title: Preparing for RICS APC Exams
intro: Before you learn a single competency, you need to understand how assessors think — and how this platform is going to prepare you to perform in front of them. This module sets that foundation.

sections.h: 1.1 Welcome — You Have Made the Right Decision
sections.body:
Becoming a Chartered Surveyor is one of the most significant professional milestones in your career. Reaching MRICS status demonstrates competence, credibility and professional standards recognised across the industry.

The fact you are here — taking active steps to prepare, improve and progress — matters. Whether you are starting early or focusing seriously now, close to submission, this platform gives you the structure, the content and the practice to move forward with confidence.

Many candidates are balancing full-time work, competing deadlines and real pressure while trying to prepare consistently. The platform works around that — structured, focused and built around what actually gets candidates through.

Here is the truth this platform is built around:

Most APC referrals are not caused by lack of knowledge. They happen because candidates know their subject but cannot demonstrate it in the way assessors are looking for.

Every module, quiz, scenario and mock interview exercise builds the way you think, speak and write as a Chartered Surveyor — not simply know the content.
sections.sprintBody:
Before you begin: The Sprint is a revision and practice tool — it assumes you have existing professional knowledge of your competencies. The revision sheets are pre-assessment reference material, not ground-up teaching content. If you need structured learning across all 11 mandatory competencies, the full 12-module programme is the right product for you.

You are closer than you think. The APC is not passed by the candidate who knows the most — it is passed by the candidate who can perform under pressure. That is what the next few weeks are about.

The global APC pass rate has held consistent at around 59% across 2023, 2024, and 2025, per RICS's own Annual Review — meaning roughly two in five candidates who sit in front of a panel don't pass first time. Not because they lacked experience. Not because they were not good enough. Because they were not prepared to perform.

You are here because you are going to be different. This Sprint programme does not care how much time you have left. It works whether you have six weeks or two weeks. What matters is what you do with the time you have.

Your journey has three phases. Know Your Stuff. Test It. Pass It. Everything in this programme is built around those three phases. Move through them at your own pace. Come back to any section. Use Michael. Use the mock interview. Use the quizzes. But keep moving forward.

Let's get started.

sections.h: Your Sprint Plan — Three Phases to Chartered
sections.body:
Forget rigid week-by-week schedules. The Sprint programme works around you — whether you have six weeks or ten days. What matters is completing all three phases before your interview.

Phase 1 — Know Your Stuff

Before you can perform, you need to know where you stand. Work through the competency modules. For each one ask yourself: can I talk about this for two minutes without hesitation? Can I give a real example from my own experience? If the answer is no, that competency needs work. Do not move to Phase 2 until you can answer yes to both questions across all your mandatory and technical competencies.

Time required: as long as it takes. Do not rush this phase.

Phase 2 — Test It

This is where most candidates underinvest — and where most candidates fail. Knowing your competencies is not the same as being able to deliver them under assessor pressure. In Phase 2 you use Michael in assessor mode and the mock interview simulator to pressure-test everything you know. You will feel uncomfortable. That is the point. The discomfort you feel here is preparation. The discomfort in the real interview is failure.

Use the quizzes at the end of every module. Use the mock interview at least three times. Ask Michael to challenge you on your weakest competency until you stop hesitating.

Time required: this phase deserves the most time you can give it.

Phase 3 — Pass It

The week before your interview is not for learning new things. It is for consolidating what you know and arriving in the right state of mind. Review your case study narrative. Practise your two-minute competency summaries out loud. Sleep. You are ready.

sections.h: S01 — Understand the Assessment
sections.body:
Before anything else, know exactly what you're walking into. Most of the anxiety around final assessment comes from uncertainty about the format itself — not the content. Fix that first.

The basic shape. Your final assessment interview runs approximately one hour, in front of a panel of two or three chartered assessors from your own pathway (RICS sets a minimum of two, maximum of three) — one of whom acts as chairperson, managing the timing and structure while all panel members ask questions and contribute to the final decision. It's typically delivered remotely (most sessions run via Microsoft Teams), though some assessment centres still run face-to-face sessions — check your specific assessment notification for which applies to you.

The actual timing breakdown:

1. Welcome and introduction (roughly 3–4 minutes). The assessors introduce themselves and the process. Low-stakes, but it sets the tone — arrive composed, not still catching your breath from rushing to log in.

2. Your case study presentation (exactly 10 minutes, not a moment more). This is entirely yours to deliver, uninterrupted — a structured account of a project you led, your role, your decisions, and the outcome. Assessors will be timing this precisely; running over doesn't get you extra credit, it gets cut off. Rehearsing to genuinely fit ten minutes, not "about ten minutes," matters.

3. Competency-based questioning (the bulk of the interview). This is where most of your hour goes. Assessors move freely across your declared competencies, probing whether you can actually operate at the levels you've claimed — not just recite what a competency means, but demonstrate reasoned judgement at Level 3 where you've declared it. Expect this to include specific time on the mandatory competencies, particularly Ethics, RICS Rules of Conduct, and professionalism.

4. Summary and close (roughly 2–3 minutes). A short wrap-up. Nothing new is usually introduced here.

The style of questioning matters more than the topic list. This isn't a fixed question bank being worked through — it's personal to you, drawn from your own submission documents (your Summary of Experience, your case study, your declared competencies and levels). Assessors are essentially saying "tell me about a time you..." and following where your answer leads, including follow-up questions that test whether your first answer was genuinely Level 3 reasoning or just a well-rehearsed script.

One current, reassuring fact worth knowing: from 1 January 2026, candidates have up to four assessment attempts per membership grade. A fifth and final attempt may be available after completing 12 months of additional experience. Attempts made before 1 January 2026 do not count toward this limit. If you're coming back after a previous attempt, this is worth knowing precisely, not assuming.

What this means for how you prepare: don't just prepare answers to guess-the-question — prepare to defend the reasoning behind every competency and level you've declared, since that's genuinely what's being tested, not topic recall.

One rule to know before you start: RICS introduced an explicit ban on using generative AI to draft APC submission documents in June 2025. AI detection checks are carried out on submissions. Michael is for revision, coaching and practice only — your Summary of Experience and case study must be written entirely in your own words.

sections.h: S02 — Build Chartered-Level Answers
sections.body:
Two or three chartered assessors from your own pathway sit on your panel — RICS sets a minimum of two, maximum of three, with one acting as chairperson. All of them have assessed dozens of candidates. They're not trying to catch you out — they're trying to establish whether you're genuinely ready to be chartered. That distinction matters for how you should think about the whole hour.

Answer at the level you've actually claimed. Level 1 is knowledge. Level 2 is application — your personal examples, describing what you specifically did, not what the team did: 'We carried out a risk assessment' scores nothing; 'I identified three hazards, proposed control measures and they were adopted' is Level 2. Level 3 is reasoned advice — you analysed options, weighed risks, advised a client and justified your recommendation: 'I considered two options. Option A carried planning risk; Option B added cost. I recommended Option B because the programme certainty outweighed the cost premium given their funding deadline.' The single most common failure pattern is a candidate answering a Level 3 question with a Level 1 answer — describing what something is instead of demonstrating they can actually advise on it. If your answer could be found in a textbook, it's not yet a Level 3 answer.

Hold your position under pressure — don't waffle. The panel will push back. They'll ask follow-up questions and challenge your answers. This usually isn't disagreement — it's a direct test of whether you can hold a reasoned position under pressure, or whether you fold at the first sign of challenge. If you're genuinely wrong about something, acknowledge it clearly and move on — that's a stronger answer than pretending certainty you don't have. But don't lose your thread and keep talking hoping to find your way back to solid ground. A clear, short answer beats two minutes of waffle every time. Silence for two seconds while you gather your thought is better than filling that silence with noise.

Speak like someone who's already operating at chartered level. Chartership is a professional threshold, and the panel is implicitly asking: would I be comfortable with this person advising my own clients? Your language, your confidence, and the judgement embedded in how you frame an answer all feed into that impression — not just the technical content itself.

A quick self-check before you move on: for each competency you've declared at Level 3, can you give a genuine example of advice you gave — not just a description of a project you worked on? If you're hesitating there, that's worth practising specifically with Michael before moving to the mock interview stage.

Defending Your Case Study

By the time you reach this programme, your case study is written — and it can't be changed. This section isn't about improving it. It's about being able to explain, justify, and reflect on it fluently, exactly as it stands.

The panel will have read it before you walk in. They'll probe it: why you made certain decisions, what you'd do differently, what the outcome was, and how you measured it.

You may now see ways you'd have written it differently. A stronger example, a clearer structure, a sharper framing — that's completely normal at this stage. There's no rewrite available, and the interview isn't a chance to fix the document. It's a chance to supply, out loud, whatever clarity or context the document itself doesn't fully capture — and to acknowledge its imperfections openly rather than pretend they're not there.

Know your narrative in one sentence. What was the situation, what did you do, and what was the result? Practise until you can deliver that without hesitation — if you can't compress it to one sentence, you don't yet know it well enough.

Anticipate the hard questions. What was the biggest risk? What would you do differently? What was the client outcome, and how did you measure success? Ask Michael each of these about your own case study and practise answering out loud — the substance, not a script.

Own your decisions. If you made a judgement call, own it. Explain your reasoning. Assessors respect candidates who demonstrate professional judgement — including the judgement to recognise, honestly, where the document itself could have been stronger.

Speak From Experience, Not Theory

The APC is not a theory exam. It’s a demonstration of your personal, real-world experience — and the language you use signals which one you’re actually giving.

The most common, entirely avoidable mistake: using hypothetical language when answering competency questions.

❌ Hypothetical (signals you haven’t actually done this):
“I would carry out a cost plan by...”
“I think I’d approach it by...”
“I would probably start with...”

✅ Personal, past-tense experience (signals genuine competence):
“On the [project name], I prepared the cost plan by...”
“When this came up on [project], I approached it by...”
“I started by...”

The moment you slip into “I would,” you tell the assessors you’re describing a theory, not an experience — even if you genuinely have done the thing you’re describing. This single shift, from hypothetical to personal past-tense, is one of the clearest signals separating a Level 2/3 answer from a referral.

Practise it now: think of one of your strongest competency examples. Say it out loud, and listen for “would,” “think I’d,” or “probably.” If you hear it, rebuild the sentence starting with what you actually did.

sections.h: 1.2 Keep Your APC Records Current — From Day One
sections.body:
Alongside your learning, continue to maintain your RICS APC graduate diary throughout this process. This is a mandatory structured record of your work experience and development — and it is one of the areas candidates most commonly neglect until it is too late.

Technical Competencies: Your diary is especially important for recording experience linked to your chosen pathway technical competencies. Record examples while projects are fresh — dates, your role, the decisions you influenced, the standards you applied.

Mandatory Competencies: These are evidenced within your Summary of Experience and final submission rather than the diary itself — but the examples you record now will become the foundation of those answers.

The best habit: Update your records regularly. Candidates who leave this until the final weeks often forget their strongest examples — the specific projects, the real decisions, the professional judgements that make the difference between a pass and a referral.

Assessors want to see candidates who actively managed their APC journey — not those who assembled their evidence under pressure at the end.

sections.h: 1.3 What the APC Really Is
sections.body:
The APC is not a traditional exam. There are no multiple choice questions on the day. No last-minute cramming the night before will save you.

It is a professional judgement assessment. A panel of two or three Chartered Surveyors (RICS sets a minimum of two, maximum of three, with one acting as chairperson) sits across from you and asks one fundamental question: can this person think, advise and behave like one of us?

That requires:

— Knowledge of your competencies
— Real examples from your own practice
— Clear reasoning under pressure
— Professional composure when questions escalate
— Sound judgement and ethical awareness

Assessors want to hear evidence that you have applied knowledge in the real world — not that you have read about it. The distinction sounds simple. In practice it is what separates candidates who pass comfortably from those who are referred.

sections.h: 1.3a The APC Routes, Rules and Requirements You Must Know
sections.body:
This section covers the procedural requirements of the APC that every candidate must understand. Missing any of these is not a content failure — it is an administrative failure that can delay your assessment by six months or more.

The Three Routes to APC

Route 1 — Structured Training (APC24)
For candidates with up to 5 years of relevant experience. Requires 24 months of structured training (minimum 400 days). Minimum 96 hours CPD over the 24-month period. You can apply for final assessment at the end of month 23 and sit after month 24.

Route 2 — Structured Training (APC12)
For candidates with 5 to 10 years of relevant experience. Requires 12 months of structured training (minimum 200 days). Minimum 48 hours CPD in the preceding 12 months. You can apply at the end of month 11 and sit after month 12.

Route 3 — Preliminary Review
For candidates with at least 5 years of relevant experience. Your submission is reviewed online first. If successful, you proceed to the final assessment interview without completing a full structured training period. Minimum 48 hours CPD required.

Route 4 — Senior Professional
For candidates with 10 or more years of senior experience, typically at director level or equivalent. An accelerated route that recognises significant professional experience. Your submission is reviewed before proceeding to final assessment.

Route 5 — Non-Structured Training
For candidates with over 10 years of relevant experience and an RICS-accredited degree. No structured training period required. Minimum 48 hours CPD in the preceding 12 months.
CPD Requirements — The Correct Figures

— APC24 (24-month route): 96 hours CPD over the 24-month period — at least half must be formal
— APC12 (12-month route): 48 hours CPD in the preceding 12 months — at least half must be formal
— Preliminary Review and Senior Professional: 48 hours CPD in the preceding 12 months

The RICS Professionalism Module

Every candidate must complete the RICS Professionalism Module before they can attend their final assessment interview. This is an online module covering ethics, professional standards and Rules of Conduct. It is not optional and it is not waived for experienced candidates. Complete it early in your training — do not leave it until the month before your assessment.

Intent to Submit — Do Not Miss This Window

Before the assessment window opens, every candidate must register their Intent to Submit through the RICS Assessment Platform. For UK candidates:
— Land and Property candidates are emailed in January to register intent
— Built Environment candidates are emailed in February to register intent

APC24 candidates must complete 23 months of training before they can register Intent to Submit. APC12 candidates must complete 11 months.

If you miss the Intent to Submit window you cannot apply for that assessment session. You must wait for the next one — typically six months away. This is one of the most avoidable reasons candidates lose an assessment window.

Once submitted, your pathway, route and counsellor details cannot be changed. Ensure these are all correct before submitting your intent.

Proposer and Seconder — A Requirement From February 2025

From 1 February 2025, all APC candidates must provide details of three Chartered Surveyors who will propose and support their application for RICS membership if successful at assessment.

The requirements:
— Three MRICS or FRICS members willing to propose and recommend you
— Your counsellor can act as proposer or seconder
— At least one must be from a different firm or organisation
— Nomination must be completed 0–2 months before your assessment date
— Approved nominations time out after 3 months
— Do not nominate someone you have not connected with personally — this can be referred to RICS Regulations

Action required: Identify your three proposers and seconders at least three months before your assessment window and request their nomination through the Assessment Platform. Do not leave this until the last moment.
Assessment attempt limits — from January 2026

From 1 January 2026, candidates have a maximum of four standard assessment attempts per membership grade. A fifth and final attempt is available only after completing a further 12 months of relevant experience. Attempts made before 1 January 2026 do not count toward this limit.

Six Months Backdating

Candidates on the structured training route can backdate their APC application by up to six months, provided the application is accompanied by a covering letter from their employer or counsellor. This means if you started your training before formally enrolling with RICS, you may be able to count that experience. Speak to your counsellor about this early.

Employment History on the Assessment Platform

All candidates must provide their full employment history on the Assessment Platform — including part-time, secondment, contract and self-employment. Each entry requires: location, employer name, start and end dates, job title and a brief role description. If you change employer during your training period, update the platform promptly. Changes can take up to 5 business days to be reflected and assessment windows may close during this time.

Turnitin — AI Detection on Submissions

RICS uses Turnitin to check submissions for AI-generated content. If the system flags concerns with your submission, this will be investigated. Every word in your Summary of Experience and case study must be written in your own words from your own professional experience. The June 2025 AI ban is enforced through automated detection — not just on trust.

The Final Assessment Interview — Correct Format

1. Ten-minute presentation by the candidate on their case study
2. Questioning on the presentation and case study — typically ten to fifteen minutes
3. Competency questioning — assessors work through your SoE testing mandatory and technical competencies
4. Professional ethics — a standard final section in every pathway

Total: approximately 60 minutes with a panel of two or three RICS professionals (RICS sets a minimum of two, maximum of three) — one acting as chairperson, the rest as assessors, all from your pathway. All panel members have equal responsibility in questioning you and contributing to the final pass or refer decision.

sections.h: 1.3b International Candidates — Using This Platform Outside the UK
sections.body:
Get Chartered AI is built on the RICS APC framework which applies identically worldwide. If you are sitting your APC in the UAE, Australia, Singapore, Hong Kong, Ireland, South Africa, Qatar or any other region — the vast majority of this platform is directly relevant to you.

What is the same everywhere:

— The 11 mandatory competencies, their descriptions and the Level 1, 2 and 3 requirements
— The APC routes — Structured Training, Preliminary Review, Senior Professional
— The submission format — Summary of Experience, logbook, case study
— The final assessment structure — ten-minute presentation, competency questioning, ethics
— The diary and logbook requirements
— The word count rules and June 2025 AI ban
— The competency choice rules — December 2025 pathway guides apply globally
— The proposer and seconder requirements
— The five attempts rule from January 2026
— The RICS Professionalism Module requirement
— The Ethics and Professionalism competency — RICS Rules of Conduct and Ethical Standards apply globally

Michael is available to you any time regardless of your time zone. You can ask it to discuss competencies in the context of your local market, legislation and professional environment. If a module section references UK legislation that does not apply in your jurisdiction, tell Michael your location and ask it to contextualise the competency for your region.
What is different by region — legislation and local standards:

The technical content in Modules 2 to 11 references UK legislation — the Building Safety Act 2022, the Renters' Rights Act 2025, UK capital allowances rates, English planning policy and so on. These are illustrative of the type of legislation knowledge assessors expect — but the specific legislation you need to know is your local equivalent.

How to apply UK legislation content to your region:

For each piece of UK legislation referenced in this platform, ask yourself: what is the equivalent in my jurisdiction? Examples:
— UK Building Safety Act → UAE Federal Law on Building Safety / Australian Building Codes
— UK CDM 2015 → Local construction health and safety regulations
— UK GDPR → UAE Personal Data Protection Law / Singapore PDPA / Australian Privacy Act
— UK Equality Act 2010 → Local anti-discrimination legislation
— UK Bribery Act 2010 → Local anti-corruption legislation plus the RICS global standard

The RICS professional standards referenced in this platform — the anti-bribery standard, the AI Standard, the Conflicts of Interest standard — apply globally and are not UK-specific. These you can use directly.

Assessment windows for international candidates:

— Americas, Europe, Middle East and Africa: candidatesupport@rics.org
— Asia Pacific: Different window dates apply — check the RICS candidates page for your region
— Ireland: Same windows as UK Built Environment and Land and Property

CPD requirements: Identical to UK candidates — 48 hours for APC12 and 96 hours for APC24 over the training period.

In your APC interview: Assessors understand that legislation varies by jurisdiction. When answering competency questions, name your local legislation equivalent confidently. Do not try to answer using UK legislation if it does not apply in your region — assessors will probe this and you will expose a knowledge gap. Your legal framework is the correct one for your context.

sections.h: 1.4 Key Documents and Requirements
sections.body:
To be eligible for the RICS APC you will need relevant qualifications or recognised equivalent experience, together with structured practical experience in your chosen pathway.

The key documents you must prepare:

Training Agreement — agreed between you, your employer and your supervisor or counsellor. Sets out the framework for your structured training.

Experience and Diary Records — your ongoing evidence of technical competency experience. Written as you go, not reconstructed at the end.

Development Action Plan — your personal goals and development priorities throughout the APC period. Keep it live and relevant.

Summary of Experience — where mandatory and technical competencies are evidenced clearly. This is where your examples need to be specific, personal and at the right level.

Case Study Submission — your opportunity to demonstrate professional judgement on a real project. More on this below.

Assessors want to hear: that you actively managed your training journey — not that you turned up to work and hoped experience would happen around you.

The Summary Sheet

The Summary Sheet is a one-page document that must be included in your submission. It captures key information about your APC submission — your pathway, your competency selection, your case study project details and your counsellor's details. It is completed on the RICS Assessment Platform as part of the submission process. If the summary sheet is missing or incomplete your submission may be treated as invalid.

The Final Assessment — Format

The final assessment is a structured interview with a panel of two or three RICS assessors (minimum two, maximum three per RICS rules), one of whom acts as chairperson. The standard format is:

— Ten-minute presentation by the candidate on their case study (some pathways vary — check your pathway guide)
— Questioning on the presentation and case study — typically ten to fifteen minutes
— Questioning on competencies — assessors work through your Summary of Experience and test your mandatory and technical competencies
— Questioning on professional ethics — a standard final section in every pathway

The total interview is typically 60 minutes. Assessors are looking for structured, concise and confident answers — not the longest or most technical ones.

A complete submission package must include:

Submission Checklist — Do Not Submit Without Checking All of These

✓ Summary Sheet — completed on the RICS Assessment Platform
✓ Logbook — structured competency record populated from your diary
✓ Summary of Experience — 1,500 mandatory section + 4,000 technical section
✓ Case Study — maximum 3,000 words with word count stated at the end
✓ Case Study Appendices — supporting documentation
✓ Competency choices validated against December 2025 pathway guide
✓ All competencies directed by day-to-day work — not aspirational
✓ Case study project involvement within 24 months of assessment date
✓ Client and employer consent obtained or project anonymised
✓ No AI-generated content in any submission document
✓ Word count checked using Microsoft Word
✓ Counsellor has reviewed and signed off the submission

sections.h: 1.4a Current RICS APC Candidate Guide Requirements — What Every Candidate Must Know
sections.body:
Current guidance checked against RICS sources: August 2026

RICS requires candidates to follow the current APC assessment rules and use the latest templates and guidance available through the Assessment Platform.

The requirements below affect your written submission, case study and assessment preparation. Make sure your documents and preparation reflect the current RICS guidance before you submit.

Use of AI in APC submissions — current RICS requirements

Your assessment submission must be your own original work.

RICS does not permit the use of generative AI to produce content for your assessment submission. This includes tools such as ChatGPT. Candidates may use tools to assist with spelling, grammar and word count, but generative AI must not be used to write submission content.

RICS carries out plagiarism and AI-detection checks on assessment submissions. If RICS suspects that submitted work is not the candidate's own, this may lead to investigation and possible regulatory action.

Get Chartered AI is a revision and practice tool — not a submission-writing tool.
Michael helps you test your knowledge, practise explaining your reasoning, strengthen your understanding of competencies and prepare for questioning. It should not be used to write your Summary of Experience, case study or other assessment submission content. Your submitted work must remain your own.

Current case study word-count requirements

The APC case study has a maximum word count of 3,000 words.

RICS calculates the case-study word count using Microsoft Word. The counted content runs from the introduction through to the end of the conclusion.

The word count includes:
— candidate-written headings and subheadings
— tables and charts included within the main body
— all written content between the introduction and conclusion

The word count does not include:
— project name
— project date
— confidentiality statement
— table of contents
— competencies demonstrated
— appendices

You are required to state the total case-study word count in the Assessment Platform when uploading your submission.

Current case study recency requirement

Your case study must be based on a project, or element of a project, in which you were personally involved during the 24 months before your assessment submission date.

The project may still be ongoing. You do not need to have been involved in the whole project, provided the element you rely on demonstrates your own professional experience and the required competencies.

Your case study should include a project or issue that enables you to demonstrate professional judgement, problem-solving and your pathway competencies, including at least one Level 3 core competency where required.

Summary of Experience word counts

Your Summary of Experience is subject to the following current word limits:
— Mandatory competencies: 1,500 words
— Technical competencies: maximum 4,000 words

RICS calculates these word counts using Microsoft Word.

Only the content entered in the Summary of Experience column is included in the count, including any source references or citations you add.

The word count does not include the competency titles or levels shown in the first two columns of the template.

Use the current RICS templates

Always use the latest Summary of Experience and Case Study templates available through the RICS Assessment Platform.

Do not rely on an older saved version simply because you started drafting in it previously.

Keep checking the current RICS guidance

RICS assessment requirements, templates, submission processes and dates can change.

Before every submission window, check:
— the current APC Candidate Guide
— the Assessment Platform
— the current submission checklist
— assessment dates and process guidance

Your counsellor should also review your submission and confirm that you have met the requirements for your pathway and route.

sections.h: 1.5 The Three Competency Levels — The Most Important Concept in the APC
sections.body:
Get this right and everything else follows. The three levels define what assessors expect from every answer you give.

Level 1 — Knowledge
You understand and can explain the subject clearly. No practical experience required at this level. Assessors ask: 'What is...' or 'Explain...'
Example: 'Explain the five Ethical Standards.' You name them clearly and accurately.

Level 2 — Application
You have applied that knowledge in real practice. This is where your personal examples live. Assessors ask: 'Tell me about a time when...' or 'Give me an example of...'
Critical rule: describe what you personally did — not what the team did. 'We carried out a risk assessment' scores nothing. 'I identified three hazards, proposed control measures and they were adopted' is Level 2.

Level 3 — Reasoned Advice
You analysed options, weighed risks, advised a client and justified your recommendation. Assessors ask: 'What options did you consider?' or 'Why did you advise that?'

Example of Level 3 thinking: 'I considered two options. Option A carried planning risk; Option B added cost. I recommended Option B to the client because the programme certainty outweighed the cost premium given their funding deadline.'

Only Ethics formally requires Level 3 — but the strongest candidates train themselves to think this way throughout the interview. Every answer benefits from it.

Assessors want to hear: what options existed, what risks mattered, what advice you gave and why that was the right route.

sections.h: 1.5a Choosing Your Competencies — The December 2025 Rules You Must Know
sections.body:
RICS updated the pathway guides in December 2025 with important clarification on competency choice. Getting this wrong can result in your submission being rejected — adding around six months to your APC journey.

The fundamental principle:
Your competency choice must reflect what you do day to day at work. It should not be aspirational or based on your degree subject. Assessors will expect a sensible and realistic choice that reflects the skills needed to fulfil the role of a surveyor in your field of practice.

Always use the latest pathway guides. If you search on Google, old versions will still appear. Always download directly from the RICS website and confirm the date on the front says December 2025.

The four rules — memorise all of them:

Rule 1 — Core technical competency required to Level 1
If your pathway includes a core technical competency required to Level 1, you CAN select this competency to Level 2 or 3 as an optional technical competency — provided the pathway guide permits it.

Example: Under the Building Surveying pathway, Fire Safety is a Level 1 core technical competency. Fire Safety also appears on the optional technical competency list and can therefore be selected to a higher level.

Rule 2 — Core technical competency required to Level 2
If your pathway includes a core technical competency required to Level 2, you CANNOT select this competency to Level 3 as an optional technical competency.

Rule 3 — Mandatory competencies in an OR list
Some pathways allow mandatory competencies to be taken to a higher level as a core or optional technical competency. Where this applies, the eligible mandatory competencies will be grouped together in a list connected by the word OR.

This means you can select only ONE of these mandatory competencies to a higher level. You CANNOT select all of them.

Example — Commercial Real Estate pathway: the mandatory competencies available at higher level are grouped with OR. A candidate can select one of them but not multiple.

Example — Building Control pathway: Client Care and Data Management are listed together with OR, while Sustainability is listed separately. This means a Building Control candidate could select either Client Care OR Data Management AND Sustainability — because Sustainability is listed separately from the OR group.

Rule 4 — Selecting from the full technical competency list
Some pathways allow candidates to select at least one competency from the full list of technical competencies in the overall pathway guide — covering requirements for all pathways, not just your chosen one.

If this applies to your pathway: you can ONLY select a mandatory competency if it is listed as a core or optional technical competency in the pathway guide. If it is grouped in an OR list, you can only select it if no other mandatory competency in that OR list has already been selected.

The practical checklist before submitting your competency selection:

— Download the December 2025 version of your pathway guide directly from the RICS website
— Check each competency you have selected against all four rules above
— Confirm your choices with your counsellor — they should be familiar with the December 2025 clarification
— If in doubt, seek specialist APC advice before submitting — do not guess

Why this matters — the risk is real:
RICS can reject your submission for invalid competency choices. If rejected, you will typically be asked to resubmit in the next assessment window — adding approximately six months to your APC journey. This is one of the most avoidable reasons for delay and one of the most important checks you can make before submitting.

Michael can help you sense-check your specific competency selection — describe your pathway and your proposed choices and it will identify whether any combination raises a flag under the December 2025 rules.

sections.h: 1.6 The Case Study — Why It Determines So Much
sections.body:
Your case study and your ability to defend it at interview account for a significant proportion of your overall APC outcome. Yet it is consistently the area candidates prepare least for.

The APC Case Study is not simply a project summary. It is designed to demonstrate professional judgement, reasoned advice, problem solving, communication skills, reflective thinking and competency achievement at Level 3.

Strong case studies do not just explain what happened. They clearly demonstrate what you did, why you did it, how you advised your client, and what you learned from the experience. The assessors are looking for clear professional reasoning and evidence of your personal involvement throughout the project.

What assessors are really looking for:

Assessors are not looking for the largest project, the most technical scheme, perfect outcomes or overly complex language. They are looking for:

— Clear communication and logical thinking
— Professional judgement under pressure
— Evidence of your own involvement and advice
— Reflective analysis demonstrating professional maturity
— Competency achievement clearly demonstrated

A strong APC Case Study should feel structured, professional, concise, easy to follow and focused entirely on your contribution.

Remember: clarity is more powerful than complexity.

sections.h: 1.7 Selecting a Strong Case Study Topic
sections.body:
Choosing the right topic is half the work. A strong topic makes the case study almost write itself. A weak topic makes it almost impossible to demonstrate Level 3 thinking regardless of how well you write.

Choose a project where:
— There was a real challenge, risk or complication requiring professional judgement
— You had genuine personal involvement in decisions and advice
— You can evidence Level 3 competency achievement across multiple competencies
— There is something meaningful to reflect on — a decision you would approach differently, or a lesson that shaped your professional thinking

A more complicated project does not automatically create a stronger case study. Clear communication and strong reasoning are more important than complexity. Many of the strongest submissions are based on relatively straightforward projects where the candidate can articulate their thinking precisely and reflect with genuine insight.

Avoid projects where:
— Your personal involvement was limited or difficult to articulate
— The outcome was entirely determined by others
— There was no meaningful challenge or professional judgement to demonstrate
— The technical complexity would take three pages to explain before you can get to the analysis

The test before you commit to a topic: can you explain in two sentences what the main challenge was, what you recommended and why? If you cannot, the topic may be too vague or too dependent on context to work well.

sections.h: 1.8 Milestones and Preparation Timeline
sections.body:
One of the most common reasons candidates are referred is poor preparation timing — not weak ability. They know their subject but run out of time to prepare properly.

The key milestones to plan for:

1. Register and confirm your pathway
2. Begin structured training and evidence capture
3. Keep diary and records updated consistently
4. Build competency examples across all mandatory and technical areas
5. Draft your case study early — not in the final weeks
6. Prepare your final submission with time to review
7. Practise mock interviews — out loud, under pressure
8. Attend your APC assessment
9. Receive your result

The single most useful thing you can do today: set your likely assessment target date and work backwards. Every milestone needs a date against it. Preparation that has no deadline has no urgency.

Assessors want to hear: a candidate who managed their APC process — not one who arrived hoping their work experience would be enough.

sections.h: 1.9 How to Use Get Chartered AI Effectively
sections.body:
This platform builds performance — not just provides information. Here is how to get the most from it.

For best results:

— Complete one module at a time and resist jumping ahead
— After each section, ask yourself: what is my personal example for this?
— Build your own answer bank as you progress — two or three real examples per competency
— Practise answering questions out loud — not just reading and nodding
— Revisit weaker competencies regularly rather than only studying what you already know
— Keep your APC diary updated alongside the course
— Use Module 12 as your final rehearsal — not your first

Even 20–30 focused minutes daily will outperform occasional long revision sessions. Consistency matters more than volume.

Monthly Access members: one module unlocks per month — use that time to go deep on each competency before the next one opens.

Annual Access members: all 12 modules are available immediately — set your own pace but build in regular review of earlier modules as you progress.

You are not revising for an exam. You are preparing to perform under professional scrutiny. Every module builds that readiness.

Important — the June 2025 RICS AI ban
RICS introduced an explicit ban on using generative AI to write APC submission documents in June 2025. AI detection checks are carried out on submissions. Michael is for revision, coaching and practice only. Your Summary of Experience and case study must be written entirely in your own words. Do not use Michael to draft, generate or substantially rewrite any part of your submission.

sections.h: 1.10 What Comes Next
sections.body:
You now have 11 modules ahead of you — one for each mandatory competency — followed by your capstone revision module.

Modules 2–11: The eleven mandatory competencies covered in depth — knowledge, application, Level 3 thinking, assessor insights and real APC scenarios for each one.

Module 12: Your final preparation module featuring:
— Full revision across all eleven competencies
— 5,000+ practice questions and answers
— Michael for coaching and answer review
— Timed 60-minute mock interview simulator
— Pathway-specific technical questions across all 22 RICS routes
— Readiness dashboard so you know where you stand before the real thing

A final thought:

The candidates who pass comfortably are not always the most technically experienced. They are the ones who prepared to perform. They understood what assessors were looking for. They had real examples ready. They could think under pressure and explain their reasoning clearly.

That is exactly what this platform builds.

Let's begin.

sections.h: S03 — Check Your Readiness
sections.body:
Before moving on, tick each competency once you feel confident you could answer an assessor's question on it — at the level shown. This is a self-check, not a test. If anything feels shaky, the link takes you straight to the relevant module.

0 of 11 confirmed— tap each row to mark it

sections.h: 1.11 Writing Your Summary of Experience — What RICS Actually Requires
sections.body:
The Summary of Experience is your written submission to RICS — and it is one of the most important documents you will produce during your APC journey. Many candidates underestimate it until it is too late.

RICS requires two distinct sections within your Summary of Experience:

Mandatory Competencies — 1,500 words total
A brief statement covering each of your mandatory competencies at the required level. This is not a detailed essay for each competency — it is a concise, evidenced statement demonstrating that you have met the standard across all eleven. The 1,500 word limit is tight. Every word must earn its place.

Technical Competencies — 4,000 words maximum
Covering your core and optional pathway competencies with real evidence of application. This is where your specific professional judgements, decisions and advice are evidenced in writing. The 4,000 word limit applies to the total — not per competency.

The principles that make a strong Summary of Experience:

1. Write in the first person about your own work. RICS is explicit: your statements must be based on your own body of work, not someone else's or a hypothetical situation. 'I advised the client...' not 'the team advised...'

2. Match your evidence to the level required. If a competency is required at Level 2, your statement must cover both Level 1 and Level 2. If Level 3, it must cover all three. Do not assume the assessor will infer the level from your narrative — state it explicitly.

3. Be specific, not general. 'I have experience of valuations' tells an assessor nothing. 'I prepared RICS Red Book compliant market valuations for three commercial investment properties, advising on yield methodology and market comparables' is evidence.

4. Use your diary as your source material. Your APC diary records are the raw material for your Summary of Experience. Candidates who update their diary consistently throughout their training write far stronger summaries than those who reconstruct it from memory at the end.

5. Reference standards and legislation naturally. Weave RICS standards, legislation and professional guidance into your examples — not as a separate list but as part of how you explain your work.

6. Get your counsellor to review it. RICS requires your submission to be reviewed by your counsellor to confirm examples are supported, contextually accurate and suitable. Do not submit without this step.

Common Summary of Experience mistakes:
— Writing about what the team did rather than what you personally did
— Using the same example for multiple competencies without distinguishing your contribution in each context
— Describing what you know rather than what you did
— Running over the word limits — RICS counts using Microsoft Word and the word count must comply
— Writing the summary in the final weeks — it should develop alongside your training, not replace it

The word count rule: RICS calculates word counts using Microsoft Word, based only on content under the Summary of Experience column. Draft your summary in Word and check the word count before submitting via the Assessment Platform.

Assessors want to hear: a Summary of Experience that reads as a coherent professional narrative — not a tick-box exercise. Every statement should leave the assessor thinking: this candidate has done this work, made these decisions and applied this knowledge in practice.

sections.h: 1.12 Writing Your Case Study — RICS Structure and What Assessors Expect
sections.body:
The case study is your single most important document in the APC submission. Assessors spend more time on it than any other part of your submission — and the first ten minutes of your interview are dedicated to probing it.

RICS requires a maximum word count of 3,000 words. From June 2025 RICS checks this using Microsoft Word and requires candidates to state their own word count at the end of the submission.

📋 WORD COUNT QUICK REFERENCE

Counts toward 3,000 words:
— Everything from Introduction through to Conclusion
— All headings and subheadings
— Charts, graphs or tables in the main body

Does NOT count:
— Project name and date
— Confidentiality statement
— Table of contents
— Appendices

State your word count at the end. Use Microsoft Word to count. Put charts and tables in appendices.


The RICS required structure:

1. Confidentiality Statement
You must obtain consent from your employer and client where project details are being disclosed. If consent is not available, anonymise project information, remove sensitive details and refer to parties generically such as 'the client' or 'the project'. Professionalism and confidentiality are essential — this is itself a demonstration of your Ethics and Professionalism competency.

2. Contents Page
Your report should include a clear contents page with accurate headings and page numbering. The report should feel professional, structured and easy to navigate.

3. Introduction
Briefly explain the project, your role and responsibilities, and key project details including project value, contract type, programme duration, location and procurement route. Keep this section concise. Avoid excessive project background. The focus should remain on your role and involvement — not the project's history.

4. Key Issues (usually two)
Your case study should focus on two significant project issues or challenges. For each key issue explain what happened, why it mattered, what risks existed, stakeholder pressures and why it became a challenge. Strong candidates focus only on relevant detail. Avoid unnecessary technical description.

5. Options Analysis
This section demonstrates professional judgement and reasoned advice. Explain what options were considered, how they were evaluated, why certain options were rejected and why the final solution was selected. Assessors want to see logical thinking, decision making, client-focused advice and risk awareness. The strongest case studies clearly explain why the chosen option was the most appropriate solution. Avoid unrealistic or weak options added purely to increase content — assessors recognise padding immediately.

6. Outcome
Explain what happened, how the solution was implemented, stakeholder responses, project outcomes, risks managed and your contribution to the final result. Strong candidates clearly explain how they influenced the outcome, how they communicated with stakeholders and what value they personally added.

7. Conclusion and Reflective Analysis
This is one of the most important sections of the APC Case Study. Reflective analysis demonstrates self-awareness, professional growth, critical thinking and learning. Explain what you learned, what you would improve next time, how your judgement developed and what future risks could be mitigated differently. Strong reflective analysis should feel honest, professional, balanced and thoughtful. This section is not about criticising yourself harshly — it is about demonstrating professional maturity and commitment to continuous improvement. Reflective analysis often separates average submissions from strong ones.

8. Appendices
Appendices may include drawings, photographs, plans, reports, cost information and supporting documentation. They should support the case study, remain relevant and be concise. Avoid excessive supporting information — appendices should improve assessor understanding, not demonstrate volume of work.

Common case study mistakes to avoid:
— Overcomplicating the project
— Writing descriptively instead of analytically
— Weak reflective analysis
— Exceeding the 3,000 word count
— Excessive technical jargon and acronyms
— Weak options analysis with unrealistic alternatives
— Focusing on team achievements instead of personal involvement
— Leaving preparation too late

The test before you submit: read your case study and ask — does every paragraph tell the assessor what I decided and why? If any paragraph simply describes what happened without explaining the reasoning behind it, it needs rewriting.

Assessors want to hear: a case study that reads as professional advice — not a project diary. The strongest candidates are often the clearest communicators, not the most technical. Focus on clarity, structure and professional reasoning throughout.

sections.h: 1.13 Writing Strong APC Diary Entries — The Foundation of Your Submission
sections.body:
Your APC diary is not a timekeeping exercise. It is the professional evidence base that your entire submission is built on. Candidates who write strong diary entries throughout their training produce stronger Summaries of Experience. Candidates who write weak diary entries — or leave them until the end — consistently struggle when the submission window opens.

What RICS requires from your diary:
For APC 24 Structured Training — a minimum of 24 months and 400 days recorded. For APC 12 Structured Training — a minimum of 12 months and 200 days. Entries must cover your core and optional technical competencies. You should not record a period of less than half a day.

What makes a strong diary entry:

1. Be specific about what you personally did.
Weak entry: 'Site visit to inspect a commercial property.'
Strong entry: 'Attended a pre-acquisition inspection of a 1980s office building. Identified potential asbestos-containing materials in the ceiling void, reviewed the existing asbestos register, confirmed specialist reinspection was required before the client could proceed. Advised client of programme implications and cost of reinspection.'

The difference is specificity and personal contribution. The weak entry describes an activity. The strong entry describes professional judgement applied to a real situation.

2. Reference the competency level you are evidencing.
Your diary should map to your competency requirements. If an entry evidences Level 2 Health and Safety — say so. Not as a separate label but woven into how you describe the work: 'I applied the five-step risk assessment model and identified three significant hazards requiring control measures before access could be granted.'

3. Write entries while projects are fresh.
The detail you capture the day after a site visit is far richer than what you can reconstruct three months later. Specific measurements, precise conversations, exact decisions — all of these fade quickly. The candidates who write the strongest Summaries of Experience are those who captured the specifics at the time.

4. Vary the competencies you evidence.
Review your diary quarterly against your competency requirements. If you have strong H&S and Client Care entries but thin Data Management and Sustainability entries, that is a signal to look actively for work that will fill those gaps — or to recognise competency evidence in work you are already doing that you have not been capturing.

5. Use professional language throughout.
Your diary may be reviewed by your counsellor and will inform your formal submission. Write it as a professional document, not as a personal note. Avoid abbreviations, casual language and shorthand that only makes sense in context.

The quarterly diary review habit:
Every three months, review your diary entries against your full competency requirements. Ask three questions:
— Which competencies are well evidenced with specific Level 2 examples?
— Which competencies are thin — either in number of entries or in depth?
— What work is coming up that will generate strong entries for the gaps?

This review takes 30 minutes and prevents the panic that hits candidates who open their diary three months before submission and find large gaps.

What happens if your diary is weak:
Your counsellor reviews your Summary of Experience for contextual accuracy and suitability. If your diary does not support the claims in your Summary, your counsellor cannot verify them. That creates a problem at submission — and an even bigger one if it surfaces at interview.

The single most useful habit: spend ten minutes at the end of each working day noting the most professionally significant thing you did. Not every activity — the one moment of professional judgement, the decision you made, the advice you gave. Over two years that habit produces an evidence base that almost writes the Summary of Experience for you.

Assessors want to hear: evidence that you actively managed your APC journey — not that you turned up to work and hoped the experience would accumulate passively. Strong diary entries are the proof that you did.

sections.h: 1.13a APC Diary vs Logbook — Two Separate Elements Confirmed by RICS
sections.body:
RICS has confirmed the APC diary and the logbook are two separate elements. Candidates frequently confuse them — and the consequences of getting this wrong at submission are serious.

Critical: If your logbook is not included in your submission documents your submission will be deemed invalid. The diary does not need to be submitted. The logbook must be submitted. These are not interchangeable.
The APC Diary

The APC diary is your day-to-day working record. You use it throughout your training period to capture your surveying experience as it happens — recording what you did, what you learned and how it relates to your competencies. The diary is a personal working document. It is your evidence base and your memory of your APC journey.

The diary is not submitted to the assessment panel. It does not form part of your formal submission documents. However it is essential — candidates who write strong diary entries throughout their training find the logbook significantly easier to complete because the detail is already captured.

The Logbook

The logbook is the formal structured document that is populated from your diary entries and submitted to the assessment panel as part of your submission. It sets out your competency experience in the required RICS format — organised by competency, showing the level you are claiming to have achieved and supported by evidence drawn from your diary.

The logbook must be included in your submission documents. If it is missing, your submission is invalid regardless of how strong your Summary of Experience and case study are.

The relationship between diary and logbook — in practice:

1. You write diary entries throughout your training — capturing real experience as it happens
2. When preparing your submission, you review your diary and select the strongest evidence for each competency
3. You populate the logbook from your diary — structured by competency, at the correct level
4. The logbook goes into your submission. The diary stays with you.

This is why diary quality from day one matters so much. A weak diary produces a weak logbook. A strong diary produces a strong logbook with specific, evidenced examples for every competency.
Common mistakes to avoid:

— Assuming the diary and logbook are the same document
— Writing diary entries retrospectively at submission time — the detail is always thinner and less convincing
— Forgetting to include the logbook in the submission package — this invalidates everything else
— Populating the logbook with generic statements rather than specific diary-derived evidence

The assessors will use your logbook to direct questioning. Entries that lack specificity give assessors a straightforward route to probe weaknesses. Entries drawn from detailed diary records tend to be precise, evidenced and confident — because the candidate was there and wrote it down at the time.

sections.h: 1.14 Illustrative Examples — What Good Looks Like in Practice
sections.body:
⚠ ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLES ONLY — NOT FOR SUBMISSION
The examples below are fictional and created purely to show candidates what strong APC writing looks like. Do not copy, adapt or submit any part of these examples as your own work. The June 2025 RICS Candidate Guide bans the use of AI-generated content in submissions and all submissions are subject to AI detection checks. Your submission must be written entirely from your own professional experience.
PART A — Summary of Experience: What Good Looks Like

The most common reason candidates underperform in the Summary of Experience is writing what they know rather than what they did. The examples below show the same competency written weakly and then strongly — so you can see the difference clearly.

EXAMPLE PATHWAY: QUANTITY SURVEYING — MANDATORY COMPETENCY: HEALTH & SAFETY — LEVEL 2
❌ Weak version — describes knowledge, not application
"At Level 2, I have an understanding of health and safety legislation including the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 and CDM Regulations 2015. I am aware of the responsibilities of the Principal Designer and Principal Contractor and understand the importance of health and safety on construction sites."
Why this fails: Describes awareness of legislation — not application. Could have been written by anyone. No personal involvement, no specific situation, no professional judgement demonstrated.
✓ Strong version — demonstrates application from personal experience
"At Level 2, I have applied my knowledge of CDM Regulations 2015 in my role as QS on a £4.2m commercial refurbishment in Manchester. When the Principal Contractor submitted a Construction Phase Plan that did not adequately address the risks associated with working adjacent to a live railway line, I identified the omission and raised this formally with the Principal Designer, recommending the plan be revised before works commenced. I prepared a cost assessment of the additional temporary works required to satisfy the revised plan and presented this to the client with a recommendation to proceed, which was accepted."
Why this works: Specific project, specific risk identified, specific personal action taken, outcome described. The assessor can visualise exactly what happened and what the candidate contributed.
QUANTITY SURVEYING — MANDATORY COMPETENCY: CLIENT CARE — LEVEL 2
❌ Weak version
"At Level 2, I have experience of dealing with clients professionally and understand the importance of managing client expectations. I have attended client meetings and communicated effectively with clients throughout projects."
Why this fails: Generic, passive, could describe any candidate on any project. No specific situation, no personal advice given.
✓ Strong version
"At Level 2, I managed the client relationship on a £1.8m residential refurbishment where the client's brief changed significantly mid-programme, requiring me to re-cost three packages of work within 48 hours and present revised cost plans at short notice. I identified that two of the client's proposed changes would create abortive costs of approximately £38,000 and advised the client against proceeding with these elements, explaining the commercial risk clearly in writing. The client accepted my advice and the final account was agreed within 2% of the revised budget."
Why this works: Specific situation, specific advice given, client impact quantified, outcome confirmed. The candidate advised — they did not just communicate.
QUANTITY SURVEYING — TECHNICAL COMPETENCY: CONTRACT PRACTICE — LEVEL 3
❌ Weak version
"At Level 3, I have provided advice on contract matters including variations, extensions of time and final accounts. I am familiar with JCT contracts and have administered contracts on a number of projects."
Why this fails: Level 3 requires advice and reasoned judgement. This describes familiarity — not advice. An assessor cannot score this at Level 3.
✓ Strong version
"At Level 3, I provided advice to a developer client on a disputed extension of time claim under a JCT Design and Build Contract 2016 where the contractor had submitted a claim for 14 weeks arising from alleged employer delays. I reviewed the contractor's delay notices against the contract programme and identified that three of the five alleged delaying events had not been notified within the contractual timescales, weakening the contractor's entitlement. I advised the client that a defensible position existed to resist approximately eight weeks of the claimed extension. I prepared a written response to the contractor setting out the basis of our position, which resulted in a negotiated settlement of four weeks — saving the client a potential liability of approximately £62,000 in liquidated damages."
Why this works: Identifies a specific dispute, explains the reasoning applied, quantifies the outcome. The candidate advised — and that advice had a clear measurable consequence. This is Level 3.
PART B — Case Study: What Good Looks Like

The example below uses a Building Surveying scenario. It shows the Introduction, Key Issue 1 and Options Analysis written to the correct standard — with annotations explaining why each element works.

EXAMPLE PATHWAY: BUILDING SURVEYING
Illustrative example only. Fictional project. Not for submission.
INTRODUCTION
"This case study concerns a pre-acquisition building survey and subsequent negotiation of a purchase price reduction for a private client acquiring a Victorian mid-terrace commercial property in Leeds, valued at approximately £475,000. The property was being acquired for conversion to serviced office accommodation. My role was to carry out the inspection, prepare the survey report and advise the client on the implications of the defects identified for the acquisition. The project ran from March 2025 to June 2025 and all activities occurred within 24 months of my submission date. Client and employer consent has been obtained to disclose project details."
✓ Why this works: States project value, location, client brief, candidate's specific role, programme dates and confirms 24-month validity. Confirms confidentiality consent. Concise — no padding.
KEY ISSUE 1 — Identification of Structural Movement
"During my inspection I identified significant diagonal cracking to the front elevation at first floor level, consistent with differential settlement at the right-hand party wall. The crack width exceeded 5mm at its widest point. My initial assessment was that the movement had occurred historically and appeared to have stabilised, however the pattern and extent of cracking was beyond what could be assessed conclusively without specialist investigation. I advised the client immediately that the defect represented a material risk to the acquisition and that I could not provide a definitive assessment of cause or stability without a structural engineer's report. I explained the potential implications clearly: if the movement was ongoing or related to inadequate foundations, remediation costs could exceed £80,000 and significantly affect the viability of the intended conversion."
✓ Why this works: Describes what was found with specific detail, explains the professional judgement applied, shows the candidate advised on risk and gave the client a quantified cost implication. Not just a description — professional judgement in action.
OPTIONS ANALYSIS
"I presented the client with three options:

Option 1 — Withdraw from the acquisition. Lowest risk but would result in the client losing legal and survey fees already incurred of approximately £4,500 and forgoing the investment opportunity.

Option 2 — Proceed unconditionally. Not recommended. In my opinion this exposed the client to unquantified structural risk that had not been adequately investigated.

Option 3 — Commission a structural engineer's report and use the findings to negotiate a price reduction or, if the findings were unfavourable, withdraw. I recommended this option as it preserved the client's position while generating the information needed to make a properly informed decision.

The client accepted my recommendation. The structural engineer's report confirmed historical movement that had stabilised. Armed with this report, I advised the client that a price reduction of £35,000 was justified on the basis of the remedial works required. The vendor accepted a reduction of £28,000 following negotiation."
✓ Why this works: Three realistic options, each evaluated. Weak options explained and rejected with reasoning. Recommendation justified. Outcome quantified. The candidate advised — and the advice had a direct financial benefit to the client. This is what Level 3 looks like.
The single most important lesson from both examples:
Weak submissions describe. Strong submissions advise. Every statement in your Summary of Experience and every paragraph in your case study should answer not just "what happened" but "what I decided, what I considered and why I concluded as I did." That shift from description to professional judgement is the difference between a pass and a referral.


🎓
Discuss this with Michael
Your APC preparation journey

"You have just finished reading about the APC process. Before we go further — tell me honestly: when you think about your assessment day, what is the feeling that comes up? Let us start there, and I will help you turn that into a preparation plan that is built around you specifically."



PART A continued — Building Surveying SoE Examples

EXAMPLE PATHWAY: BUILDING SURVEYING
MANDATORY COMPETENCY: HEALTH & SAFETY — LEVEL 2
❌ Weak version
"At Level 2, I understand the importance of health and safety when carrying out building inspections. I follow my firm's health and safety procedures at all times and wear appropriate PPE when visiting sites."
Why this fails: Describes compliance with procedures — not application of professional judgement. Any surveyor could have written this. No specific situation, no personal decision, no risk identified and managed.
✓ Strong version
"At Level 2, I applied CDM Regulations 2015 principles during a pre-acquisition survey of a vacant commercial property where I identified an unlabelled substance in a plant room that I suspected was asbestos-containing material. I immediately halted the inspection, secured the area and informed the client in writing that the survey could not be completed until a licensed asbestos survey had been carried out. I advised the client that proceeding without this survey would expose them to significant legal and financial risk under the Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012. The client accepted my recommendation and the subsequent survey confirmed the presence of ACMs, which materially affected the acquisition price."
Why this works: Specific situation, specific regulation applied, professional judgement exercised under uncertainty, personal action taken, client protected, outcome quantified. The candidate did not just follow a procedure — they made a professional judgement that protected the client from a real risk.
TECHNICAL COMPETENCY: BUILDING PATHOLOGY — LEVEL 3
❌ Weak version
"At Level 3, I have extensive experience in diagnosing building defects including damp, structural movement and roof failures. I provide professional advice to clients on remediation options and cost implications."
Why this fails: Generic, could describe any Building Surveyor. No specific defect, no specific advice, no specific consequence. "Extensive experience" is not evidence — it is a claim.
✓ Strong version
"At Level 3, I provided advice to a residential investor client on a Georgian mid-terrace property where I identified extensive penetrating and rising damp affecting three ground floor rooms. The vendor's surveyor had attributed the dampness to condensation and recommended only ventilation improvements. Having analysed the moisture patterns, the solid wall construction, the absence of a DPC and the external ground levels, I advised the client that the cause was penetrating damp through the solid masonry combined with bridged DPC at the rear elevation, not condensation. I recommended independent specialist investigation before proceeding and prepared a condition schedule identifying eighteen separate defects with remediation costs totalling approximately £34,000. The client negotiated a price reduction of £28,000 using my report as the basis for negotiation."
Why this works: Specific defect with a specific diagnosis that contradicted a previous professional. The candidate explains their reasoning — why they reached a different conclusion and on what basis. Specific financial consequence. This is what Level 3 looks like — reasoned professional advice that made a real difference to a real client.


Building Surveying SoE — Level 2 Illustrative Example
Inspection and defect analysis context

❌ Weak version
"At Level 2, I applied my understanding of building pathology by carrying out inspections of residential properties and identifying defects. I understand the importance of correctly diagnosing defects and providing appropriate advice to clients. I always ensure that my reports are clear and that clients understand the findings."
Why this fails: Every sentence describes general practice or awareness — not a specific situation where professional judgement was applied. There is no named defect, no diagnosis, no specific advice given and no identifiable outcome. An assessor cannot score this at Level 2.
✅ Strong version
"At Level 2, I applied my understanding of building pathology when instructed to carry out a pre-purchase survey on a 1930s semi-detached property. During inspection I identified significant cracking to the front bay window at first floor level with associated bowing to the external masonry. I diagnosed the cause as differential settlement related to a shallow foundation bearing on shrinkable clay, exacerbated by an adjacent mature tree. I produced a written report advising the client of the structural risk, recommending intrusive investigation by a structural engineer before exchange, and explaining the implications for mortgage valuation. The client instructed the investigation which confirmed my diagnosis. I subsequently advised on remediation options and their respective cost implications, enabling the client to renegotiate the purchase price."
Why this works: Specific property type, specific defect, named diagnosis with cause and contributing factors, specific professional advice given, client action taken, confirmed outcome, further advice on remediation. Every element of Level 2 is present — situation, application of knowledge, advice given, outcome evidenced.

sections.h: 1.15 If You Have Been Referred — Read This First
sections.body:
This section is written directly for candidates who have been referred. If this is your first attempt, this section is still worth reading — because understanding what referral actually means is part of understanding what the APC is actually testing.
What a referral actually means

A referral is not a verdict on your ability as a surveyor. It is a specific finding that on this occasion, in this room, the evidence you presented did not demonstrate competence to the standard required for independent chartered practice.

That is a precise and limited conclusion. It is not a statement about your intelligence, your professional worth or your future. Most referred candidates are good surveyors who were not yet ready to demonstrate it in the specific format the APC requires. Those are different problems — and the second one is solvable.

What the referral report is actually telling you

Read your referral report as a brief, not a judgement. Every line in it is a specific instruction. If it says your Ethics answer lacked depth at Level 3 — that tells you exactly what to prepare. If it says your case study options analysis was weak — that tells you exactly what to rewrite.

The most common referral reasons, in order of frequency:

1. Describing rather than demonstrating — the candidate explained what happened rather than what they advised and why. This is the most common single reason. Every answer in your resit needs to contain your personal judgement, your reasoning and the consequence of your advice.

2. Weak reflective analysis in the case study — assessors wanted to hear what the candidate learned and would do differently. Generic reflection does not score. Specific professional growth does.

3. Thin options analysis — the candidate presented options but did not show genuine evaluation. Strong options analysis rejects weak options with a reason and defends the chosen option under scrutiny.

4. Competency evidence that did not reach the required level — a Level 3 competency answered at Level 1. The candidate knew the subject but described their knowledge rather than evidencing reasoned professional advice.

5. Unable to handle follow-up questions — the initial answer was adequate but the candidate could not extend their thinking when probed. Assessors always go deeper. Preparing an answer is not the same as understanding it well enough to defend it.

How candidates who pass on their resit approach it differently

They do not simply revise harder. They revise differently. The specific changes that make the difference:

— They rewrite every competency statement from scratch, not from their original submission. The original got them referred. Starting over forces fresh thinking.

— They practise answering follow-up questions out loud, not just in writing. The room is a conversation. The page is not preparation for a conversation.

— They read their referral report before every practice session. Every session has a specific target drawn from that report.

— They get challenged. They do not just review material — they ask someone or something to probe their answers, name the level and tell them what is missing.

Michael in Module 12 is built for this moment.
Switch to Assessor Mode. Tell it you have been referred on a specific competency. Ask it to probe you the way the panel did. That discomfort — answering a follow-up question when you are not sure what comes next — is the preparation that the first attempt did not include for most referred candidates.
One more thing

The candidates who pass their resit are not exceptional. They are the ones who were honest with themselves about what went wrong, addressed it specifically and practised being challenged rather than avoiding the discomfort.

You have already shown you are serious enough to get this far. The distance between where you are and where you need to be is smaller than it feels tonight.
