title: Ethics, Conduct & Professionalism
intro: Ethics is the first competency assessed at interview. It is the most frequently examined. And it is the fastest route to referral if you get it wrong. This module gives you everything you need to answer with confidence at every level.

sections.h: Sprint Ethics — What the Panel Will Ask You
sections.body:
Ethics is not a topic you can wing. It is the one area where a weak answer can end your interview regardless of how well everything else has gone. The panel will ask you at least one ethics scenario. Possibly more. Here is what you need to know.

The RICS Five Ethical Standards are: Act with integrity. Always provide a high standard of service. Act in a way that promotes trust in the profession. Treat others with respect. Take responsibility. You need to know these by name and be able to apply them to a scenario without hesitation.

The panel does not ask ethics questions to catch you out. They ask them to confirm you think and behave like a professional. The bar is not perfection — it is judgment.

The four scenarios assessors use most

Scenario 1 — The conflict of interest

A client asks you to act on a transaction where you or your firm has a competing interest. What do you do?

The answer assessors want: You identify the conflict immediately. You do not proceed until you have disclosed it to all parties. You assess whether it can be managed with appropriate safeguards. If it cannot be managed, you decline to act. You document everything.

What risks referral: "I would tell my client and carry on." Disclosure alone is not enough. You must assess whether acting is appropriate at all.

Scenario 2 — The client asks you to do something improper

A client pressures you to overstate a valuation, omit a material fact from a report, or sign off something you are not comfortable with. What do you do?

The answer assessors want: You refuse. Clearly, professionally, and without equivocation. You explain that you cannot act in a way that compromises your professional obligations. You document the conversation. If necessary, you withdraw from the instruction.

What risks referral: Any answer that suggests you might comply under pressure, or that the client's instruction takes priority over your professional judgment.

Scenario 3 — You discover a colleague has done something wrong

You become aware that a colleague or another professional has acted improperly or potentially in breach of RICS standards. What do you do?

The answer assessors want: You do not ignore it. Depending on severity you raise it internally first — with a senior colleague or compliance officer. If the issue is serious and not being addressed, you understand that RICS members have obligations to report significant breaches. You do not cover it up to protect relationships.

What risks referral: "It is not my problem" or "I would speak to my colleague quietly and leave it there." The panel is testing whether you understand professional responsibility extends beyond your own conduct.

Scenario 4 — The bribery or hospitality question

A contractor offers you tickets to a major sporting event, an expensive gift, or a benefit that could influence your professional judgment. What do you do?

The answer assessors want: You decline or escalate. You refer to your firm's gifts and hospitality policy. You understand the Bribery Act 2010 and that accepting benefits that could influence professional judgment is unacceptable regardless of intent. You document the offer.

What risks referral: "It depends on the value." It depends on whether it could influence your judgment — not just whether it does.

Three things to say in any ethics scenario

  1. "My first obligation is to act with integrity and in accordance with RICS ethical standards."
  2. "I would document this and seek guidance if I was uncertain about the right course of action."
  3. "The client's instruction does not override my professional obligations."

These three statements, delivered with confidence, tell the panel everything they need to know about your ethical judgment.

The question behind every ethics question

Can we trust this person to act professionally when no one is watching? That is what chartership means. That is what the panel is deciding. Your answer to every ethics question should make the answer to that question obvious.

sections.h: 2.1 Introduction — The Competency That Can End Your APC Before It Starts
sections.body:
Assessors take ethics seriously because RICS takes it seriously. Every Chartered Surveyor carries public trust. The moment a panel suspects you do not understand your professional obligations — the interview changes tone.

Ethics is not a standalone competency. It runs through every other competency. When you manage a client — that is ethics. When you handle confidential data — that is ethics. When you face pressure to adjust advice — that is ethics.

The good news: Ethics is also one of the most straightforward competencies to master once you understand what assessors are actually looking for.

Assessors want to hear: not a recitation of the five Ethical Standards — anyone can memorise a list. They want to hear how you applied ethical judgement under pressure.

sections.h: 2.2 Module Objectives and Level Breakdown
sections.body:
After this module you will:

— Name and explain the five RICS Ethical Standards with confidence
— Apply the Rules of Conduct to real scenarios
— Recognise conflicts of interest before they become problems
— Handle pressure to act unethically and explain exactly what you would do
— Answer at Level 1, 2 and 3 without hesitation

Level 1: Know the Ethical Standards, Rules of Conduct, CHP, PII, conflicts of interest.
Level 2: Show how you applied ethical judgement in real situations.
Level 3: Give clear, balanced, compliant advice on ethical matters — weighing options and justifying your position.

Assessors want to hear: a candidate who has genuinely thought about ethics in practice — not one who has memorised the RICS website.

sections.h: 2.3 The Five Ethical Standards
sections.body:
Memorise these. Know them in your sleep. Assessors will ask — and hesitating on something this fundamental sends the wrong signal immediately.

1. Act with Integrity — honest, transparent, not misleading. Doing what is right even when it is inconvenient.

2. Always Provide a High Standard of Service — competent, responsive, client-focused. Doing what you said you would do, when you said you would do it.

3. Always Act in a Way that Promotes Trust in the Profession — protecting RICS reputation. Behaving in a way that makes the profession proud.

4. Treat Others with Respect — fairness and consideration for all stakeholders regardless of seniority or commercial value.

5. Take Responsibility — own your work, acknowledge mistakes, act on them. Not passing the blame.

Assessors want to hear: the five standards named correctly and then — crucially — at least one example of how you have applied them in your real work.

sections.h: 2.4 What Professional Conduct Actually Looks Like
sections.body:
Professional conduct is not a concept — it is a daily habit. It shows in how you write emails. How you respond when a client is unreasonable. How you handle a mistake. Whether you escalate a concern or hope it goes away.

RICS expects all surveyors to demonstrate:

Integrity — acting honestly, avoiding misleading behaviour, prioritising what is right over what is easy.
Independence — providing objective, impartial advice even under commercial pressure.
Accountability — owning your work, decisions and mistakes.
Transparency — clear reasoning, clear documentation, clear communication.
Respect — working with fairness, considering others' perspectives.
Competence — keeping skills up to date through CPD, only accepting work you are qualified for.
Confidentiality — protecting client information and only sharing on a need-to-know basis.

Assessors want to hear: specific behaviours, not definitions. Not 'I always act with integrity' — but a real example of when you did.

sections.h: 2.5 Demonstrating Professionalism Under Pressure
sections.body:
Any candidate can behave professionally when everything is going well. Assessors want to know what you do when it is not.

Typical pressure points in surveying practice:
— A client pressing you to soften advice that might delay their transaction
— A colleague cutting corners on a report
— A contractor asking you to overlook a compliance issue
— An error in work you have already delivered to a client
— A situation where commercial interest and professional duty conflict

The professional response follows the same logic every time:
1. Stay calm — do not react emotionally
2. Focus on facts and your professional obligations
3. Refer to RICS standards and firm policy
4. Escalate where needed — and document that you did
5. Never prioritise commercial interest over public interest

Public interest always overrides commercial interest. If you remember nothing else from this module, remember that.

Assessors want to hear: that you have faced professional pressure and handled it correctly — not that you have always worked in a perfectly straightforward environment.

sections.h: 2.6 Conflicts of Interest
sections.body:
More candidates are referred for failing to identify or properly manage a conflict of interest than almost any other ethics issue.

A conflict of interest arises when your personal, financial or professional interests could compromise — or appear to compromise — your impartiality.

You must:
— Identify conflicts proactively, not wait to be asked
— Declare them to all relevant parties immediately
— Follow firm and RICS procedures for managing them
— Put client and public interest before personal interest

The test: ask yourself at the start of every instruction — is there any reason, however small, why my judgement on this matter might be seen as compromised? If in doubt, declare. The risk of over-declaring is far lower than the risk of a conflict that surfaces later.

Assessors want to hear: that you understand what a conflict is, that you know how to identify one, and — ideally — that you have recognised and managed one in practice.

sections.h: 2.7 Confidentiality, GDPR and Duty of Care
sections.body:
Confidentiality is a professional obligation, not just a policy.

Everything a client tells you — their financial position, their plans, their concerns — is shared in professional confidence. It is not yours to share, discuss informally, or reference in other contexts.

In practice this means:
— No client details in casual conversation
— No sensitive documents sent via personal email
— No discussion of client matters in public places
— Secure storage of all client files and correspondence

GDPR reinforces these obligations legally. Personal data must be collected lawfully, used only for its stated purpose, kept accurate, stored securely and not retained longer than necessary.

Duty of care: you are professionally obligated to only accept work you are competent to undertake, to seek supervision when needed, and to refer instructions beyond your expertise.

Assessors want to hear: that confidentiality is a genuine professional habit — not something you only think about when reminded.

sections.h: 2.8 APC Scenario Practice
sections.body:
These are the scenarios assessors use. Practise your answer to each one out loud before your interview.

Scenario 1 — The client wants you to adjust your valuation.
A client calls and says your valuation is too low for their loan application. They ask you to revise it upward.
Strong answer: 'I would explain that my valuation reflects the evidence available and that RICS Red Book standards require me to report my honest professional opinion. I would document the conversation, decline to amend the figure, and inform my supervisor. If pressure continued I would consider whether I could continue acting.'

Scenario 2 — You discover an error.
You find a significant error in a report already sent to a client.
Strong answer: 'I would notify my supervisor immediately, contact the client to explain the error and issue a corrected report. I would log the incident under our quality management process and consider whether any third parties needed to be informed.'

Scenario 3 — A colleague behaves unprofessionally.
You overhear a colleague discussing confidential client details in a public area.
Strong answer: 'I would speak to my colleague privately, explain the confidentiality issue and ask them to move the conversation. If the behaviour continued I would escalate to our compliance officer and document what I witnessed.'

Scenario 4 — You are offered a gift.
A contractor offers you hospitality worth £300.
Strong answer: 'I would politely decline and record the offer in our gifts and hospitality register. Accepting could create a perceived conflict of interest and our firm policy requires declaration of anything over £25.'

Assessors want to hear: calm, structured, professional responses that reference RICS obligations — not panic, evasion or over-qualification.

sections.h: 2.9 2026 RICS Updates — AI Standard and CPD Framework
sections.body:
Two significant RICS changes came into effect in early 2026 that every APC candidate must know.

RICS Responsible Use of AI Standard (9 March 2026)
This is now a mandatory RICS professional standard. It requires:
— Written records of AI-assisted decisions in professional practice
— A risk register identifying where AI tools are used and what risks they carry
— Client notification when AI outputs materially affect professional advice or services
— Human oversight and professional accountability — AI does not remove your professional responsibility

The standard applies directly to surveyors using AI tools for valuations, reports, market analysis or client advice. If you use any AI tool in your professional work, you must be able to demonstrate compliance with this standard.

Updated RICS CPD Framework (January 2026)
RICS introduced a new 3-year rolling CPD requirement. Mandatory topics now include:
— Ethics
— Sustainability
— Artificial Intelligence

This means AI literacy is now a professional obligation — not optional development. Candidates must be able to demonstrate structured CPD across all three mandatory topics over the rolling 3-year period.

Assessors want to hear: that you are aware of the AI standard, understand your obligations under it, and can explain how it affects your professional practice — particularly if you use any AI-assisted tools in your work.

sections.h: 2.10 Bribery, Corruption and the RICS Professional Standard
sections.body:
Bribery and corruption is a core Ethics and Professionalism topic. Every APC assessor can ask about it. Every candidate must understand the RICS mandatory requirements, the red flag indicators and the built environment examples.

The RICS Professional Standard

The RICS professional standard Countering bribery, corruption, money laundering and terrorist financing (2nd edition) aims to help RICS members and regulated firms detect, prevent and respond to risks relating to bribery, corruption, money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions. It applies globally and takes precedence except where local legislation stipulates otherwise — in which case local law applies and the departure must be recorded in writing.

The RICS Rules of Conduct Rule 1 also stipulates that members and firms must not facilitate any financial crime including money laundering, tax evasion, bribery or corruption.

Mandatory requirements — RICS Members

— Must not offer or accept, directly or indirectly, anything that could constitute a bribe
— Must have adequate knowledge of bribery and corruption to comply with the professional standard
— Must report any activity they are aware of that breaches applicable anti-bribery laws to the nominated reporting officer or senior management

Mandatory requirements — RICS Regulated Firms

— Must not offer or accept anything that could constitute a bribe
— Must have plans in place to comply with applicable anti-bribery laws and ensure they are followed
— Must report any activity that may give rise to suspicion of anti-corruption law breach
— Must conduct periodic written risk evaluations of bribery and corruption risks facing the firm
— Must document and retain information detailing how the firm has met the requirements of the professional standard

Facilitation Payments

Facilitation payments — sometimes called grease payments — are small, unofficial payments made to a public official to speed up or secure routine administrative actions the payer is already entitled to. They do not change the outcome of a decision; they simply speed up the process.

Facilitation payments are illegal in the UK under the Bribery Act 2010. Most firms prohibit them. They must not be made unless explicitly authorised by senior management — and even where legal locally, they are discouraged within the RICS professional standard. In your APC interview, the correct answer is always that facilitation payments are prohibited unless explicitly authorised, and your default position should be not to make them.

Departures from the professional standard

Where the professional standard conflicts with local legislation, local law takes precedence. All departures must be recorded in writing noting the conflict, the deviation taken and any additional reporting or controls implemented.

The Five Red Flag Categories

The RICS Red Flag Indicators document identifies five categories of concern:

1. The Client — secretive about their identity, source of funds or reason for the transaction

2. The Parties — reside in or have connections to high-risk regions (Algeria, Ecuador, Ethiopia, Syria, Yemen, Iraq, Iran, North Korea) or connections that cast doubt on the genuine nature of the transaction

3. The Source of Funds — large cash payments, unexplained third-party payments or loans from non-institutional lenders

4. The Transaction — unusual size, regularity of payments, complicated structures or unusual steps in completing transactions

5. The Instructions — client is not local yet chose your services, willingness to pay high fees or regularly changes legal advisers

Built environment examples of bribery and corruption

Assessors will ask you to give examples. Know at least three of these:

— Bribery: A contractor gives a project manager a hospitality package — concert tickets, luxury travel — in exchange for being awarded a subcontract without competitive tender

— Artificially inflated prices: A supplier agrees with the QS to submit an inflated quote. The inflated amount is hidden within rate buildups and shared between supplier and QS

— Kickbacks: A site manager awards a landscaping contract to a specific firm. Once paid, the firm transfers 10% back to the manager as a thank-you

— Introduction payments: An architect receives an undisclosed fee from a cladding contractor for recommending them to the client despite better value alternatives

— Inflated timesheet hours: A supervisor approves timesheets showing 60 hours when only 40 were worked, in exchange for cash from the labour agency

— Planning consent: A developer gives gifts to a planning officer to ensure an application is approved quickly with fewer constraints

What a firm's anti-bribery policy must include

— A risk assessment, updated annually
— Appropriate governance and controls proportionate to the firm's work
— Registers for gifts, hospitality, charitable donations and conflicts of interest
— Clear staff guidance on their role in preventing bribery
— A designated contactable person for compliance and ethics matters
— A published code of conduct
— Due diligence on third-party suppliers
— Larger firms should formally appoint a compliance and ethics champion

In your APC interview: If asked about bribery or corruption, demonstrate that you know the RICS professional standard exists, understand the five red flag categories, can give specific built environment examples and know what to do if you suspect a breach — report immediately to the nominated reporting officer or senior management.

Money Laundering — The Three Stages

Every APC candidate must know the three stages of money laundering with built environment examples for each:

1. Placement — introducing criminal proceeds into the financial system. In property: paying cash deposits on property purchases, overpaying on a purchase and requesting a refund by legitimate bank transfer, using cash-intensive businesses to mingle criminal funds.

2. Layering — disguising the trail to prevent detection. In property: multiple rapid property transactions between connected parties, offshore ownership structures, using shell companies to obscure beneficial ownership, misrepresenting property values in transactions.

3. Integration — reintroducing laundered funds into the legitimate economy. In property: selling a property acquired through placement or layering and receiving clean proceeds, using rental income from a property purchased with criminal funds as legitimate income.

The RICS Professional Standard — Countering Financial Crime requires all RICS regulated firms to:
— Appoint a Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO)
— Carry out Customer Due Diligence (CDD) on all clients before accepting instructions
— Apply Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) for higher-risk clients, Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs) and complex or unusual transactions
— File a Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) with the National Crime Agency when they know or suspect money laundering — and never tell the client (tipping off)
— Maintain records of all CDD checks for five years

Professional Indemnity Insurance

PI insurance is mandatory for all RICS regulated firms carrying out regulated work. It protects clients and third parties against financial loss arising from negligent professional advice or work carried out by the firm.

Key points every candidate must know:
— RICS sets minimum PI insurance levels based on fee income
— PII must be maintained for a minimum of six years after the firm ceases trading (run-off cover)
— A firm must not carry out regulated work without adequate PII in place
— If a firm's PII lapses, it must notify RICS and cease regulated work immediately
— Candidates who are asked informally for professional advice by friends or family after chartership must be aware that their firm's PII may not cover informal instructions — and they should decline or formally appoint through the firm

Whistleblowing

A Chartered Surveyor who becomes aware of professional misconduct — by a colleague, their firm or a third party — has an obligation to act. The RICS Rules of Conduct and the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 both protect employees who raise genuine concerns in good faith.

In practice: raise internally first, document everything, escalate to RICS if the firm does not act, and never be deterred by seniority of the person involved. A candidate who says *"I would raise it with my line manager"* and stops there is not demonstrating Level 3 — they need to describe what happens if the line manager does nothing.

sections.h: 2.11 Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing, Sanctions and the ECCTA
sections.body:
Money laundering, terrorist financing and the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 are all live assessment topics for Ethics and Professionalism at Level 3.

Mandatory AML obligations for regulated firms

— Must not facilitate money laundering
— Must report suspicions to the relevant authority (Suspicious Activity Report — SAR)
— Must not tip off — informing a client that a SAR has been filed or an investigation is underway is a criminal offence
— Must carry out customer due diligence and verify client identity
— Must retain information securely
— Must periodically review money laundering and terrorist financing risks
— Must conduct enhanced checks where risks are higher (including cryptocurrency transactions)
— Must examine supply chains
— Must ensure reliance on third parties is appropriate

Tipping Off

Tipping off is informing a client that a suspicious activity report has been filed or that an investigation is underway. It is a criminal offence in most jurisdictions because it compromises investigations. If you have filed or are considering filing a SAR, you must not discuss the matter with the client under any circumstances until you have received legal advice or clearance from the relevant authority.

Customer Due Diligence — Standard Process

1. Identify the client
2. Verify identification against reliable, independent documentation
3. Perform additional risk-based checks where necessary

Enhanced Due Diligence — When Required

Enhanced due diligence is required when:
— The client is high-risk
— The transaction is unusual or complex
— The jurisdiction presents higher risk
— Digital currency (cryptocurrency) is used
— The client's wealth profile does not align with the transaction

Digital Currency and Cryptocurrency Risk

Digital assets can obscure the source of funds and are frequently used in money laundering and terrorist financing. RICS regulated firms must carry out enhanced due diligence for cryptocurrency transactions, including verifying origin, beneficial ownership and transaction purpose. This is an increasingly tested area as cryptocurrency use in property transactions grows.

Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML)

TBML involves disguising criminal proceeds using trade transactions. In real estate and construction it may appear as incorrect invoicing, refund requests or over and underpayments between parties. Any such irregularity should be escalated to compliance immediately. Assessors may ask you to identify a TBML scenario — know this term and be able to give a property-specific example.

Sanctions

Firms must:
— Not transact with specially designated nationals or sanctioned parties
— Implement effective systems and controls to screen clients
— Train staff on sanctions awareness
— Periodically review sanctions risks

If you suspect a client is sanctioned or a specially designated national, seek advice immediately from senior management and do not continue business until the risk is clarified.

The Role of a Compliance and Ethics Champion

A senior individual appointed to oversee customer due diligence, ethics and money laundering controls. Their role is to support good practice, identify emerging risks and assist internal investigations. Larger RICS regulated firms are expected to formally appoint one.

Whistleblowing Policies

Larger firms should have a formal whistleblowing policy explaining reporting methods and protections. Smaller firms may use simpler processes but must still support a culture of speaking up. If you have not reported a concern because you feared consequences — that is the gap the policy is designed to close.

The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 — Failure to Prevent Fraud

On 1 September 2025 the Failure to Prevent Fraud offence introduced by ECCTA 2023 came into force. This is an entirely new offence and assessors are already testing it.

What the offence does: Makes large organisations criminally liable if an associated person — employee, agent, subsidiary or contractor acting on the organisation's behalf — commits a fraud offence for the organisation's benefit, and the organisation did not have reasonable fraud-prevention procedures in place.

Which organisations does it apply to? Large organisations only — those meeting two of the following three criteria:
— More than 250 employees
— Turnover in excess of £36 million
— Balance sheet total in excess of £18 million

Who can trigger the offence? Any associated person acting for or on behalf of the organisation — employees, agents, subsidiaries, contractors or consultants.

There is no need to prove senior management involvement — making this similar in structure to the Failure to Prevent Bribery offence under the Bribery Act 2010.

The six prevention principles an organisation must demonstrate:
1. Proportionate procedures — controls proportionate to the risks faced
2. Top-level commitment — leadership visibly committed to fraud prevention
3. Risk assessment — identifying fraud risks across the organisation
4. Due diligence — on associated persons and third parties
5. Communication and training — staff understand their obligations
6. Monitoring and review — procedures kept current and tested

In your APC interview: If asked about financial crime, demonstrate that you know ECCTA 2023 came into force on 1 September 2025, understand what the Failure to Prevent Fraud offence means for firms, know the six prevention principles and can distinguish it from the older Bribery Act 2010 offence. This is recent legislation and assessors will reward candidates who know it.

🎓
Discuss this with Michael
Ethics in your professional life

"Imagine it is Monday morning. A client asks you to do something that feels slightly wrong — not illegal, but not quite right. You have thirty seconds to decide how to respond. Tell me about a moment like that in your own work. I will help you shape it into a strong Ethics statement."

title: Client Care
intro: Client care is not about being pleasant. It is about managing professional relationships with precision — from the first conversation to the final invoice. Done well, it prevents disputes before they start.

sections.h: Sprint Client Care — What the Panel Will Ask You
sections.body:
Client Care is mandatory for every candidate on every pathway. The panel will test it. Not with abstract theory — with scenarios from real practice. Here is what they ask and what they want to hear.

At its core, Client Care is about one thing: did you act in your client's best interests while maintaining your professional obligations? Every scenario the panel gives you comes back to that question.

The three scenarios assessors use most

Scenario 1 — The unhappy client

A client is dissatisfied with your service. They are threatening to complain. What do you do?

The answer assessors want: You listen. You acknowledge their concern without immediately admitting liability. You explain your firm's complaints procedure clearly and promptly. You attempt to resolve the issue at the earliest opportunity. You document everything. If the complaint cannot be resolved internally, you explain their right to escalate to the RICS or an alternative dispute resolution service.

What risks referral: "I would explain why they are wrong." The panel is not testing whether you can win an argument. They are testing whether you can handle a complaint professionally.

Scenario 2 — Scope creep

A client asks you to do something outside the agreed scope of your instruction. What do you do?

The answer assessors want: You clarify the original scope. You explain what is and is not included. If the additional work is appropriate, you agree revised terms in writing before proceeding. You do not simply absorb additional work without updating your terms of engagement — that creates risk for both you and the client.

What risks referral: "I would just do it to keep the client happy." Undefined scope creates liability. Protecting the client means being clear about what you are doing and on what terms.

Scenario 3 — Communicating bad news

You need to tell a client something they do not want to hear — a valuation is lower than expected, a defect is more serious than thought, a transaction is unlikely to proceed. How do you handle it?

The answer assessors want: You communicate clearly, promptly and in writing. You do not delay difficult news. You explain the implications objectively and present available options. You document the conversation. You remain professional and client-focused even when the message is unwelcome.

What risks referral: Delaying bad news, softening it to the point of misleading the client, or avoiding the conversation altogether. The panel is testing professional courage as much as communication skill.

Two principles for every client care question

  1. The client's interests and your professional obligations are not in conflict — they are the same thing. Acting professionally IS acting in the client's best interests.
  2. Document everything. Verbal conversations become disputes. Written records protect both you and your client.

What the panel is really asking

Would I trust this person to look after my client? That is the client care question. Answer it with every response.

sections.h: 3.1 Learning Objectives
sections.body:
After this module you will:

— Explain what client care means in professional surveying practice
— Understand RICS expectations and mandatory compliance requirements
— Set clear scope, manage expectations and handle variations professionally
— Use communication to prevent disputes rather than manage them
— Demonstrate Level 1 and Level 2 APC-ready examples

Assessors want to hear: that you manage client relationships proactively — not reactively.

sections.h: 3.2 What Client Care Really Means
sections.body:
Client care is about managing professional relationships from first contact through to completion. It links directly to the RICS Ethical Standard 'Always Provide a High Standard of Service' — which means it is not optional, it is a professional obligation.

In practice it includes:

— Understanding what the client actually needs, not just what they say they want
— Setting clear scope and managing expectations before problems arise
— Communicating proactively — not waiting to be chased
— Keeping accurate records of every instruction and agreement
— Handling variations, complaints and difficulties professionally

Assessors want to hear: that you understand client care as a professional discipline — not just common courtesy.

sections.h: 3.3 Why Client Care Matters in APC Practice
sections.body:
Poor client care has consequences that are hard to reverse. Complaints create formal paper trails. Misunderstandings escalate into disputes when communication breaks down. A client who feels ignored escalates.

Good client care, on the other hand:
— Builds trust that leads to repeat instructions and referrals
— Reduces disputes before they happen through clear communication
— Protects your professional reputation
— Creates the written evidence trail that protects you if things do go wrong

Assessors want to hear: that you understand the commercial and professional consequences of poor client care — not just the theoretical benefits of getting it right.

sections.h: 3.4 Level 1 and Level 2 Breakdown
sections.body:
Level 1 — Knowledge: You must understand the client lifecycle, service level agreements, scope of service, complaints procedures and the fundamentals of service delivery.

Level 2 — Application: You must show that you have managed real instructions — setting and agreeing scope, managing expectations when things change, handling variations and documenting communication.

There is no Level 3 for Client Care as a mandatory competency — but a strong Level 2 answer that shows you managed a difficult situation with clarity and professionalism demonstrates real professional maturity.

Assessors want to hear: 'I managed a situation where...' — not 'I know how to manage situations where...'

sections.h: 3.5 The Client Lifecycle and Setting Clear Scope
sections.body:
Every instruction passes through the same lifecycle. Understanding each stage is the foundation of good client care.

1. Enquiry — clarify needs, assumptions and constraints before agreeing anything.
2. Proposal — set out your fee, scope and service level clearly in writing.
3. Instruction — confirm written terms, deliverables and dates before starting work.
4. Delivery — communicate proactively, flag risks early, manage expectations.
5. Handover — report clearly, give advice on next steps, close out properly.
6. Aftercare — follow up, seek feedback, close the relationship professionally.

The golden rule that prevents most disputes: if it is not written and recorded, it is not agreed. Every variation, every additional instruction, every change to scope must be confirmed in writing before the work is done.

Assessors want to hear: that you understand scope management as a risk management tool — not just an administrative formality.

sections.h: 3.6 Communication Essentials
sections.body:
The majority of client complaints are rooted in communication failure — not technical failure. A client who feels informed and respected rarely complains. A client who feels ignored escalates.

The habits that prevent complaints:
— Confirm everything in writing, even if already agreed verbally
— Acknowledge receipt of instructions quickly — even if you cannot respond fully straight away
— Provide proactive updates rather than waiting to be chased
— Explain risks and delays clearly and early, not after the fact
— Maintain a professional tone even in difficult conversations
— Follow up every significant meeting or call with a written summary

If it is not in writing, it did not happen. That principle protects you as much as it serves your client.

Assessors want to hear: that your communication discipline is a professional habit — not something you apply only when a situation becomes difficult.

sections.h: 3.7 Managing Complaints and Difficult Situations
sections.body:
Complaints happen in every surveying practice. How you handle them is what matters.

RICS requires every firm to have a two-stage Complaints Handling Procedure:

Stage 1 — Internal review by a senior member of staff not involved in the matter.
Stage 2 — Independent redress mechanism such as CEDR or the property ombudsman.

When a complaint arises:
— Listen fully before responding
— Acknowledge the complaint factually and calmly, not defensively
— Refer back to the written scope and timeline
— Escalate internally if the matter requires senior involvement
— Maintain a clear written record throughout
— Stay professional — a well-handled complaint can strengthen a client relationship

Assessors want to hear: that you have faced a difficult client situation and managed it with professionalism and structure.

sections.h: 3.8 APC Exam-Style Examples
sections.body:
Use these as a framework for building your own answers.

Example 1 — Managing a deadline that cannot be met.
You identify that a client's deadline cannot be met due to third-party delays outside your control.
Strong approach: inform the client early; explain the cause clearly; reset the timeline in writing; offer a revised programme; document everything.

Example 2 — A client adds scope mid-instruction.
A client asks you to add three additional properties to your inspection the day before the visit.
Strong approach: explain the impact on fee, time and programme; issue revised terms before proceeding; wait for written confirmation; do not start additional work until agreed.

Example 3 — A client disputes your fee.
A client says your invoice is higher than they expected.
Strong approach: refer to the original proposal and scope; walk through the basis of the fee calmly; identify if scope variations were not documented; negotiate a fair resolution; record the outcome in writing.

Assessors want to hear: clear scope and clear communication running through every answer. Those are the two pillars every client care response should rest on.

sections.h: 3.9 2026 Residential Property Law Updates
sections.body:
Two significant pieces of legislation affecting residential property came into force or were extended in 2026 with direct implications for surveyors advising landlords, tenants and housing providers.

Renters' Rights Act (May 2026)
This Act fundamentally changes the private rented sector in England. Key provisions:
— Abolition of Section 21 'no-fault' evictions — landlords can no longer end a tenancy without grounds
— All tenancies become periodic from the outset — fixed terms are abolished
— New rental review processes — landlords must follow a statutory process to increase rent
— Private Rented Sector Landlord Ombudsman — mandatory membership for all private landlords
— New possession grounds — landlords can still recover possession but only on defined statutory grounds

Commercial implications for surveyors:
— Valuation of buy-to-let and residential investment portfolios must reflect the new tenancy regime
— Landlord clients need advice on the implications for their management strategy and exit planning
— Property managers must update their processes to comply with the new rent review and possession requirements
— The loss of Section 21 changes the risk profile of residential investment assets

Awaab's Law
Awaab's Law came into force for the social rented sector from 27 October 2025, following the death of Awaab Ishak from damp and mould exposure. Stage one requires social housing providers to respond to emergency hazards within 24 hours and to investigate and begin remediation of significant damp and mould within prescribed timeframes. Stage two, expected from October 2026, will extend obligations to cover additional significant hazards in social housing. Extension to the private rented sector is subject to government consultation — no confirmed implementation date has been set. Key requirements for social housing providers from 27 October 2025:
— Emergency hazards: action required within 24 hours
— Significant damp and mould: investigation and remediation within prescribed timeframes
— Written record-keeping of all hazard investigations and remediation
Note: the 14-day investigation and 24-hour emergency timescales apply to the social rented sector only — they are not currently legally enforceable in the private rented sector

Private Rented Sector (PRS) Database
The PRS Database is a new mandatory national registration system being introduced under the Renters' Rights Act, with a phased launch expected from late 2026. Key details:
— Mandatory registration for all private landlords, their properties, and compliance information
— Phased regional rollout beginning late 2026, with full national registration through 2027
— Penalties up to £7,000 for basic non-compliance; up to £40,000 for serious non-compliance or fraud
— The Private Rented Sector Landlord Ombudsman becomes mandatory from 2028
Surveyors advising landlord clients should flag registration obligations and the reputational and financial risks of non-compliance.

Assessors want to hear: that you understand the Renters' Rights Act implications for residential investment advice and valuation, that you are aware of Awaab's Law obligations for surveyors working in or advising the social housing sector, and that you can explain the PRS Database registration requirements and penalties to a landlord client.

sections.h: 3.10 RICS Consumer Protection Requirements and the Equality Act 2010
sections.body:
RICS Consumer Protection Requirements and the Equality Act 2010 are both directly tested under Client Care. Every candidate must understand what they require in practice.

RICS Consumer Protection Requirements

RICS regulatory requirements place significant emphasis on the protection of consumer clients. The RICS Rules of Conduct, effective from February 2022, set mandatory standards for all members and regulated firms. When acting for residential consumer clients, these requirements are reinforced by supporting professional statements covering transparency, competence, complaints handling, conflicts of interest and professional indemnity insurance. These requirements cover five key areas:

1. Transparency — firms must be clear about who they are, what services they provide, their fees and how complaints are handled. All material information must be provided upfront, not buried in small print.

2. Conflicts of Interest — firms must identify, disclose and manage conflicts of interest. Where a conflict cannot be managed it must be declined. The RICS Conflicts of Interest professional standard applies.

3. Complaints Handling — firms must have a written complaints procedure, acknowledge complaints promptly and keep clients informed of progress. Where a complaint cannot be resolved internally, clients must be directed to an approved redress scheme. For residential property firms this is typically the Property Ombudsman or the Property Redress Scheme.

4. Competence — firms must only take on work they are competent to carry out and must maintain that competence through CPD.

5. Professional Indemnity Insurance — firms must hold appropriate PII cover. Candidates must be able to explain what PII is, why it exists and what it covers — this is tested in Client Care interviews across all pathways.

In your APC interview: If asked about Client Care compliance, demonstrate you know RICS consumer protection requirements, understand the five key areas and can describe how your firm's complaints procedure works in practice. Assessors frequently ask: what happens when a client complains? Know the answer specifically — acknowledge, investigate, respond within a defined timeframe, refer to redress scheme if unresolved.

The Equality Act 2010

The Equality Act 2010 is the primary UK legislation prohibiting discrimination. It applies directly to surveying practice in two ways:

Service provision — it is unlawful to discriminate against a client or service user on the basis of any of the nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. RICS regulated firms must not treat clients less favourably on any of these grounds.

Reasonable adjustments duty — service providers have a positive duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people where a provision, criterion or practice puts them at a substantial disadvantage. In a surveying context this includes physical access to premises, communication formats (large print, audio), and flexibility in service delivery. The duty is anticipatory — firms must not wait for a disabled person to request an adjustment before thinking about it.

Employment — the Equality Act also governs how firms recruit, manage and develop staff. Relevant for Team-Working and Diversity, Inclusion and Teamworking competency answers.

In your APC interview: Know the nine protected characteristics. Know what reasonable adjustments means in practice for a surveying firm. Be ready to describe how your firm addresses the Equality Act in its client-facing work.

Sustainability connection — ESG and client sustainability expectations

Sustainability is increasingly embedded in client care obligations. Clients — particularly institutional investors — now expect ESG reporting, green building credentials and net zero pathways as standard. When advising clients on property strategy, a Chartered Surveyor is expected to be aware of how sustainability affects asset value, lettability and compliance. BREEAM ratings, EPC bands and embodied carbon are all areas where client questions are increasingly focused. The depth on sustainability legislation and net zero is in Module 10 — this note ensures you can connect sustainability awareness to your Client Care competency where relevant in your SoE.


🎓
Discuss this with Michael
Client Care in your practice

"Think of the client interaction in your career that was hardest to manage — the one where you had to deliver news they did not want to hear, or where expectations were difficult to align. Tell me what happened. I will show you how that moment is evidence for your Client Care competency."



Terms of Engagement

Every APC candidate must understand what terms of engagement are, why they are required and what they must contain. Terms of engagement form the contractual basis for every instruction — without them, the firm has no documented agreement with the client about scope, fee, liability or complaints process.

RICS requires terms of engagement to include:
— The scope of services to be provided
— The fee basis and payment terms
— The identity of the client and the property or matter
— The complaints handling procedure and the right to refer to an approved redress scheme
— Any limitation of liability (subject to RICS minimum PI requirements)
— Confirmation of professional indemnity insurance
— GDPR / data protection statement

Terms of engagement must be issued before work commences or as soon as reasonably practicable. For residential consumer clients, RICS regulatory requirements demand greater transparency, earlier disclosure of material information and clear communication of fees and scope before the instruction commences.

Client Money Protection

Client money is money held by a firm on behalf of a client — deposits, rent collected, sale proceeds, and so on. RICS regulated firms that hold client money must:
— Hold client money in a designated client account separate from the firm's own money
— Be registered with an RICS-approved client money protection scheme
— Account to clients promptly and maintain accurate records
— Never mix client money with office money
— Carry out regular reconciliations of client accounts

Mishandling client money is one of the most serious disciplinary matters in the profession. Candidates who manage rent, deposits or sale proceeds must be able to describe their firm's client money procedures in specific terms.

Confidentiality Obligations

A Chartered Surveyor owes a duty of confidentiality to their client. Information obtained during an instruction must not be disclosed to third parties without the client's consent — except where required by law (for example, SAR filing under AML obligations or court order).

Key points:
— Confidentiality continues after the instruction ends
— Acting for two parties in the same transaction creates a confidentiality conflict — information obtained for one client cannot be used for the other
— Social media and informal conversations are covered — a Chartered Surveyor discussing a client's affairs casually is a breach
— Data protection (GDPR) runs alongside professional confidentiality — they are distinct but complementary obligations

title: Communication & Negotiation
intro: Every surveying activity depends on communication. Every professional relationship involves negotiation. This is not a soft skill — it is the mechanism through which all your technical knowledge reaches your client.

sections.h: Sprint Communication & Negotiation — What the Panel Will Ask You
sections.body:
The APC interview is itself a communication test. Every answer you give is being assessed not just for content but for how you deliver it. Clarity, confidence and structure matter as much as technical knowledge.

Communication & Negotiation is also one of the competencies where candidates most commonly undersell themselves. They know more than they demonstrate because they do not structure their answers well under pressure.

The three scenarios assessors use most

Scenario 1 — Tell me about a negotiation you were involved in

This is an invitation to demonstrate Level 2 — application. The panel wants a real example with a clear structure: what was the situation, what were the competing interests, what approach did you take, what was the outcome.

The answer assessors want: A specific example. Not "I often negotiate on behalf of clients" — that is Level 1. They want: "I was instructed on a lease renewal where the landlord's initial position was X. I prepared by understanding the tenant's priorities and the landlord's likely constraints. I used a collaborative approach and the outcome was Y." Outcome matters. Lessons learned matter more.

What risks referral: A vague answer with no specific example, or an example where you describe what happened without explaining your role or judgment.

Scenario 2 — How do you communicate complex technical information to a non-technical client?

The answer assessors want: You adapt your communication to your audience. You avoid jargon. You use analogies, visual aids or written summaries where appropriate. You check understanding. You follow up in writing to confirm key points. You give a real example.

What risks referral: "I explain it clearly." That is not an answer. The panel wants to know HOW you do it — your actual approach.

Scenario 3 — A negotiation breaks down. What do you do?

The answer assessors want: You do not escalate immediately. You seek to understand why the breakdown occurred. You consider whether the other party's position has changed or whether there is new information. You explore whether alternative solutions exist. You advise your client on options including mediation, arbitration or other dispute resolution routes where appropriate.

What risks referral: "I would tell the client to go to court." The panel is testing whether you exhaust professional options before escalating.

The PREP framework for every answer

Use this structure for any communication or negotiation question:

  • P — Point: State your answer clearly in one sentence
  • R — Reason: Explain why
  • E — Example: Give a specific real example from your experience
  • P — Point again: Reinforce your answer

This structure works for every APC answer — not just Communication & Negotiation. Candidates who use it consistently sound more confident and more prepared.

What the panel is really assessing

Can this person communicate professionally under pressure? You are demonstrating the answer in real time. Every response is evidence.

sections.h: 4.1 Learning Outcomes
sections.body:
After this module you will:

— Communicate clearly and professionally in written, verbal and non-verbal form
— Use the PREP framework to structure every professional answer
— Adapt your communication style to different audiences and situations
— Demonstrate active listening and effective questioning
— Understand negotiation styles, BATNA and when to use each
— Handle difficult conversations professionally and follow up correctly

Assessors want to hear: structured, evidence-based answers — not fluent rambling. The candidate who uses PREP consistently throughout their interview stands out immediately.

sections.h: 4.2 Why This Competency Matters
sections.body:
Strong communication reduces risk. Weak communication creates it.

Misunderstandings that become disputes almost always have a communication failure at their root. A fee that was never confirmed in writing. A scope that was discussed but not documented. Advice that was given verbally but not followed up.

RICS expects Chartered Surveyors to:
— Present technical advice clearly to clients and stakeholders
— Use structured reasoning when giving recommendations
— Lead and participate in meetings effectively
— Negotiate professional outcomes fairly and ethically
— Document advice, decisions and agreements properly

This competency supports every other competency. You cannot demonstrate strong Client Care without strong communication. You cannot manage Conflict Avoidance without it either.

Assessors want to hear: that your communication is deliberate and structured — not just friendly and fluent.

sections.h: 4.3 Learning Levels Breakdown
sections.body:
Level 1 — Knowledge: Understand the principles of communication; barriers to effective communication; verbal, written and non-verbal channels; negotiation theory and terminology.

Level 2 — Application: Show that you communicate effectively in real professional situations — negotiating fees, managing difficult conversations, documenting agreements, chairing or supporting meetings.

The gap between Level 1 and Level 2 is not knowledge — it is evidence. For every principle you can explain at Level 1, you should have a real example of having applied it at Level 2.

Assessors want to hear: 'When X situation arose, I communicated by doing Y, which resulted in Z.'

sections.h: 4.4 Principles of Effective Communication
sections.body:
Effective professional communication must be:

— Clear — no ambiguity about what you mean
— Concise — no unnecessary words or padding
— Structured — logical flow from point to conclusion
— Relevant — tailored to the purpose and audience
— Confirmed in writing — verbal communication followed up on paper

Poor communication leads to confusion, delays, disputes, complaints and loss of professional credibility — in that order.

Always adapt your style to your audience. A letter to a client reads very differently from a site instruction to a contractor. A technical report for a lender uses different language from advice to a first-time buyer.

Assessors want to hear: that you think about who your audience is before you communicate — not after.

sections.h: 4.5 Communication Channels and the PREP Framework
sections.body:
The three communication channels:
— Written — emails, letters, reports, meeting minutes. Always the preferred record.
— Verbal — face-to-face, telephone, video call. Always followed up in writing.
— Non-verbal — posture, eye contact, tone, body language. More powerful than most candidates realise, especially in interview.

PREP — the framework that transforms your APC answers:

P — Point. State your recommendation or position clearly upfront.
R — Reason. Explain why. One clear justification.
E — Example. Evidence from your real practice. This is where Level 2 lives.
P — Point. Repeat and confirm your recommendation.

Example: 'I recommend a measured survey (Point) because the existing plans are significantly outdated (Reason). On a previous instruction, relying on outdated plans caused a three-week programme delay (Example). A measured survey at this stage will eliminate that risk (Point).'

Assessors want to hear: PREP applied to every answer. It is the single most visible sign of a well-prepared candidate.

sections.h: 4.6 Active Listening, Written Communication and Verbal Skills
sections.body:
Active listening is not simply waiting for the other person to finish. It involves:
— Full attention with no interruption
— Clarifying questions to confirm understanding
— Summarising back what you have heard
— Acknowledging the other person's position before responding

In negotiation and in APC interviews, active listening is as important as what you say. Candidates who listen carefully give better, more targeted answers.

Written communication best practice:
— Write for the reader, not for yourself
— Use plain English — technical jargon impresses no one
— Structure with clear headings and logical flow
— Confirm every verbal discussion in writing with a clear summary

Non-verbal communication in interview: maintain eye contact, sit with open posture, speak at a measured pace. Avoid filler words — 'um', 'like', 'you know' — they undermine perceived confidence even when the content is strong.

Assessors want to hear: structured, measured verbal communication — not speed and volume.

sections.h: 4.7 Negotiation Essentials
sections.body:
Surveyors negotiate constantly — fees, timelines, access arrangements, contract terms, variations, disputes. It is not an occasional skill, it is a daily one.

The five negotiation styles:
— Competitive — win/lose. Rarely appropriate in professional relationships.
— Collaborative — win/win. The preferred approach in surveying practice.
— Compromising — balanced trade-offs. Useful when time is limited.
— Avoiding — delaying or sidestepping. Almost never the right approach.
— Accommodating — prioritising the other party's interests. Can damage your position over time.

Collaborative negotiation is preferred because it protects professional relationships and produces agreements that both parties can commit to.

Assessors want to hear: that you understand which negotiation style to use and why — not just that you are good at reaching agreement.

sections.h: 4.8 BATNA — Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement
sections.body:
BATNA is your fallback position if negotiation fails. Knowing it before you enter any negotiation keeps you grounded — it tells you the point at which walking away is better than accepting a poor deal. Without it, you negotiate from weakness.

Preparing for any negotiation:
— Know your ideal outcome and your minimum acceptable position
— Understand the other party's priorities and constraints
— Prepare facts and evidence rather than opinions
— Ask open questions: 'What is most important to you about this?'
— Always document the final agreement

Difficult conversations: stay calm and measured. Listen before responding. Acknowledge concerns before countering them. Use facts, not emotions. Reframe rather than refuse — instead of 'That is not possible' say 'The alternative we can offer is...'

Assessors want to hear: a real negotiation you handled, what your preparation was, how you approached it, and what the outcome was.

sections.h: 4.9 APC Examples and Handling Scenarios
sections.body:
Use these to build your own evidence.

Example 1 — Negotiating a timeline.
A client requested delivery of a report within 24 hours. You identified compliance and quality risks with that timeline.
Strong approach: explain the risk clearly; propose a phased approach with a draft in 24 hours and final report within 48; confirm the revised agreement in writing. Outcome: client's deadline met safely, risk managed.

Example 2 — Managing conflict through communication.
A contractor challenged your measurement of completed works, claiming it was undervalued.
Strong approach: review the evidence before responding; arrange a joint inspection with the contractor present; reach agreement on measurement methodology. Outcome: dispute resolved without formal escalation.

Example 3 — Stakeholder communication on a complex project.
Multiple consultants were receiving different scope information from different client contacts.
Strong approach: identify the communication breakdown; propose a single coordinated weekly update issued to all parties; agree reporting lines with the client. Outcome: misalignment prevented before it caused programme delay.

Assessors want to hear: effective communication is structured, clear and evidence-based. Those three words should define every answer in this competency.

sections.h: 4.10 Measurement Standards — IPMS, GEA, GIA, NIA and Key Conversions
sections.body:
Measurement standards and conversions are frequently tested in APC interviews across Commercial Real Estate, Valuation, Building Surveying, Facility Management and Retail pathways.

IPMS — International Property Measurement Standards

IPMS is a global framework developed by a coalition of over 80 professional organisations including RICS, designed to create consistent property measurement worldwide. Before IPMS, the same building measured under different national standards could produce floor area figures varying by up to 24% — creating significant risk in international investment decisions.

The current standard is IPMS: All Buildings (published January 2023), which consolidated all previous asset-class specific standards into one unified framework. RICS members are required to use IPMS: All Buildings or the RICS Code of Measuring Practice as appropriate, and must document which basis they have used.

The three key IPMS measurements:
— IPMS 1 — External measurement. The total floor area measured to the outer face of the external walls including everything within the external envelope
— IPMS 2 — Internal measurement, broadly equivalent to Gross Internal Area (GIA). Measured to the internal dominant face of the perimeter walls
— IPMS 3 — Occupier measurement, broadly equivalent to Net Internal Area (NIA). The usable space the occupier actually occupies

RICS Code of Measuring Practice — traditional UK standards:
— GEA (Gross External Area) — measured to the outside of external walls. Used for rating, council tax and building cost estimates
— GIA (Gross Internal Area) — measured to the inside of external walls. Standard for valuing industrial, warehouse and retail warehouse properties, and for construction cost estimates
— NIA (Net Internal Area) — the usable floor space excluding toilets, plant rooms, stairwells, lift shafts, permanent corridors, structural walls and columns. Used for office and retail valuations and lettings

Which standard when:
— Offices and residential: IPMS required for new instructions
— Industrial, retail, mixed-use: RICS Code of Measuring Practice still applies
— Always document which basis has been used

Zone A — Retail Zoning

Zone A is the measurement and valuation methodology used for retail units. It divides a shop floor into zones of equal depth (typically 6.1 metres) running from the shopfront backwards, with each zone having a different rental value.

— Zone A — the frontmost 6.1m of the unit, highest value, 100% weighting
— Zone B — the next 6.1m, typically 50% of Zone A value
— Zone C — the next 6.1m, typically 25% of Zone A value
— Remainder — any space beyond Zone C, typically 12.5% or less

The total rental value is expressed in terms of Zone A rate (ITZA) — in terms of Zone A — which allows comparison between units of different shapes and sizes. Deeper units have proportionally less valuable rear space. An irregular unit is reduced to its Zone A equivalent for comparison purposes.

This is tested frequently in Commercial Real Estate and Valuation APC interviews. Assessors will ask you to explain the principle, calculate an ITZA rate from given dimensions and explain why it matters to rental valuation.

Key Measurement Conversions — memorise these

1 square metre = 10.764 square feet
To convert sq m to sq ft: multiply by 10.764
To convert sq ft to sq m: divide by 10.764
Practical: a 100 sq m unit = approximately 1,076 sq ft

1 hectare = 2.471 acres
To convert hectares to acres: multiply by 2.471
To convert acres to hectares: divide by 2.471
Practical: a 10 hectare site = approximately 24.7 acres

Assessors will ask you these directly. Know the conversion figures. Do not guess. If you cannot recall the exact figure in the room, say so and give the approximate — "approximately 10.8 square feet to a square metre" is far better than silence or a wrong answer stated with confidence.

sections.h: 4.11 Cat A and Cat B Fit-Out — Definitions, Differences and APC Application
sections.body:
Cat A and Cat B fit-out is a core topic for Commercial Real Estate, Building Surveying, Project Management and Facility Management APC pathways.

Cat A Fit-Out

Cat A is the base level of fit-out provided by a landlord to a tenant to create a blank canvas. It makes the space technically functional and legally compliant but contains nothing specific to a particular occupier.

A Cat A fit-out typically includes:
— Raised access floors with grid installed
— Suspended plenum ceilings with standard grid and lighting
— Heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) distributed to the floor plate
— Electrical services to the floor plate
— Fire detection and suppression to the floor plate
— Male, female and accessible WC facilities
— Lift lobbies and common parts finished
— Painted walls and ceilings

The space is habitable and code-compliant but has no partitions, no occupier-specific features and no personalisation. A prospective tenant walks into a Cat A space and sees a functional open floor plate ready for their own fit-out.

Cat B Fit-Out

Cat B is the occupier-specific fit-out carried out by or for the tenant within the Cat A shell. It turns the blank canvas into a functioning workplace specific to that occupier's requirements.

A Cat B fit-out typically includes:
— Internal partitioning — meeting rooms, offices, breakout spaces
— Bespoke ceiling features, feature lighting and finishes
— Raised floor coverings — carpet tiles, hard flooring
— Occupier-specific HVAC controls
— Kitchen and tea-point facilities
— Reception and branded entrance features
— Data cabling and AV infrastructure
— Furniture, fixtures and equipment
— Decorative finishes specific to the occupier's brand

The distinction in practice:

The landlord typically delivers Cat A at their cost as part of the letting terms. The tenant funds Cat B. The dividing line is occasionally contested — some landlords offer a Cat A+ which includes some basic elements of Cat B (carpet, kitchen, some partitions) to reduce tenant fit-out cost and incentivise occupation.

Why this matters in your APC:
In Commercial Real Estate — understanding what is included in Cat A informs rent-free period negotiations, dilapidations at lease end and reinstatement obligations
In Building Surveying — Cat A and Cat B are part of dilapidations and condition assessment work
In Project Management — the distinction defines scope, cost planning and programme for fit-out projects

A plenum ceiling (referenced in Cat A) is the void space between a suspended ceiling and the structural floor or roof above it. This space is used to route mechanical and electrical services — ductwork, cabling, sprinkler pipes — without them being visible from the occupied space below. In modern commercial buildings the plenum is pressurised as part of the HVAC system, which is where the term originates.

sections.h: 4.12 Building Inspection — Frame Type, BMS and Structural Identification
sections.body:
Identifying structural frame type and understanding building management systems is tested across Building Surveying, Commercial Real Estate and Facility Management APC pathways.

How to identify concrete or steel frame from inspection

In many APC interviews — particularly Building Surveying — candidates are asked how they would determine whether a commercial building has a concrete or steel structural frame. You cannot always see the frame itself, but the following indicators allow an experienced surveyor to form a view:

Indicators of a concrete frame:
— Columns tend to be square or rectangular in section
— Column sizes are larger and walls between columns may be thicker
— Exposed concrete soffit (underside of structural floor) visible in plant rooms, car parks or service areas
— No visible bolt plates or cleats at column/beam junctions
— Post-tensioning ducts or tendons sometimes visible at cut edges
— Flat slab construction is almost always concrete
— Fire protection not typically visible — concrete is inherently fire resistant

Indicators of a steel frame:
— Columns tend to be narrow I-section or H-section profile
— Bolt plates, cleats or welded connections visible at beam-to-column junctions
— Fire protection casing around columns and beams — intumescent paint, board casing or sprayed protection
— Profiled metal decking (ComFlor or similar) visible at edges or in service voids — steel frames typically use composite metal deck floors
— Lighter, longer spans than equivalent concrete construction
— Hollow sections (CHS/RHS) for secondary steelwork

On a surveying inspection you would not typically open up fabric to investigate, but plant room access, car park levels, service risers and any exposed structure in maintenance areas usually reveal sufficient evidence to form a reasoned view.

BMS — Building Management System

A Building Management System (BMS) is a computer-based control system installed in a building that monitors and manages the building's mechanical and electrical equipment.

What a BMS does:
— Controls and monitors heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC)
— Manages lighting systems — occupancy sensing, daylight dimming, zoning
— Monitors electrical systems — energy consumption, power distribution
— Controls fire alarm and detection systems
— Manages access control and security systems
— Monitors lifts and escalators
— Tracks energy use and generates performance reports
— Provides fault alerts and predictive maintenance data

Why a BMS matters in commercial property:
— EPC ratings and energy performance are directly linked to how effectively the BMS optimises building services
— Landlord and tenant service charge disputes often involve BMS data on energy consumption
— Under the RICS AI Standard and sustainability obligations, BMS data is increasingly used to evidence carbon performance
— In dilapidations, the BMS installation and its condition can be a significant item
— Facility managers use BMS data daily for planned preventative maintenance scheduling

In your APC interview: If you have worked in commercial property, you should be able to describe a BMS you have encountered, what it controlled, and how it affected your advice to a client on energy performance, service charges or maintenance obligations.
