title: Health & Safety in Surveying
intro: Health and safety is not bureaucracy. It is a legal duty. The most common reason a surveyor is sent off site is failing to follow procedure — and the most common procedure candidates cannot explain in APC interviews is RAMS. This module changes that.

sections.h: Sprint Health & Safety — What the Panel Will Ask You
sections.body:
Health & Safety is mandatory and non-negotiable. The panel will ask about it. A weak answer here — regardless of how well everything else has gone — raises serious concerns about your readiness for chartership.

The good news: H&S questions follow predictable patterns. Here is what to expect and how to answer.

The three scenarios assessors use most

Scenario 1 — You arrive on site and identify an immediate safety risk. What do you do?

The answer assessors want: You stop. You do not proceed past an unsafe condition. You identify the risk, assess whether it presents an immediate danger and take proportionate action. If there is immediate danger to life you stop works, clear the area and notify the relevant parties. You document everything. You do not continue your inspection until the risk is controlled.

What risks referral: "I would note it in my report and carry on." Immediate risks require immediate action — not a footnote.

Scenario 2 — What are your responsibilities under CDM 2015?

The answer assessors want: You understand the role relevant to your practice. As a designer or principal designer you have specific duties to eliminate or reduce foreseeable risks during design. You understand that CDM applies to all construction projects and that your responsibilities depend on your role. You know the difference between the principal designer, principal contractor and client duties.

What risks referral: Confusion between roles, or describing CDM as something that only applies to large projects. CDM 2015 applies to all construction work.

Scenario 3 — A contractor on site is working unsafely. What do you do?

The answer assessors want: You raise it immediately. You do not ignore unsafe practices because it is not your direct responsibility. Depending on your role you instruct the contractor to stop, notify the principal contractor and document the incident. If the unsafe practice continues and presents serious risk you have an obligation to escalate. H&S responsibilities on site are shared — they do not belong only to the contractor.

What risks referral: "It is the contractor's responsibility, not mine." The panel is testing whether you understand that everyone on site has H&S obligations.

Three things every candidate must know cold

  1. The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 — the principal legislation placing duties on employers, employees and the self-employed
  2. CDM 2015 — Construction Design and Management Regulations — your duties depend on your role
  3. The 5-step risk assessment model — identify hazards, identify who might be harmed, evaluate risks and controls, record findings, review

What the panel is really assessing

Would I be comfortable with this person on site making safety decisions? That is the H&S question. Your answer needs to make the answer obvious.

sections.h: 5.1 Introduction — Why H&S Matters More Than You Think
sections.body:
Surveyors are on site regularly. They inspect buildings in poor condition. They attend construction sites with active operations. They work alone in unoccupied properties. Every one of these scenarios carries real physical risk — and real professional liability.

RICS expects all surveyors to put public protection first. Not because it is a compliance exercise, but because a surveyor who gets this wrong can cause serious harm — to themselves, to third parties, or to the clients relying on their advice.

Assessors want to hear: that you take H&S seriously as a professional responsibility — not just a box to tick before you enter a building.

sections.h: 5.2 Learning Outcomes
sections.body:
After this module you will:

— Explain the key H&S legislation relevant to surveying practice
— Apply the risk assessment 5-step model
— Understand CDM 2015 roles and your responsibilities within them
— Explain what RAMS are, why they matter and what to do when they are missing
— Demonstrate safe site behaviour and lone working procedures
— Answer APC questions at Level 1 and Level 2 with confidence

Assessors want to hear: specific procedures applied in real situations — not a recitation of legislation.

The Gateway Process — Higher-Risk Buildings

The Building Safety Act 2022 introduced a mandatory three-gateway process for new higher-risk buildings (broadly those over 18 metres or 7 storeys with at least two residential units):

Gateway 1 — at planning application stage. The BSR provides a statutory consultee role. The applicant must demonstrate how fire safety has been considered in the design before planning permission is granted. No construction can commence without Gateway 1 clearance.

Gateway 2 — before construction commences. The principal dutyholder must submit a building control approval application to the BSR including full design and fire safety information. The BSR must approve before any higher-risk building work begins. This replaced the old building notice process for HRBs.

Gateway 3 — at completion, before occupation. A completion certificate application must be submitted to the BSR including the Golden Thread of information — a digital record of all building safety information maintained throughout design and construction. The BSR must issue a completion certificate before the building can be occupied.

The Golden Thread — a digital record of all building safety information that must be maintained throughout the life of the building. It begins at design and continues through construction, occupation and refurbishment. The Accountable Person is responsible for maintaining it during occupation.

COSHH — Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002

COSHH requires employers to control substances that are hazardous to health. In construction and surveying contexts this includes asbestos, dust, solvents, paints and chemicals used in construction or remediation.

The COSHH hierarchy of control:
1. Eliminate the substance
2. Substitute with a less hazardous alternative
3. Enclose the process
4. Extract at source
5. Reduce exposure through engineering controls
6. PPE as a last resort

Work at Height Regulations 2005

Work at height means any work where a person could fall and be injured — including working on roofs, scaffolding, ladders and in excavations. The Regulations require:
— Avoid work at height where reasonably practicable
— If work at height cannot be avoided, use work equipment or other measures to prevent falls
— Where the risk of a fall cannot be eliminated, use work equipment to minimise the distance and consequences of a fall

For surveyors carrying out inspections, this applies to roof access, ladder use and inspection of elevated structures. A candidate must be able to describe how their firm's risk assessment process applies to inspection activities involving height.

sections.h: 5.3 Learning Levels Breakdown
sections.body:
Level 1 — Knowledge: You must understand the core legislation, risk assessment principles, hazard identification, CDM roles and basic H&S terminology.

Level 2 — Application: You must show evidence of applying H&S in real practice — conducting safe site visits, reading and understanding RAMS, identifying hazards, wearing appropriate PPE, following emergency procedures.

The candidates who struggle with this competency at interview are those who can recite the Health and Safety at Work Act but cannot describe a single site visit from an H&S perspective.

Assessors want to hear: 'Before attending site, I always...' followed by a specific, detailed account of your real practice.

sections.h: 5.4 Key H&S Legislation and Terminology
sections.body:
Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974
The foundation of all UK H&S law. Employers and employees must ensure safety 'so far as reasonably practicable.' This duty cannot be delegated or ignored.

Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999
Requires employers to: carry out risk assessments; appoint competent persons; provide information and training.

CDM Regulations 2015
Applies to construction projects. Key roles include Client, Principal Designer, Designers, Principal Contractor and Workers. Surveyors often fall under 'Designer' or 'Client Advisor' — both carry specific H&S duties.

Key terms you must know:
— Hazard: anything with potential to cause harm
— Risk: the likelihood and severity of that harm occurring
— Control measure: action taken to eliminate or reduce risk
— PPE: Personal Protective Equipment
— RAMS: Risk Assessment and Method Statement
— Near miss: an incident that could have caused harm but did not

Assessors want to hear: these terms used correctly in context — not just defined in isolation.

sections.h: 5.5 Risk Assessment — The 5-Step Model
sections.body:
Risk assessment is a practical tool, not a bureaucratic exercise. Its purpose is to identify what could cause harm, who might be affected, and what to do about it — before harm occurs.

The five steps:
1. Identify the hazards
2. Decide who might be harmed and how
3. Evaluate the risk and decide on control measures
4. Record your findings
5. Review and update regularly

The approach must be proportionate. A simple site visit to a well-maintained commercial office requires a different level of assessment than a survey of a derelict industrial building. The key is that it is done by someone competent, it is documented, and it is kept current.

Assessors want to hear: that you understand risk assessment as a live process — not a document you complete once and forget.

sections.h: 5.6 Site Hazards and Control Measures
sections.body:
The hazards surveyors face regularly:

— Slips, trips and falls on uneven or wet surfaces
— Working at height including on roofs and scaffolding
— Asbestos-containing materials in older buildings
— Confined spaces with limited ventilation or access
— Moving plant and vehicles on active construction sites
— Structural instability in dilapidated buildings
— Live electrical, gas and water services
— Lone working in remote or unoccupied properties

Control measures you should be applying:
— Appropriate PPE: hard hat, safety boots, hi-vis, gloves, eye protection
— Barriers, signage and safe access routes
— Pre-visit risk assessment and site-specific planning
— Asbestos management survey review before any intrusive work
— Emergency procedures and contact arrangements

Assessors want to hear: specific hazards relevant to your pathway and real measures you have taken to manage them.

sections.h: 5.7 CDM Responsibilities and Incident Reporting
sections.body:
Under CDM 2015, surveyors acting as designers must:
— Identify and communicate foreseeable hazards to the project team
— Ensure their designs take health and safety into account
— Provide adequate pre-construction information
— Cooperate with the principal designer and contractor

Incident and near-miss reporting:
If an incident occurs: make the area safe immediately; provide first aid; report internally; record the details accurately; review and implement prevention measures.

RIDDOR 2013 requires reporting to the HSE of: deaths; specified serious injuries; worker incapacitation for more than seven consecutive days; dangerous occurrences.

The threshold is seven consecutive days of incapacitation — not 24 hours. This is a common error in APC answers and assessors will correct you on it.

Assessors want to hear: that you understand CDM not as a theoretical framework but as something that affects how you work on every project.

sections.h: 5.8 Safe Working on Site
sections.body:
Before any site visit, your preparation should be consistent and thorough:

— Complete a pre-visit risk assessment based on available information
— Obtain and read any RAMS for the site or works being carried out
— Confirm PPE requirements
— Ensure someone at your firm knows your location and expected return time
— Identify any lone working procedures that apply

On site:
— Sign in and attend any induction
— Follow all site rules and instructions without exception
— Stay alert and maintain a safe distance from operations
— Never walk under suspended loads
— Report hazards you identify — do not simply note them

Assessors want to hear: a consistent, thorough routine that demonstrates H&S is embedded in how you work — not something you improvise on arrival.

sections.h: 5.9 RAMS — Risk Assessment and Method Statement
sections.body:
RAMS is one of the most examined H&S topics in APC interviews and one of the most poorly answered.

RAMS = Risk Assessment + Method Statement. Before attending any site where works are being carried out, you must read and understand the contractor's RAMS to know:

— What hazards exist on site
— What risks those hazards present
— What control measures are in place
— What PPE is required
— Whether you as a visitor are permitted access to specific areas
— Whether the work is safe to proceed

If RAMS are missing or inadequate — you do not proceed. You do not enter the site. You request updated RAMS before any access is given.

This is the correct professional response. APC panels ask about RAMS specifically because many candidates do not know this.

Real scenario: demolition site. RAMS showed the building was partially unstable. You arranged an escorted visit with exclusion zones rather than a solo inspection.
Real scenario: asbestos risk. RAMS included the asbestos register showing ACMs in the area you needed to survey. You arranged specialist attendance before proceeding.

Assessors want to hear: that RAMS are a genuine part of your site visit routine — and that you know exactly what to do when they are missing.

sections.h: 5.10 End-of-Module Summary
sections.body:
You should now be able to demonstrate APC-ready knowledge across all H&S areas:

— Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 — the legal foundation
— CDM 2015 — your specific duties as a surveyor
— Risk Assessment 5-step model — applied consistently
— RAMS — what they are, why they matter, what to do when they are absent
— RIDDOR — seven consecutive days is the incapacitation threshold, not 24 hours
— Site behaviour — a consistent, professional routine every time

The strongest candidates in this competency are not those who can quote the most legislation. They are those who can describe a real site visit from an H&S perspective in specific, credible detail.

Safety is a legal duty. Not optional, not assumed, not delegated.

sections.h: 5.11 2026 Building Safety Updates
sections.body:
Three significant building safety changes came into effect in 2026 that are directly relevant to surveying practice.

Building Safety Regulator (BSR) — Full Independence (January 2026)
The BSR is now a fully independent regulatory body exercising strict oversight on higher-risk buildings — broadly those 11 metres or above or with 5 or more storeys. Note: the formal higher-risk building definition under the Building Safety Act 2022 is 18 metres or 7+ storeys. The government's remediation programme targets all residential buildings over 11 metres with potentially unsafe cladding. Its key functions include:
— Oversight of the design and construction of new higher-risk buildings
— Assessment and registration of existing higher-risk buildings
— Enforcement action against non-compliant dutyholders
— Increased scrutiny on structural integrity, fire safety and building control

Surveyors working on or advising on higher-risk buildings must understand their duties under this new regime.

Building Safety Levy (1 October 2026)
A new direct levy on most new residential developments in England, payable before building work is completed. Key implications:
— Must be factored into development viability assessments from inception
— Affects residual land value calculations
— Applies broadly to new residential development — exemptions are limited

Two Staircase Rule (30 September 2026)
New residential buildings over 18 metres must now include two staircases. This requirement affects:
— Floor plate design and net-to-gross ratios
— Unit numbers and development density
— Viability of high-rise residential schemes
— Refurbishment feasibility for existing tall buildings

Surveyors advising on residential development schemes above 18 metres must factor this requirement into feasibility, design and cost advice from the outset.

Assessors want to hear: that you are aware of the BSR independence, the levy and the two staircase rule — and that you understand their commercial and practical implications for the projects you advise on.

🎓

"Health and Safety is the competency that often feels like a checkbox — until something goes wrong. Tell me about a health and safety situation you have encountered in your work, however small. I will help you see why it matters more than you might think — and how it becomes Level 2 evidence."

title: Accounting Principles & Procedures
intro: You do not need to be an accountant to pass this competency. You need to understand financial information well enough to give commercially aware advice. That is what assessors are testing — and it is a skill every Chartered Surveyor needs.

sections.h: Sprint Accounting Principles — What the Panel Will Ask You
sections.body:
Accounting Principles is the competency candidates most commonly underestimate. It is not about being an accountant. It is about demonstrating that you understand the financial context in which your clients operate and that you can give commercially aware advice.

The panel will not ask you to prepare a balance sheet. They will ask you to demonstrate that you understand what financial information means and how it affects your advice.

The three scenarios assessors use most

Scenario 1 — A client asks you to advise on a property acquisition. What financial information would you want to see?

The answer assessors want: You think beyond the physical property. You want to understand the client's financial position, cash flow requirements, borrowing capacity and investment objectives. You would want to review relevant financial statements to understand the client's ability to fund acquisition costs, ongoing liabilities and any remediation or refurbishment requirements.

What risks referral: Answering purely in terms of the property condition or valuation without any reference to the client's financial context. The panel is testing commercial awareness — not just technical surveying knowledge.

Scenario 2 — What is the difference between cash flow and profit?

The answer assessors want: A business can be profitable but cash poor — revenue recognised does not equal cash received. Cash flow measures the actual movement of money in and out of a business. Profit measures income against expenditure over a period. A property company may show strong profits on paper while facing serious cash flow pressure if rental income is delayed or void periods extend. Understanding this distinction helps you give better client advice.

What risks referral: Confusing the two, or giving a textbook definition with no practical application to surveying practice.

Scenario 3 — Your client is considering a significant capital expenditure. How would you advise them?

The answer assessors want: You consider the financial implications alongside the technical ones. You discuss capital allowances where relevant, the impact on cash flow, the difference between capital and revenue expenditure for tax purposes, and the client's overall financial objectives. You do not give tax advice — but you know enough to flag the issues and refer to appropriate specialists.

What risks referral: Advising purely on the technical or physical aspects without any reference to financial implications. Or claiming to give detailed tax advice outside your competence.

Three things every candidate must know cold

  1. The difference between capital and revenue expenditure — and why it matters for tax
  2. Capital allowances — main pool WDA is reducing to 14%, special rate pool remains 6%
  3. Cash flow vs profit — a business can be profitable and insolvent at the same time

What the panel is really assessing

Can this person give commercially aware advice? Technical knowledge without commercial awareness is not enough for a chartered surveyor. Show them you understand the financial world your clients operate in.

sections.h: 6.1 Introduction
sections.body:
Accounting Principles is a mandatory APC competency at Level 1 — knowledge and understanding only. No application examples are required. But that does not make it easy to pass.

Surveyors interact with financial information daily — client budgets, project viability assessments, fee proposals, cost reports. Understanding the basics ensures you can read that information, understand what it is telling you, and give advice that reflects commercial reality.

The candidates who struggle with this competency are not those who lack financial knowledge. They are those who have learned the definitions but cannot explain the concepts in plain language under interview pressure.

Assessors want to hear: clear, confident explanations of financial concepts — not hesitant recitals of textbook definitions.

sections.h: 6.2 Learning Outcomes
sections.body:
After this module you will:

— Explain the three key financial statements and what each one tells you
— Define core accounting terms accurately and confidently
— Explain the difference between cash and profit — and why it matters in practice
— Understand budgeting, variance analysis and cost control
— Explain VAT, capital allowances and audit processes at a basic level
— Demonstrate commercially aware thinking in your APC answers

Assessors want to hear: financial concepts explained in the context of surveying practice — not abstract accounting theory.

Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT)

SDLT is a tax on the purchase of land and property in England and Northern Ireland. Every candidate advising on property transactions must understand the basic structure. Note: the nil-rate threshold reverted from £250,000 to £125,000 from 1 April 2025 when the temporary relief ended:

Residential SDLT rates (standard):
— £0 to £125,000: 0%
— £125,001 to £250,000: 2%
— £250,001 to £925,000: 5%
— £925,001 to £1.5m: 10%
— Above £1.5m: 12%
An additional 3% surcharge applies to second homes and buy-to-let purchases. A 2% surcharge applies to non-UK resident purchasers.

Non-residential SDLT rates (commercial):
— Up to £150,000: 0%
— £150,001 to £250,000: 2%
— Above £250,000: 5%
For commercial leases, SDLT is charged on the Net Present Value of rent over the lease term.

Key assessor question: A client is purchasing a commercial property for £500,000. What is the SDLT liability? Answer: £0 on the first £150,000 + £2,000 on the next £100,000 (2%) + £12,500 on the remaining £250,000 (5%) = £14,500.

Value Added Tax on Property

VAT treatment of property is complex and frequently tested:
— New commercial buildings: standard rated (20%)
— Existing commercial buildings: generally exempt, but the owner can opt to tax
— Residential new builds: zero rated
— Listed buildings: zero rated for approved alterations
— Conversions from commercial to residential: 5% reduced rate

Option to tax: A commercial property owner can opt to tax their property, making supplies of that property subject to VAT at 20%. This allows them to recover input VAT on costs but means tenants who cannot recover VAT (charities, banks, insurers) face an additional cost. Candidates advising on commercial acquisitions must consider whether the property is opted to tax.

sections.h: 6.3 Fundamentals of Surveying Accounts
sections.body:
Three financial statements form the foundation of business financial reporting. Every APC candidate should be able to explain each one clearly.

Profit and Loss (P&L) Statement
Shows revenues, costs and expenses over a specific period. Answers the question: is the business profitable? Surveyors encounter P&L when assessing project viability, reviewing firm performance or advising clients on the financial health of a business they are acquiring.

Balance Sheet
A snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity at a specific point in time. Answers the question: what does the business own and what does it owe? Important for understanding financial stability and solvency.

Cash Flow Statement
Tracks cash in and cash out over a period. Answers the question: does the business have enough cash to operate? This is the statement surveyors most commonly encounter in client advice situations.

Assessors want to hear: a clear explanation of each statement and when it is relevant — not just what it contains.

sections.h: 6.4 Key Accounting Terms
sections.body:
These are the terms assessors test most frequently. Know them precisely.

Revenue — income earned from providing services or selling goods.
Costs and Expenses — money spent to deliver services, including labour, materials and overheads.
Gross Profit — Revenue minus direct costs. Measures trading profitability before overheads.
Net Profit — Gross profit minus overheads. The actual bottom line.
Margin — Profit expressed as a percentage of revenue.
Overhead — Fixed costs not directly tied to a specific project: rent, salaries, insurance, administration.
Depreciation — The reduction in the value of an asset over time, recorded as a cost.
Variance — The difference between actual and budgeted performance. Positive variance means better than budget.
Accrual accounting — Recording revenues and expenses when they are incurred, not when cash changes hands.
Matching Principle — Expenses must be recorded in the same period as the revenues they help generate.

Assessors want to hear: these terms used naturally in context — not recited from a list.

sections.h: 6.5 VAT, Tax and Audit Processes
sections.body:
VAT must be charged on professional fees if the business is VAT-registered. It is not optional and not at the surveyor's discretion. Understanding VAT is essential when advising clients on the total cost of professional services and property transactions.

Capital allowances provide tax relief on qualifying capital expenditure — most commonly fixed mechanical and electrical installations forming part of plant in a commercial building. When advising on a commercial property acquisition or refurbishment, understanding which elements qualify for capital allowances is directly relevant to the client's financial position.

Internal audit exists to ensure financial controls are working, compliance obligations are met and risk is being managed effectively. Its purpose is to protect the business and its clients.

Assessors want to hear: that you understand these concepts in the context of client advice — not as standalone accounting theory.

sections.h: 6.6 Understanding Cash Flow
sections.body:
Cash flow management is often more important to a business than profitability — and this surprises many APC candidates when they first encounter the concept.

A business can be profitable on paper — showing strong revenues and healthy margins — and still be unable to pay its suppliers, its staff or its rent. This happens when clients are slow to pay invoices, when upfront costs are high before income is received, or when project delays shift the timing of cash receipts.

This distinction matters in surveying practice because:
— Clients often need advice on cash flow as much as profit
— Schedule delays on a development project affect a client's cash position directly
— Fee proposals should reflect not just the work involved but when cash will be received

Assessors want to hear: that you understand the cash flow concept and can explain why it matters in a practical client scenario.

sections.h: 6.7 Cash vs Profit and the P&L Account
sections.body:
Profit is an accounting measure of financial performance over a period. It tells you whether revenues exceeded costs.

Cash flow is the actual movement of money into and out of the business. It tells you whether the business has enough money to operate right now.

A business can be profitable and still fail if it runs out of cash. This is known as insolvency despite profitability — and it is more common than most people realise.

The P&L Account shows:
— Revenue at the top
— Direct costs deducted to give gross profit
— Overheads deducted to give net profit

APC candidates need to understand the structure and purpose of the P&L — not prepare one themselves.

Assessors want to hear: 'A business can be profitable and still fail because profit and cash are not the same thing.' That single sentence demonstrates the level of understanding required.

sections.h: 6.8 Balance Sheet and Cash Flow Statements
sections.body:
The Balance Sheet is a snapshot of financial position at a specific moment in time. It shows three things:

Assets — what the business owns. Current assets (cash, debtors, inventory) and fixed assets (property, plant, equipment).

Liabilities — what the business owes. Current liabilities due within 12 months, long-term liabilities due beyond that.

Equity — the net value. Assets minus liabilities. What the business is worth to its owners.

The fundamental accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. It always balances — hence the name.

The Cash Flow Statement shows cash in, cash out and the net cash position at the end of the period. Used to assess short-term financial health and the business's ability to meet its obligations.

Assessors want to hear: the difference between a balance sheet and a P&L explained clearly and confidently.

sections.h: 6.9 Budgeting and Cost Control
sections.body:
Budgeting is how a business plans its financial future. Cost control is how it manages against that plan in practice.

Surveyors work with budgets in many contexts — feasibility studies, cost management, project viability assessments, departmental planning.

A budget contains:
— Forecasted revenue — what the business expects to earn
— Forecasted costs — what it expects to spend
— Time periods — monthly, quarterly, annual
— Variance analysis — actual versus budget, and the reason for any difference

Variance Analysis: Variance = Actual minus Budget. A positive variance means better than budget. A negative variance signals a problem requiring investigation and corrective action.

Assessors want to hear: that you can explain budgeting and variance in the context of a surveying project or firm — not as an abstract financial concept.

sections.h: 6.10 Commercial Awareness and Cost Control
sections.body:
Commercial awareness is what connects accounting knowledge to professional advice. It is the ability to understand the financial implications of your recommendations and factor them into the advice you give.

In surveying practice this means:
— Understanding a client's budget constraints before recommending a course of action
— Recognising when a project's financial viability is at risk
— Understanding how delays, variations and procurement decisions affect cost
— Knowing when to recommend a specialist financial adviser rather than opining beyond your expertise

The surveyors who give the best commercial advice are not those who know the most accounting — they are those who ask the right questions about their client's financial position before they start advising.

Assessors want to hear: that your advice always reflects an awareness of its commercial consequences — not just its technical accuracy.

sections.h: 6.11 APC Examples and Scenarios
sections.body:
Although Level 1 does not require practical application, you can strengthen your answers by referencing financial knowledge in context.

Example 1 — Reading a budget.
You reviewed a departmental cost report and identified that the variance between budget and actual was being driven by a single overhead category that had been mis-allocated. You flagged this to your supervisor and the report was corrected before the board meeting.

Example 2 — Fee proposal viability.
Before submitting a fee proposal for a large inspection programme, you used margin calculations to confirm the fee would cover direct costs and contribute appropriately to overheads.

Example 3 — Client cash flow advice.
A client was proceeding with a development based on strong projected profit. You highlighted that the cash flow profile — with significant upfront costs and delayed sales receipts — created a funding gap at month nine. The client restructured their financing before committing.

Revision scenarios:
— A client's project is profitable but cash flow is negative. How do you explain this?
— A feasibility study shows strong revenue but high fixed costs. How do you assess viability?
— A budget review shows rising overheads. What are the financial implications?

Assessors want to hear: that accounting knowledge informs your advice — it does not sit in a separate box labelled 'mandatory competency.'

sections.h: 6.14 End-of-Module Summary
sections.body:
You should now be able to demonstrate APC Level 1 accounting knowledge with confidence:

— The three financial statements and what each one tells you
— Revenue, gross profit, net profit, margin and variance defined and used accurately
— The difference between cash and profit — and why it matters
— Budgeting, cost control and variance analysis explained in context
— VAT, capital allowances and audit understood at an appropriate level
— Commercial awareness running through every answer

The single sentence that demonstrates Level 1 mastery: 'A business can be profitable and still fail — because profit is an accounting measure and cash flow is a financial reality.' Everything else in this module builds from that insight.

sections.h: 6.15 2026 Capital Allowances — Key Legislative Changes
sections.body:
Significant changes to UK capital allowance legislation took effect in April 2026. Every APC candidate should understand these as they directly affect advice on commercial property acquisitions, fit-outs and equipment investment.

New 40% First-Year Allowance (FYA) — from 1 January 2026
Available for new and unused plant and machinery (excluding cars and second-hand assets). For the first time, this allowance extends to assets used for UK leasing — a major departure from previous rules. Note: overseas leasing is excluded. Available to both companies and unincorporated businesses.

Reduced Main Rate Writing-Down Allowance (WDA)
From 1 April 2026 (Corporation Tax) or 6 April 2026 (Income Tax), the main pool writing-down allowance reduces from 18% to 14%. This reduces the annual tax relief on existing plant and machinery pools — a material change for long-term asset owners and investors modelling after-tax returns.

Permanent Full Expensing
Companies continue to benefit from 100% first-year tax relief on new qualifying main pool plant and machinery under the permanent Full Expensing regime. This remains one of the most generous capital allowance provisions available and is particularly relevant when advising clients on timing of capital investment.

The practical implications for surveyors:
— Development viability models must reflect the new 14% WDA rather than 18%
— Clients acquiring commercial property should be advised on the availability of the 40% FYA for qualifying fit-out and equipment
— The extension of the FYA to leasing opens new planning opportunities for clients with equipment leasing arrangements
— Timing of capital expenditure now carries greater tax planning significance given the interaction between Full Expensing and the new FYA

Assessors want to hear: that you understand these changes and can explain their practical implications for client advice — not simply recite the rates.

sections.h: 6.14 Working Capital, Gearing and Key Financial Ratios
sections.body:
Working capital and gearing are the two most frequently tested financial ratio topics in APC accounting competency interviews. Know both clearly and be able to calculate them from given figures.

Working Capital

Working capital is the difference between a firm's current assets and current liabilities. It measures whether a business has enough short-term assets to cover its short-term obligations.

Formula: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities

Current assets include cash, trade debtors, stock and prepayments. Current liabilities include trade creditors, bank overdrafts and accruals due within 12 months.

A positive working capital figure means the business can meet its short-term obligations. A negative figure — more current liabilities than current assets — signals potential liquidity risk.

Working Capital Ratio (Current Ratio)
Formula: Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities
A ratio above 1.0 indicates positive working capital. A ratio of 1.5 to 2.0 is generally considered healthy. Below 1.0 suggests potential short-term cash flow problems.

Quick Ratio (Acid Test)
Formula: (Current Assets − Stock) ÷ Current Liabilities
A stricter measure that excludes stock, which may not be quickly convertible to cash. Used for businesses where stock cannot be liquidated rapidly.

Why it matters in surveying practice:
In Client Care and Business Planning contexts, a candidate advising a developer or investment client needs to be able to assess whether that client has sufficient working capital to proceed with a project. A client who runs out of working capital mid-project is a significant commercial risk. At Level 1 you need to understand the concept. At Level 2 you should be able to apply it to a real client situation.

Gearing

Gearing (also called leverage) measures how much of a business is financed by debt relative to equity. It indicates financial risk — highly geared businesses have significant debt obligations that must be serviced regardless of trading performance.

Formula: Gearing = Total Debt ÷ Total Equity × 100 (expressed as a percentage)

Alternative formula sometimes used: Total Debt ÷ (Total Debt + Total Equity) × 100

A gearing ratio above 50% is generally considered high — the business is more debt-financed than equity-financed. Very high gearing increases insolvency risk because interest and capital repayments must be made even when income falls.

Why it matters in surveying practice:
In property finance and development contexts, gearing is directly relevant to investment advice. A highly geared property investor is more vulnerable to interest rate rises and falling property values — two risks that are highly relevant in the current 2026 commercial environment. Capital allowances strategy, refinancing decisions and development appraisals all require an understanding of gearing.

Other key financial ratios assessors may ask about:

— Return on Capital Employed (ROCE): Operating Profit ÷ Capital Employed × 100. Measures how efficiently a business uses its capital to generate profit
— Gross Profit Margin: Gross Profit ÷ Revenue × 100. The proportion of revenue retained after direct costs
— Net Profit Margin: Net Profit ÷ Revenue × 100. The proportion retained after all costs
— Debtor Days: Trade Debtors ÷ Revenue × 365. How long on average clients take to pay — a rising debtor days figure signals cash flow pressure

In your APC interview: Be ready to calculate working capital and gearing from a simple set of figures. The assessor may present a balance sheet extract and ask what it tells you about the business. A Level 2 answer explains the calculation and draws a practical conclusion about what the figures mean for the client's financial position.

Sustainability connection — Sustainability costs and capital allowances

Sustainability has direct accounting implications for surveying clients. Capital allowances on energy-efficient plant and machinery (40% FYA from April 2026), the cost of EPC improvement works, embodied carbon costs in new construction and the Building Safety Levy all have financial statement implications. When evidencing Accounting Principles at Level 1, awareness of how sustainability obligations translate into costs and allowances demonstrates commercial breadth. The depth on specific sustainability legislation and net zero frameworks is in Module 10.

title: Business Planning
intro: Business Planning is assessed at Level 1 — knowledge only. But assessors want to know that you understand how the business you work in actually operates. That requires real commercial awareness, not just textbook knowledge.

sections.h: Sprint Business Planning — What the Panel Will Ask You
sections.body:
Business Planning is typically held at Level 1 — knowledge and understanding. The panel is not expecting you to have written a business plan. They are testing whether you understand what one is, why it matters and how it applies to surveying practice.

This is one of the competencies where a confident, concise answer scores well. Do not overcomplicate it.

The two scenarios assessors use most

Scenario 1 — What is a business plan and what does it contain?

The answer assessors want: A business plan sets out an organisation's objectives, the strategy for achieving them, the resources required and the financial projections. Key components include an executive summary, market analysis, operational plan, financial forecasts, KPIs and risk assessment. You can relate this to your own firm or a client context.

What risks referral: "A business plan is a document that explains what a business does." That is Level 0. The panel wants to know you understand purpose, components and application.

Scenario 2 — How does business planning apply to your role as a surveyor?

The answer assessors want: You understand that surveyors operate within commercial contexts — whether as employees, practice owners or advisers. You can relate business planning principles to fee forecasting, resource allocation, client pipeline management and risk assessment in your own practice context. If you have been involved in any business planning activity — even informally — this is the place to use it.

What risks referral: Treating this as purely theoretical with no connection to your actual experience or practice context.

Two things every candidate must know cold

  1. The components of a business plan — objectives, strategy, resources, financials, KPIs, risk
  2. KPIs — Key Performance Indicators — how performance is measured against objectives

What the panel is really assessing

Does this candidate understand the commercial context they work in? Business Planning is about showing you think like a professional — not just a technician.

sections.h: 7.1 Introduction
sections.body:
Surveyors do not work in isolation. They work within firms that have financial targets, market strategies, resource constraints and commercial risks. Understanding how that business operates — and how your work contributes to it — is part of what RICS expects of a Chartered Surveyor.

Business Planning is one of the competencies where candidates most often give thin, generic answers. 'A business plan sets out goals and how to achieve them' is accurate but demonstrates nothing. The candidates who perform well are those who can connect the theory to the commercial reality of their own firm.

Assessors want to hear: that you understand business planning in the context of how a surveying firm actually operates — not as an abstract management concept.

sections.h: 7.2 Learning Outcomes
sections.body:
After this module you will:

— Explain what a business plan is and what it contains
— Describe how surveying firms plan their services, resources and finances
— Understand SWOT and PESTLE as analytical frameworks
— Explain KPIs and how firms use them to monitor performance
— Identify and articulate commercial risks facing a surveying business
— Answer Level 1 APC questions with commercial confidence

Assessors want to hear: three commercial risks facing a surveying firm — named, explained and linked to how the firm responds. This question comes up in almost every APC interview.

sections.h: 7.3 What is Business Planning?
sections.body:
A business plan is a structured document that sets out what the business wants to achieve, how it will achieve it, what resources are required, how performance will be measured and what risks may affect delivery.

In a surveying firm context this means planning:
— Which service lines to offer and to which clients
— How many fee earners are needed to deliver those services
— What revenue and profitability targets are realistic
— What market conditions and risks could affect those targets
— How technology and infrastructure support delivery

Business planning is not a one-off exercise done when a firm is founded. It is an ongoing discipline that every commercial surveying practice uses to manage growth, respond to market changes and allocate resources effectively.

Assessors want to hear: that business planning is a live, practical tool — not a document that sits on a shelf.

sections.h: 7.4 Components of a Business Plan
sections.body:
A complete business plan contains seven elements:

1. Vision and Mission — the long-term aim and the business's purpose. Why does the firm exist and where is it going?

2. Objectives — SMART goals: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Not 'grow the business' but 'increase fee income from residential surveys by 20% within 12 months.'

3. Market Analysis — understanding client segments, competitor landscape, market trends and external risks. This is where PESTLE sits.

4. Services and Value Proposition — what the firm offers and why clients should choose it over competitors.

5. Operational Plan — staffing, technology, processes, quality management and how services are delivered.

6. Financial Plan — revenue forecast, cost forecast, profit margins, cash flow projections and budget framework.

7. Risk Management — market downturn, regulatory change, staffing issues, reputational risk and contingency planning.

Assessors want to hear: these seven components named and explained — with at least one connected to the surveying context you actually work in.

sections.h: 7.5 Key Performance Indicators
sections.body:
KPIs are the metrics a firm uses to monitor whether it is on track to meet its business plan objectives. For a surveying firm they typically include:

— Utilisation rate: what proportion of available time is being charged to clients
— Fee recovery: how much of the budgeted fee is actually invoiced and collected
— Revenue per fee earner: total fee income divided by number of fee earners
— Client satisfaction scores: measured through feedback or repeat instruction rates
— Project profitability: margin achieved on individual instructions versus budget
— H&S metrics: incident rates, near misses, compliance scores
— Compliance indicators: CPD completion rates, conflicts declared

Assessors may ask you to name three commercial risks facing a surveying firm. PESTLE gives you the framework — Political (regulatory change), Economic (market downturn), Social (talent shortage), Technological (digital disruption), Legal (liability exposure), Environmental (sustainability compliance costs).

Assessors want to hear: KPIs connected to the commercial performance of the business — not just a list of metrics.

sections.h: 7.6 Resource Planning
sections.body:
A business plan is only as good as its resource planning. A surveying firm that wins more instructions than it has capacity to deliver faces exactly the same commercial risk as one that has too few.

Resource planning covers:
— Staffing: the right number of people with the right skills at the right time
— Training and CPD: keeping the team competent and compliant
— Technology: software, hardware and digital infrastructure to support delivery
— Outsourcing decisions: which services to deliver in-house and which to refer
— Equipment: PPE, measuring tools, access equipment and vehicles

Surveyors contribute to resource planning by estimating time requirements for projects accurately, flagging capacity issues early and managing their own workload in a way that does not create bottlenecks.

Assessors want to hear: that you understand resource planning as a commercial discipline — not just a staffing question.

sections.h: 7.7 Risk and Opportunity Planning
sections.body:
Every business plan must address risk — not just to satisfy a template but because unmanaged risk destroys profitable firms faster than anything else.

Key risks a surveying firm faces:
— Market downturn reducing instruction volumes
— Key staff departures taking client relationships with them
— Regulatory change increasing compliance costs
— Technology disruption changing client expectations
— Reputational risk from a high-profile claim or complaint

Opportunity planning considers the opposite:
— New service lines that could generate additional revenue
— New geographies or client segments with unmet need
— Partnership or referral arrangements with complementary practices
— Technology investment that improves efficiency or capability

SWOT analyses internal strengths and weaknesses alongside external opportunities and threats. PESTLE analyses the external environment across six dimensions.

Assessors want to hear: risk and opportunity framed in the specific commercial context of a surveying business — not generic management theory.

sections.h: 7.8 Business Planning in Surveying Practice
sections.body:
In day-to-day surveying practice, business planning appears in many forms:
— Feasibility studies that assess whether a project is commercially viable
— Fee proposals that balance competitiveness with profitability
— Budget versus actual tracking on service lines or departments
— Pipeline management — monitoring live instructions and anticipated income
— Client development plans targeting specific organisations or sectors

These are not activities reserved for directors and partners. Every surveyor who manages instructions, prepares fee proposals or monitors project costs is engaging with business planning in practice.

Assessors want to hear: that you recognise business planning activity in your day-to-day work — not just in the boardroom.

sections.h: 7.9 Level 1 Understanding and APC Mini Scenarios
sections.body:
At Level 1 the key questions are: What is a business plan and what does it contain? What does SWOT analysis show? What is PESTLE and why is it useful? Name three commercial risks facing a surveying firm. What are KPIs and how does a firm use them?

APC Mini Scenarios:

Scenario 1: Your firm is planning to expand into a new service line. What does the business plan need to include?
Strong answer: market analysis of client demand and competitor presence; resource requirements including staffing and training; financial forecast including revenue projections and cost of establishment; risk assessment including timeline and break-even point.

Scenario 2: Your team has missed its revenue target for the quarter. What business planning tools help identify the cause?
Strong answer: variance analysis comparing actual versus budgeted fee income; utilisation rate review; pipeline assessment showing whether new instructions are entering the system.

Scenario 3: A client asks why your firm is better positioned than a competitor to advise on their portfolio.
Strong answer: value proposition from your firm's business plan — specific experience, sector knowledge, team capability, quality management and track record.

Assessors want to hear: that you can apply business planning concepts to realistic surveying scenarios — not just define them in the abstract.

sections.h: 7.9a 2026 Business Planning — Legislative and Commercial Context
sections.body:
The 2026 legislative and commercial environment is directly relevant to business planning for surveying firms and their clients. Assessors expect Level 1 candidates to show awareness of how the external environment affects business decisions.

Capital Allowances — April 2026

From April 2026 the Written Down Allowance (WDA) for main pool assets the Written Down Allowance (WDA) for main pool assets reduces from 18% to 14% — affecting the tax efficiency of investment in qualifying plant and machinery. The special rate pool WDA remains at 6%. The 40% First Year Allowance (FYA) remains available for qualifying energy-efficient and low-emission assets. In a business planning context, these changes affect investment timing decisions and the financial case for capital expenditure.

Building Safety Levy — October 2026

The Building Safety Levy applies to most new residential development in England from October 2026, payable before practical completion. Development appraisals and business plans for residential schemes must factor in this additional cost. For surveying firms advising developer clients, this affects the viability advice given at feasibility stage.

The RICS AI Standard — March 2026

The RICS AI Standard came into mandatory effect in March 2026. For surveying firms this creates a compliance obligation in business planning — firms must assess how AI is used within their practice, ensure appropriate governance and oversight, and document their approach. Business plans for firms using AI tools must address the standard's requirements.

Renters' Rights Act 2025

The abolition of Section 21 no-fault evictions and the introduction of the Private Rented Sector Database directly affect the business model of firms providing residential property management services. Business plans for firms in the residential sector must reflect the changed legal framework and the new compliance obligations on landlords.

In your APC interview: If asked about business planning in a 2026 context, show that you understand the external environment affects business strategy — capital allowances affect investment decisions, building safety costs affect development viability, and the RICS AI Standard creates new compliance requirements for firms using technology.

Sustainability connection — Sustainability risk in business planning

Sustainability is a material business planning consideration for any surveying practice or developer client. The commercial drivers include regulatory compliance costs (Future Homes Standard, Building Safety Levy), ESG investor requirements, green premium on assets and the reputational risk of non-compliance with net zero commitments. When evidencing Business Planning at Level 1, you should be able to explain how sustainability factors appear in a business plan — both as risk and as commercial opportunity. The depth on sustainability frameworks and legislation is in Module 10.

title: Conflict Avoidance & Dispute Resolution
intro: Most disputes in surveying practice were preventable. This module shows you how to prevent them — and what to do when prevention has not worked. It is one of the most practically useful competencies you will study.

sections.h: Sprint Conflict Avoidance & Dispute Resolution — What the Panel Will Ask You
sections.body:
Conflict Avoidance is one of the competencies where candidates most clearly demonstrate professional maturity. The panel is not just testing whether you know the dispute resolution routes — they are testing whether you have the judgment to avoid disputes in the first place.

The candidate who says "I would go to court" in response to a dispute scenario has already failed this question.

The three scenarios assessors use most

Scenario 1 — A dispute has arisen between your client and a third party. What steps would you take?

The answer assessors want: You exhaust informal resolution first. You attempt direct negotiation. If that fails you consider structured options in order of proportionality — negotiation, mediation, adjudication, arbitration, litigation. You advise your client on the cost, time and risk implications of each route. You always consider whether the dispute can be resolved without escalation.

What risks referral: Jumping straight to litigation or arbitration without demonstrating awareness of less adversarial options. The competency is called Conflict AVOIDANCE for a reason.

Scenario 2 — How would you avoid a dispute arising in the first place?

The answer assessors want: Clear terms of engagement from the outset. Regular communication throughout the instruction. Managing client expectations proactively. Documenting decisions and advice in writing. Addressing concerns early before they become formal complaints. Prevention is always preferable to resolution.

What risks referral: Treating conflict avoidance as something that happens after a dispute arises. The panel wants to hear about proactive professional practice.

Scenario 3 — What is the difference between mediation, adjudication and arbitration?

The answer assessors want:

  • Mediation — a neutral third party facilitates negotiation. Non-binding. The parties reach their own agreement.
  • Adjudication — a quick, binding decision by an adjudicator. Commonly used in construction disputes under the Housing Grants Act. Decision is temporarily binding.
  • Arbitration — a formal, binding process similar to litigation but private. The arbitrator's award is final and enforceable.

What risks referral: Confusing the routes or describing them all as "going to a third party to decide." The panel expects you to know the distinctions.

Two things every candidate must know cold

  1. The dispute resolution hierarchy — negotiation → mediation → adjudication → arbitration → litigation
  2. Without prejudice communications — what they are and why they matter

What the panel is really assessing

Does this candidate resolve problems or create them? Conflict avoidance is about professional judgment, communication and proportionality. Show the panel you are the kind of surveyor who prevents disputes — not one who escalates them.

sections.h: 8.1 Introduction
sections.body:
Conflict is inevitable in a profession where multiple parties have competing interests, tight budgets and significant financial stakes. A landlord and tenant see a dilapidations claim very differently. Two surveyors produce different valuations of the same property.

What distinguishes a Chartered Surveyor is not the ability to avoid disagreement — it is the professional skill to prevent disagreements becoming formal disputes, and to resolve them when they do.

RICS places strong emphasis on conflict avoidance precisely because disputes are expensive, time-consuming and damaging to professional relationships.

Assessors want to hear: that you see conflict avoidance as a professional responsibility — not just a preference.

Expert Determination

Expert determination is a binding dispute resolution process where an independent expert is appointed to decide a dispute based on their specialist knowledge, rather than legal argument. Unlike arbitration, the expert is not acting as a judge — they apply their own expertise to reach a decision. It is commonly used in:
— Rent review disputes
— Valuation disputes
— Dilapidations quantum disputes
— Business sale disputes involving property assets

The expert's decision is final and binding (unless fraud is proven) and cannot be appealed on the merits. This makes it faster and cheaper than arbitration for suitable disputes.

RICS Dispute Resolution Service (DRS)

The RICS Dispute Resolution Service provides a range of ADR services including arbitration, expert determination, independent expert valuation, adjudication and mediation. Candidates must know that the DRS exists and what services it offers. When a firm's complaints procedure fails to resolve a complaint, residential consumer clients have the right to refer to an approved redress scheme — for many RICS firms, the RICS Dispute Resolution Service provides this function alongside the Property Ombudsman and Property Redress Scheme.

PACT — Professional Arbitration on Court Terms

PACT is a scheme for resolving unopposed Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 lease renewal disputes. Where a landlord and tenant agree that the lease should be renewed but cannot agree the new terms (typically rent or other lease terms), either party can apply to have the terms determined by an independent person under the PACT scheme rather than going to court. It is faster, cheaper and more property-specialist than county court proceedings.

The Construction Act — Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996 (as amended)

The Construction Act gives parties to construction contracts the right to refer any dispute to adjudication at any time. Key provisions:
— Any party to a qualifying construction contract can refer a dispute to adjudication — the 28-day timetable is tight and designed for speed
— The adjudicator's decision is temporarily binding — it must be complied with immediately even if the losing party intends to challenge it through arbitration or litigation
— The Act also gives contractors a right to stage payments and restricts pay when paid clauses
— Applies to construction contracts in writing (or evidenced in writing) for construction operations in England, Wales and Scotland

In your APC interview: Be clear on the distinction between adjudication (statutory, any time, 28 days, temporarily binding) and arbitration (contractual, final and binding, longer). Many candidates confuse them under pressure.

sections.h: 8.2 Learning Outcomes
sections.body:
After this module you will:

— Explain what conflict avoidance means and why it matters in surveying practice
— Identify the early warning signs that a disagreement is escalating
— Apply professional tools to prevent conflicts from becoming formal disputes
— Explain the five dispute resolution routes in order of escalation
— Understand the RICS Conflict Avoidance Pledge and reference it by name
— Explain 'without prejudice' communications and when they are used
— Demonstrate APC Level 2 competence with real examples

Assessors want to hear: that you have identified and acted on early signs of conflict in practice — not just that you know the theory.

sections.h: 8.3 What is Conflict Avoidance?
sections.body:
Conflict avoidance is not about avoiding difficult conversations. It is about managing them early enough that they do not become formal disputes.

In practice it means:
— Communicating clearly from the outset so there is no room for misunderstanding
— Documenting instructions, assumptions and agreements as they happen
— Addressing ambiguity as soon as it is identified
— Flagging concerns early rather than waiting until they are impossible to ignore
— Keeping professional relationships intact even when disagreements arise

The goal is early, informal resolution — at a cost and effort that bears no comparison to formal dispute proceedings.

Assessors want to hear: a specific example of how you identified a potential conflict early and took steps to resolve it before it escalated.

sections.h: 8.4 Why Conflict Occurs
sections.body:
Understanding why conflicts arise makes them easier to prevent. The most common causes in surveying practice:

— Poorly defined scope: each party understood the instruction differently
— Undocumented assumptions: something was assumed but never agreed
— Ambiguous contract terms: the contract did not clearly address the situation
— Delays or changes: one party's expectations were not updated when circumstances changed
— Poor communication: updates were not given or messages were unclear
— Conflicting expert evidence: two professionals reached different conclusions
— Commercial pressure: one party feels the financial terms are unfair

Early warning signs that a conflict is developing:
— Tone of communications becomes more formal or guarded
— Responses slow down or become incomplete
— Parties stop collaborating and start protecting their positions
— Disagreements that were resolved informally before start being recorded formally

Assessors want to hear: that you recognise these early signals and respond to them before they escalate.

sections.h: 8.5 Professional Tools for Conflict Avoidance
sections.body:
The most effective conflict avoidance tools are not sophisticated — they are disciplined professional habits applied consistently.

Clear instructions: scope, deliverables, fees and timelines set out unambiguously before work begins.
Documented assumptions: any uncertainty written down and confirmed. 'We assume access will be available for three days as discussed' — confirmed in writing.
Regular communication: proactive updates prevent misunderstandings. A client who is kept informed does not need to chase.
Audit trails: every significant instruction, decision and change confirmed in writing and retained.
Professional behaviour: calm, impartial and solution-focused even when the situation is difficult.
Early clarification: address ambiguity and disagreement as soon as they arise.

The RICS Conflict Avoidance Pledge: a commitment by signatory firms to build collaborative, non-adversarial behaviours into their professional practice. Reference it by name in APC answers — it demonstrates current awareness and is a differentiating detail that most candidates miss.

Assessors want to hear: the Conflict Avoidance Pledge mentioned specifically.

sections.h: 8.6 Dispute Resolution Routes
sections.body:
When conflict cannot be avoided, RICS expects surveyors to advise clients on the most proportionate resolution mechanism available.

1. Negotiation — the first and best option. Informal, quick, cheap. The parties reach an agreement themselves. No third party involvement.

2. Mediation — a neutral mediator facilitates structured discussions. Non-binding unless the parties reach a settlement. Good for preserving relationships.

3. Adjudication — most commonly used in construction contracts. A decision is delivered within 28 days. Binding but temporarily — either party can refer to arbitration or litigation afterwards.

4. Arbitration — formal, private, binding. An arbitrator considers the evidence and delivers a final decision. More expensive than adjudication but less public than court.

5. Litigation — court proceedings. The most expensive, most public and slowest route. A last resort, not a first choice.

The escalation order matters: Negotiation, Mediation, Adjudication, Arbitration, Litigation. Each step up increases cost, formality and damage to professional relationships.

Assessors want to hear: the five routes named in order and — for Level 2 — a real example of advising a client on which route was most appropriate.

sections.h: 8.7 Without Prejudice Communications
sections.body:
'Without prejudice' is a legal concept that protects settlement negotiations from being used as evidence in subsequent legal proceedings.

When correspondence is marked 'Without Prejudice' it means:
— The communication is made genuinely for the purpose of settling a dispute
— The content cannot be used as evidence in court (with limited exceptions)
— The party making the communication is not weakening their formal legal position

This protection allows parties to negotiate freely without fear that an offer of compromise will be held against them if negotiations fail.

The common mistake: marking correspondence 'Without Prejudice' when it is not genuinely a settlement negotiation. The courts look at the substance, not just the label. Mislabelling does not create legal protection.

Assessors want to hear: a clear explanation of what 'without prejudice' means, when it is used, and the risk of incorrect labelling.

sections.h: 8.8 Your Professional Role in Conflict Avoidance
sections.body:
As a surveyor your professional duty in conflict avoidance is not neutral. You are expected to:
— Maintain impartiality even when under pressure from one party
— Provide evidence-based advice rather than opinion-based advocacy
— Keep clear, accurate, factual records at all times
— Escalate concerns appropriately — internally first, then formally if needed
— Manage expectations proactively so surprises do not become grievances
— Act with integrity and transparency even when the situation is commercially difficult

Failure to manage conflict professionally can result in complaints against you personally, negligence claims against your firm, or regulatory action by RICS.

Assessors want to hear: that you understand your personal professional duty in conflict situations — not just the general principles.

sections.h: 8.9 APC-Level Scenarios
sections.body:
Use these to prepare your Level 2 evidence.

Scenario 1 — Scope ambiguity.
Two parties disagree about what the original instructions included.
Strong approach: refer to the written scope; clarify the assumptions that were documented; propose an updated scope note that both parties agree and sign. Do not take sides until the evidence is clear.

Scenario 2 — Fee dispute.
A client disputes your invoice, claiming it exceeds what was agreed.
Strong approach: refer to the original fee proposal; walk through the basis of the invoice calmly; identify whether scope variations were not properly documented at the time; negotiate a fair resolution; record the outcome in writing.

Scenario 3 — Conflicting expert reports.
Two consultants have produced opposing findings on a defect cause.
Strong approach: decline to express an informal view before reviewing both reports fully; assess the evidence base for each conclusion; provide a reasoned professional opinion once you have done so.

Scenario 4 — Contractor confrontation.
A contractor becomes aggressive in a meeting, disputing your measurement of completed works.
Strong approach: remain calm and professional; do not escalate the tone; propose a joint inspection with all parties present to resolve the measurement question with evidence; document the incident.

sections.h: 8.10 Professional Dos and Don'ts and End-of-Module Summary
sections.body:
Always:
— Use calm, neutral, professional language even when the situation is tense
— Keep thorough written records of every instruction, decision and communication
— Clarify ambiguity and address concerns early
— Focus on solutions and evidence rather than positions and blame
— Know when to escalate and do so without hesitation when needed

Never:
— Make assumptions and proceed without documenting them
— Avoid difficult conversations because they are uncomfortable
— Become emotionally involved in a dispute between other parties
— Allow ambiguity to continue when it could be resolved

The Chartered Surveyor who manages conflict well does not avoid difficult conversations — they manage them better than anyone else in the room.

sections.h: 8.11 2026 Building Safety — Remediation Bill
sections.body:
The Building Remediation Bill was announced in the King's Speech on 13 May 2026 and is currently progressing through Parliament. It introduces a legal duty on responsible persons (freeholders) to identify, assess and remediate unsafe cladding on residential buildings within fixed statutory timeframes, with unlimited fines and criminal prosecution for serious failures. This has direct implications for surveyors involved in dispute resolution, contract management and professional advice on affected buildings.

What the Bill will introduce:
— A legal duty on responsible persons (freeholders) to identify, assess and remediate unsafe cladding
— High-rise residential buildings over 18 metres must complete remediation by end of 2029
— All residential buildings over 11 metres must complete remediation by 2031
— Construction product manufacturers will be required to contribute to remediation costs
— Sanctions include unlimited fines and criminal prosecution for serious failures
— Enhanced enforcement powers for the Building Safety Regulator

Conflict and dispute implications for surveyors:
The remediation programme has already generated significant dispute activity — between freeholders and leaseholders over liability, between contractors and building owners over scope and cost, and between residents and housing providers over timescales. The Remediation Bill is expected to intensify this activity by:
— Creating hard deadlines against which performance can be measured
— Generating enforcement actions where deadlines are missed
— Increasing pressure on all parties to resolve outstanding liability disputes quickly

Surveyors acting as expert witnesses, contract administrators or professional advisers on higher-risk buildings must understand the Remediation Bill framework and its implications for their professional duties and advice.

Assessors want to hear: awareness of the Remediation Bill in the context of building safety dispute resolution — particularly for candidates in building surveying, project management and residential pathways.

sections.h: 8.12 Dilapidations — Multi-Let and Single Dwelling Settlements
sections.body:
Dilapidations is a core competency topic for Building Surveying, Commercial Real Estate and Property Management APC pathways.

What is a dilapidations claim?

Dilapidations are breaches of a tenant's obligations under a lease relating to the condition, repair, decoration and reinstatement of a property at or during the lease term. At lease end, the landlord serves a Schedule of Dilapidations setting out the alleged breaches and the cost of remedying them.

Multi-let versus single dwelling — key differences in approach:

Multi-let commercial property (office building, retail park, industrial estate with multiple tenants):
— The landlord's claim is limited by the diminution in value cap under Section 18(1) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1927
— The cap limits the claim to the reduction in the value of the landlord's reversion caused by the disrepair — if the landlord intends to redevelop, the disrepair may cause no diminution at all
— In a multi-let building, the landlord must also consider whether defects are demised to a specific tenant or fall within the common parts (landlord's responsibility under the service charge)
— Vacant possession value versus occupied value with other tenants is relevant to the Section 18 valuation
— Service charge provisions affect which repairs are recoverable from the individual tenant versus spread across the estate

Single dwelling residential property:
— Dilapidations in residential leases operate under different statutory frameworks including the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985, which implies repairing obligations on landlords for dwellings below certain annual rent thresholds
— The Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018 and Awaab's Law impose additional obligations on landlords
— Residential dilapidations are typically resolved through deposit deductions under the tenancy deposit scheme rather than formal Schedule of Dilapidations procedure
— For long residential leases, disrepair obligations and their enforcement are more complex — involving forfeiture risk and statutory protections

The dilapidations settlement process:
1. Landlord instructs surveyor to prepare a Terminal Schedule of Dilapidations at or near lease end
2. Tenant's surveyor responds with a Counter Schedule
3. Section 18 valuation is obtained where a cap is in dispute
4. Negotiation between surveyors — most claims settle without litigation
5. Settlement is typically a cash sum reflecting agreed remediation costs

RICS Dilapidations Protocol 2016 — sets out the pre-action requirements for dilapidations disputes including the timetable for serving schedules and the requirement for a Section 18 valuation where relevant.

In your APC interview: Be prepared to explain a dilapidations situation from your experience, describe the Section 18 cap and how it affected the settlement, and distinguish between the landlord's and tenant's position in the negotiation.

Tell me about a conflict or dispute you have encountered — even a minor one. I will show you how it evidences one of the most underestimated competencies in the APC."
