title: Data Management
intro: Data management may be the least glamorous mandatory competency. It is also one of the most practically important. A surveying career involves handling sensitive client information every day — and the professional and legal consequences of handling it badly are significant.

sections.h: Sprint Data Management — What the Panel Will Ask You
sections.body:
Data Management is typically held at Level 1 but do not underestimate it. GDPR questions catch candidates out regularly — not because the law is complex but because candidates give vague answers when the panel wants specifics.

This is also the competency where the 2026 RICS AI Standard is most likely to come up. If you use AI tools in your practice, be ready to talk about it.

The three scenarios assessors use most

Scenario 1 — A data breach occurs in your firm. What do you do?

The answer assessors want: You act immediately. You contain the breach — stop further data loss. You assess the nature and scale of the breach. You notify your data protection officer or senior management. If the breach is likely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, you notify the ICO within 72 hours. If individuals are at high risk you notify them directly. You document everything throughout.

What risks referral: "I would tell my manager." That is the beginning of an answer — not a complete one. The panel wants to know you understand the 72-hour ICO notification requirement and the criteria for notifying affected individuals.

Scenario 2 — What are the key principles of GDPR and how do they apply to your work?

The answer assessors want: The six principles — lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality. You can apply at least two or three to a surveying context: you only collect data you need, you store it securely, you do not retain it longer than necessary, you ensure clients understand how their data is used.

What risks referral: Listing the principles without any application to practice. Or only knowing two or three of the six.

Scenario 3 — How do you ensure data security in your day-to-day practice?

The answer assessors want: Practical measures — secure file storage, access controls, encrypted communications where appropriate, clear desk policy, secure disposal of physical documents, not using personal devices for client data without authorisation. You demonstrate that data security is part of your professional practice — not an IT department problem.

What risks referral: "I use a password on my laptop." The panel wants professional awareness — not just basic hygiene.

Three things every candidate must know cold

  1. The six GDPR principles — lawfulness, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality
  2. 72 hours — the ICO notification window for reportable data breaches
  3. The RICS AI Standard 2026 — if you use AI tools you must be able to explain how you ensure data protection and professional accountability

What the panel is really assessing

Does this candidate take data protection seriously as a professional obligation — not just an administrative requirement? Show them it is part of how you practise.

sections.h: 9.1 Introduction
sections.body:
Surveyors handle data constantly — client instructions, valuation inputs, lease documents, site photographs, inspection notes, financial records, personal details. Every piece of that data carries an obligation: to keep it accurate, secure, accessible when needed and properly disposed of when it is not.

GDPR brought legal enforcement to data obligations that were always professional requirements. A data breach is no longer just an embarrassment — it can result in regulatory action, significant fines and serious reputational damage.

Assessors want to hear: that data management is an embedded professional habit — not a compliance exercise you perform reluctantly.

Building Information Modelling (BIM)

BIM is a process for creating and managing digital information about a built asset throughout its lifecycle. It is not just a software tool — it is a collaborative way of working that uses a shared digital model to coordinate design, construction and operation.

BIM levels:
— Level 0: Unmanaged CAD — 2D drawings, no collaboration
— Level 1: Managed CAD with some 3D, files shared via common data environment
— Level 2: Collaborative working — federated information models, each discipline maintains its own model. Required on all UK government-funded projects since 2016.
— Level 3 (ISO 19650): Single shared project model — fully integrated, real-time collaboration

ISO 19650 is the international standard for managing information over the whole lifecycle of a built asset using BIM. It replaced the UK PAS 1192 standards from 2019.

For APC candidates: Know what BIM is, what Level 2 requires and how it affects information management on your projects. Be ready to describe how BIM affects your role — even if your firm does not use full BIM, you should understand the Common Data Environment (CDE), IFC file formats and the Employer's Information Requirements (EIR).

Data Retention

RICS regulated firms must retain client and project records for defined periods. GDPR does not specify retention periods but requires data is not kept longer than necessary — the ICO recommends firms define and document their own retention schedule.

In surveying practice the typical retention periods are:
— Valuation reports: minimum 6 years (limitation period for negligence claims), recommended 15 years
— Contract documents: 12 years (deeds) or 6 years (simple contracts) after practical completion
— Inspection records: minimum 6 years
— CDD records for AML: 5 years from the end of the business relationship
— Employment records: 6 years after employment ends

A firm must have a documented data retention policy, apply it consistently and be able to demonstrate compliance to the ICO or RICS if requested.

sections.h: 9.2 Learning Outcomes
sections.body:
After this module you will:

— Explain the data lifecycle from creation through to secure disposal
— Name and apply the six GDPR principles to surveying scenarios
— Understand the different types of data and the obligations each carries
— Describe data security best practices and why they matter
— Explain audit trails, version control and their role in professional practice
— Respond correctly to a data breach
— Demonstrate Level 1 APC knowledge with confidence

Assessors want to hear: the six GDPR principles named correctly — and at least one applied to a practical surveying scenario.

sections.h: 9.3 What is Data Management?
sections.body:
Data management is the set of policies, processes and professional behaviours that ensure data is handled correctly throughout its entire lifecycle — from the moment it is created to the moment it is securely destroyed.

In surveying practice, the data you handle includes:
— Client personal information: names, contact details, financial position, intentions
— Commercial information: lease details, valuations, rent schedules, transaction details
— Technical data: drawings, surveys, inspection records, site photographs, measurements
— Financial data: fee records, invoices, cost reports
— Health and safety information: RAMS, site inspection records, incident reports

Each category carries different obligations. Personal data carries GDPR obligations. Commercial information carries confidentiality obligations. Technical data carries version control and accuracy obligations.

Assessors want to hear: that you understand data management as something that applies to the specific types of data you handle in your own practice.

sections.h: 9.4 Types of Data
sections.body:
Understanding what type of data you are handling tells you what level of protection is required.

Personal Data is any information that relates to an identifiable individual — a name, an address, an email address, a phone number, a photograph. Under GDPR, personal data must be handled in accordance with the six principles.

Special Category Data is a subset of personal data that is particularly sensitive — health records, biometric data, racial or ethnic origin, religious beliefs. It requires explicit consent or a specific legal basis to process, and carries a higher standard of security obligation.

Commercial Data — lease details, valuations, transaction records, client instructions. Often commercially sensitive and subject to confidentiality obligations even where GDPR does not directly apply.

Technical Data — drawings, models, survey records, measurements. Subject to version control and accuracy obligations and often critically important in dispute situations.

Assessors want to hear: the distinction between personal data and special category data explained clearly — a common area of confusion.

sections.h: 9.5 GDPR Principles — What Assessors Expect
sections.body:
Six principles govern how personal data must be handled under GDPR. Know them precisely — assessors will ask.

1. Lawfulness, fairness and transparency — you must have a lawful basis for processing personal data and must be transparent about how it is used.

2. Purpose limitation — personal data must only be used for the purpose for which it was collected. You cannot collect data for one purpose and use it for another.

3. Data minimisation — collect only the data you actually need. Not everything that might be useful — only what is necessary.

4. Accuracy — keep data up to date. Inaccurate data must be corrected or deleted promptly.

5. Storage limitation — do not retain data indefinitely. When data is no longer needed for its purpose, it should be securely disposed of.

6. Integrity and confidentiality — keep data secure from unauthorised access, loss, destruction or damage.

Assessors want to hear: all six principles named and at least one applied to a real surveying scenario. 'Storage limitation' is the most commonly forgotten — make sure you know it.

sections.h: 9.6 Data Security and Storage
sections.body:
Good data security is a combination of technology and professional discipline. Technology alone is not enough — human behaviour is the most common source of data breaches.

The professional habits that protect data:
— Strong, unique passwords and multi-factor authentication for all work systems
— Approved cloud storage or firm servers — not personal file sharing accounts
— Encrypted devices when working off-site — a stolen unencrypted laptop is a notifiable breach
— Secure transfer methods — never send sensitive client data via personal email
— Regular backups so data cannot be permanently lost
— Controlled access permissions — the least-privilege principle: people should only access the data they need to do their job
— Never use public Wi-Fi for sensitive files without a VPN

Assessors want to hear: specific security practices you apply in your daily work — not a generic list of cybersecurity measures.

sections.h: 9.7 Audit Trails and Version Control
sections.body:
In professional surveying practice, the ability to demonstrate what was agreed, what was delivered and when is often the difference between a defensible position and an indefensible one.

Audit trails require:
— Version-controlled documents with clear version numbers and dates
— Change logs showing what changed, why and when
— Email trails confirming key instructions and decisions
— Dated inspection records and site notes
— Retained evidence of advice given and how clients responded

When a dispute arises — and in a long career it will — the surveyor with clear, complete, contemporaneous records is in a fundamentally different position to the one without them.

Version control also prevents the common error of teams working from different versions of the same document simultaneously. A single master document, clearly version-controlled, prevents errors that are otherwise almost impossible to avoid in complex projects.

Assessors want to hear: that audit trails and version control are professional disciplines you apply as a matter of course.

sections.h: 9.8 Data Retention and Disposal
sections.body:
Data retained for longer than necessary creates risk — regulatory risk under GDPR's storage limitation principle, and practical risk if old, inaccurate information is used in error.

Surveying firms typically retain records for 6 to 15 years depending on the nature of the work, with some categories retained longer for insurance or regulatory reasons.

When data is no longer needed it must be securely disposed of:
— Physical documents: shredded, not recycled or binned
— Electronic files: wiped using approved deletion software, not simply moved to the recycle bin
— Devices being retired: fully wiped before disposal or reuse

Simply deleting a file from your desktop does not destroy it — the data remains recoverable until it is properly overwritten.

Assessors want to hear: that retention and disposal are managed through firm policy — not ad hoc decisions by individual surveyors.

sections.h: 9.9 Data Breaches
sections.body:
A data breach is any incident that results in the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data.

Breaches are not always caused by hackers. The most common causes are: sending an email to the wrong recipient; losing a device; unauthorised access by a third party; accidental deletion; a colleague sharing data they should not have.

When a breach occurs, the correct professional response is:
1. Report internally to your data protection officer or firm management immediately — do not delay
2. Document the breach accurately: what happened, when, what data was affected
3. Follow your firm's data breach procedure
4. Notify the ICO within 72 hours if the breach is likely to result in risk to individuals
5. Notify affected individuals if the breach creates a high risk to their rights
6. Review what happened and implement measures to prevent recurrence

Assessors want to hear: this six-step response described accurately — including the 72-hour ICO notification requirement, which candidates frequently omit.

sections.h: 9.10 Level 1 Requirements and APC Scenarios
sections.body:
At Level 1 the questions are straightforward — but the answers must be precise. The questions assessors ask most frequently: What are the six GDPR principles? What is the 72-hour rule? What do you do when a data breach occurs? What is special category data?

APC Mini Scenarios:

Scenario 1 — Email to wrong recipient.
You accidentally send a confidential valuation report to the wrong client email address.
Strong response: report internally immediately; document the incident; contact the recipient and request deletion; follow firm GDPR breach procedure; notify the ICO if required.

Scenario 2 — Laptop stolen.
Your work laptop is stolen from your car.
Strong response: report to IT immediately to confirm whether the device was encrypted; log the incident; follow the firm's data breach policy; notify the ICO if unencrypted personal data was at risk.

Scenario 3 — Version control failure.
Two teams have been working from different versions of the same report, resulting in contradictory advice being given to different parties.
Strong response: identify the master version; implement version control going forward; communicate a corrected position to all parties; review how the error occurred.

Assessors want to hear: GDPR knowledge applied to practical situations — not recited as a list in isolation from professional context.

sections.h: 9.11 Data Management Module Summary
sections.body:
You should now be able to demonstrate APC Level 1 data management knowledge with confidence:

— The six GDPR principles named and applied
— The distinction between personal data and special category data
— Data security practices described specifically
— Audit trails and version control understood as professional disciplines
— The correct response to a data breach including the 72-hour ICO notification
— Retention and disposal managed through policy not individual judgement

The principle that runs through all of it: protect client data as if it were your own. Accuracy, security and confidentiality are not optional — they are the professional standard.

sections.h: 9.12 RICS AI Standard 2026 — Data and Professional Obligations
sections.body:
The RICS Responsible Use of AI Standard (effective 9 March 2026) introduces specific data management obligations that sit directly within this competency.

What the standard requires:
— Written records of where AI tools are used in professional decision-making
— A risk register documenting AI tool usage, the decisions they inform and the risks they carry
— Client notification when AI outputs materially affect professional services or advice
— Demonstration that human professional judgement — not AI output alone — underpins all professional advice

Why this matters for data management:
AI tools process data. The GDPR obligations that apply to client data do not stop applying because the processing is AI-assisted. A surveyor using an AI tool to analyse comparable evidence, generate a report draft or assess risk is still responsible for:
— The accuracy of the data fed into the AI
— The security of client data processed by or shared with AI tools
— The lawfulness of using client data in AI systems — particularly where the AI tool is a third-party service
— Retaining records of what the AI produced and how professional judgement was applied to review it

Practical steps:
— Check that any AI tools used in practice are listed in your firm's risk register
— Never input personal client data into a public AI tool without checking your firm's policy
— Document clearly in your records where AI was used and what human review was applied
— Be prepared to explain your AI usage to a client if asked

Assessors want to hear: that you understand the intersection of GDPR, data management and the new RICS AI standard — and that you handle AI-assisted work with the same professional discipline you apply to all client data.

sections.h: 9.13 Residual Valuation and Investment Yield — Key Concepts
sections.body:
Residual valuation and investment yields are core topics for Valuation, Commercial Real Estate and Property Finance APC pathways.

The Residual Valuation

A residual valuation is used to assess the value of a development site by working backwards from the completed development value to determine what a developer can afford to pay for the land.

The formula:
Gross Development Value (GDV)
minus Development Costs
minus Developer's Profit
= Residual Land Value

The key inputs and where risk lies:
— GDV — estimated value of the completed development, based on comparable sales or lettings. The greatest risk of error — a small change in GDV has a disproportionate impact on residual land value
— Build costs — typically using BCIS (Building Cost Information Service) rates adjusted for location, specification and market conditions
— Professional fees — typically 10-15% of build costs
— Finance costs — interest on land purchase and build costs during the development period
— Marketing and sales costs — agents' fees, marketing, legal
— Developer's profit — typically 15-25% of GDV for residential, sometimes higher for commercial development reflecting risk
— Contingency — typically 5% of build costs

The yield question — what yield is used?

In a residual valuation for a commercial development, the GDV for the income-producing element (offices, retail, industrial) is calculated by capitalising the estimated rental value (ERV) at an appropriate yield:

GDV = ERV ÷ Yield

The yield used is the market capitalisation rate for that property type and location — reflecting current investment market conditions, covenant strength assumptions, vacancy risk and comparable transactions. For prime Central London offices this might be 4-5%. For secondary regional retail it might be 8-10% or more.

The yield input is critical. A 1% change in yield on a significant commercial development can change GDV by millions of pounds — which flows directly through to residual land value. This is why residual valuations are highly sensitive to yield assumptions and why assessors probe this in Valuation and Property Finance interviews.

In your APC interview: Be ready to explain the residual method from first principles, identify where the greatest sensitivity lies (GDV, and therefore yield), and describe a situation where you applied or reviewed a residual valuation in practice.

Sustainability connection — ESG data and sustainability reporting

ESG (Environmental, Social and Governance) reporting is now a significant data management obligation for larger firms and their clients. Sustainability data — energy consumption, carbon emissions, water use, waste — must be collected, stored, verified and reported to an increasing standard of accuracy. The RICS AI Standard (mandatory March 2026) includes specific provisions around data used in sustainability assessments. When evidencing Data Management at Level 1, you should be able to explain what ESG data is and why its accurate management matters. The depth on sustainability frameworks is in Module 10.


🎓

"Data management is the competency candidates write least confidently — because it sounds technical and dry. But you manage data every day. Tell me how information flows through a typical project you work on — who records what, where does it go, who relies on it. I will help you find the competency hiding in plain sight."

title: Sustainability
intro: Sustainability is no longer a specialism — it is a mainstream professional obligation. Clients, investors, lenders and regulators are all demanding higher standards of environmental performance from built assets. Surveyors who cannot advise on sustainability are already behind the curve.

sections.h: Sprint Sustainability — What the Panel Will Ask You
sections.body:
Sustainability is no longer a specialist topic. It is a mainstream professional obligation. The panel will test it — and they will expect you to know the current landscape, not just the theory.

This is also one of the areas where demonstrating current awareness scores well. If you know what changed in 2025 and 2026, say so.

The three scenarios assessors use most

Scenario 1 — A client asks you to advise on the sustainability performance of a commercial property they are considering acquiring. What would you consider?

The answer assessors want: You consider the EPC rating and its implications for lettability — from April 2023 it has been unlawful to let most commercial properties below EPC E, with further tightening ahead. You consider the building's energy consumption, carbon footprint, potential for improvement and the cost implications of any required upgrades. You flag the risk of stranded assets — properties that may become difficult to let or sell as standards tighten. You advise on the commercial implications alongside the technical ones.

What risks referral: "I would check the EPC." That is the starting point — not a complete answer. The panel wants commercial awareness, not just compliance checking.

Scenario 2 — What is Biodiversity Net Gain and how does it affect development?

The answer assessors want: Biodiversity Net Gain became mandatory for most new developments in England in February 2024 under the Environment Act 2021. Developers must deliver at least a 10% net gain in biodiversity. Gain can be achieved on-site, off-site or through the purchase of statutory biodiversity credits. You understand this affects development viability, land value and planning strategy.

What risks referral: Not knowing BNG is now mandatory or confusing it with general environmental assessment requirements.

Scenario 3 — What is a net zero carbon building and how does it differ from an energy efficient building?

The answer assessors want: An energy efficient building minimises energy consumption. A net zero carbon building goes further — it balances the carbon emitted through its construction, operation and end of life against carbon removed or offset. Operational net zero focuses on in-use energy. Whole life net zero includes embodied carbon in construction materials. This distinction matters because clients increasingly need advice on both operational performance and embodied carbon.

What risks referral: Using "net zero" and "energy efficient" interchangeably. The panel is testing whether you understand the distinction.

Three things every candidate must know cold

  1. EPC minimum standards for commercial lettings — currently EPC E, with further tightening proposed
  2. Biodiversity Net Gain — mandatory 10% net gain for most developments from February 2024
  3. Net zero carbon — the difference between operational carbon and embodied carbon

What the panel is really assessing

Is this candidate keeping up with one of the most rapidly changing areas of property practice? Current awareness in sustainability is a proxy for professional engagement. Show them you are paying attention.

sections.h: 10.1 Introduction
sections.body:
Ten years ago, sustainability was an optional add-on in surveying practice. Today it sits at the centre of investment decisions, planning policy, building regulation and client strategy.

The RICS APC reflects this shift. Sustainability is a mandatory competency — not because it is fashionable but because no surveyor practising today can give commercially credible advice without understanding how sustainability affects the assets they are advising on.

This module gives you the foundation to demonstrate Level 1 knowledge confidently and to connect sustainability to the commercial and valuation advice you give at Level 2.

Assessors want to hear: sustainability knowledge connected to real commercial implications — not abstract environmental principles.

sections.h: 10.2 Learning Outcomes
sections.body:
After this module you will:

— Define sustainability and explain the ESG framework
— Explain why sustainability matters to real estate value, investment decisions and compliance
— Understand the key legislation — Building Regulations, MEES, SECR, Climate Change Act 2008
— Explain EPCs, BREEAM and their commercial implications
— Describe renewable and low carbon technologies at a level appropriate for client advice
— Advise clients on sustainability risks and valuation impacts

Assessors want to hear: sustainability explained in terms of its commercial impact on specific assets and transactions — not as a set of environmental principles.

NABERS UK

NABERS (National Australian Built Environment Rating System) was adapted for the UK commercial office market in 2020. Unlike BREEAM and EPC which measure designed or predicted performance, NABERS UK measures actual operational energy performance — what a building really uses, not what it was designed to use.

NABERS UK Energy ratings run from 1 to 6 stars:
— 1 star: poor performance
— 3 stars: average market performance
— 5-6 stars: market leading, net zero aligned

Why it matters: The performance gap between designed EPC rating and actual energy use has been a significant problem in the commercial sector. NABERS addresses this by measuring metered energy consumption. Institutional investors and major occupiers are increasingly requiring NABERS ratings as part of their ESG due diligence. For candidates on commercial, valuation and project management pathways, NABERS is a live market issue that assessors are testing in 2026.

MEES — Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards

The Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES) Regulations require commercial properties to have a minimum EPC rating of E before they can be let. The trajectory:
— From April 2023: unlawful to continue letting a commercial property with an EPC below E
— Proposed from 2027: minimum rating of C for new lettings
— Proposed from 2030: minimum rating of B for new lettings

For residential properties, MEES applies to new tenancies and renewals. The government's proposed trajectory for residential is EPC C for all rental properties by 2030.

A property below the MEES threshold cannot be lawfully let. Candidates advising landlord clients on investment strategy must factor the cost of EPC improvement works into their advice and cash flow projections.

sections.h: 10.3 What is Sustainability?
sections.body:
The Brundtland Report definition has stood for decades: 'Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.'

In practice, sustainability in the built environment rests on three pillars:

Environmental — carbon emissions, energy consumption, waste, biodiversity, water use. The pillar most visible in building regulation and compliance.

Social — wellbeing, accessibility, community impact, fair working practices. Increasingly important to institutional investors and planning authorities.

Economic — lifecycle cost efficiency, long-term asset value, financial viability. The pillar most directly connected to surveying advice.

Together these three pillars form the ESG framework — Environmental, Social, Governance — which is now the dominant lens through which institutional property investors make decisions.

Assessors want to hear: the three pillars and ESG defined and then applied to how they affect the advice you give in practice.

sections.h: 10.4 Sustainability in Surveying Projects
sections.body:
Sustainability is not something that happens at the end of a project. It needs to be considered from inception — in design, specification, procurement, delivery and long-term operation.

In surveying practice this means:
— Evaluating the long-term environmental and social impact of development proposals
— Specifying materials and systems that reduce whole-life carbon and operational cost
— Ensuring projects comply with current and anticipated future building regulations
— Advising clients on sustainability risks before they become compliance failures
— Understanding how sustainability performance affects the value and lettability of assets

The surveyors who add most value on sustainability are those who connect environmental performance to commercial outcome. An F-rated building is not just environmentally poor — it is potentially unlettable, harder to finance and at risk of becoming a stranded asset.

Assessors want to hear: sustainability considerations connected to specific project types and commercial consequences.

sections.h: 10.5 Why Sustainability Matters in Real Estate
sections.body:
The commercial case for sustainability is now overwhelming — and it affects every surveying discipline.

Poor sustainability performance affects property through:
— Income risk: MEES non-compliance can make a building unlettable, eliminating rental income entirely
— Capital value: stranded assets — buildings too expensive to upgrade or impossible to let — are repriced significantly downward
— Financing: lenders increasingly require minimum EPC ratings before agreeing terms
— Occupier demand: corporate occupiers with ESG commitments will not take leases in buildings that undermine those commitments
— Regulatory risk: tightening MEES standards and net zero obligations create ongoing compliance exposure

The investor who buys a commercially attractive asset today without understanding its sustainability profile may own a stranded asset in five years.

Assessors want to hear: that you understand sustainability as a commercial risk management issue — not just an environmental one.

sections.h: 10.6 Key Legislation and Requirements
sections.body:
Building Regulations (England and Wales)
Part L governs the conservation of fuel and power. Part F governs ventilation. Part O addresses overheating mitigation. Surveyors must understand the compliance principles even if they are not the designer responsible for meeting them.

Energy Act 2011 and MEES (Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards)
Commercial buildings must achieve a minimum EPC rating to be let. The current minimum is E. Higher standards are anticipated ahead of 2030. Surveyors advising on commercial lettings, acquisitions and portfolio management must understand MEES implications thoroughly.

Climate Change Act 2008
The UK's legally binding commitment to net zero by 2050. This drives building regulation, planning policy, investment criteria and client sustainability strategies.

SECR — Streamlined Energy and Carbon Reporting
Applies to large companies. Requires annual disclosure of energy usage, carbon emissions and efficiency measures. Relevant when advising corporate occupier and investor clients.

Assessors want to hear: these pieces of legislation named correctly and connected to specific scenarios in your practice area.

sections.h: 10.7 Energy Act and Performance Certificates
sections.body:
Energy Performance Certificates are one of the most practically relevant sustainability tools in everyday surveying.

What EPCs show: an energy efficiency rating from A (best) to G (worst), based on the building's physical characteristics and systems. They do not show actual energy consumption — they show potential performance based on standard assumptions.

When EPCs are required: on the construction, sale or letting of most buildings. Commercial buildings over 500 square metres frequently visited by the public must also display their certificate.

MEES and its commercial consequences: F and G-rated commercial buildings cannot lawfully be let without first improving their rating to at least E. A landlord with a non-compliant asset faces void risk, compliance cost and potential enforcement action.

Validity: EPCs issued before the 2026 methodology change are valid for ten years. From the second half of 2026, EPCs issued under the new multi-metric methodology are expected to carry a 5-year validity — a significant change that affects letting strategies, acquisition due diligence and portfolio management. If improvements are made to the building the EPC may be out of date and a new one should be commissioned. From 2026 the shorter 5-year validity period makes proactive EPC management even more important for landlords with large portfolios.

Assessors want to hear: EPCs connected to letting risk, acquisition due diligence and valuation — not just defined as a certificate with a rating.

sections.h: 10.8 Energy and Carbon Reporting and Metering and Billing
sections.body:
SECR in practice: large companies meeting qualifying thresholds must report annually on energy consumption, carbon emissions and the efficiency measures they have taken. Surveyors advising corporate occupier clients need to understand these obligations and factor them into accommodation strategy advice.

Heat Network (Metering and Billing) Regulations: apply to landlords and building owners operating district heating or cooling networks. Obligations include metering individual units, notifying OPSS of the network's existence and billing end users based on actual consumption. Relevant when advising on large mixed-use schemes and apartment buildings.

These requirements are becoming increasingly common in urban development contexts. A surveyor who understands them adds commercial value to clients managing complex assets.

Assessors want to hear: awareness of these obligations in the context of assets they are likely to encounter in your specific pathway.

sections.h: 10.9 Climate Change and Sustainability Assessment Tools
sections.body:
The Climate Change Act 2008 establishes the legal framework for the UK's net zero journey. Its 2050 target is legally binding — not a policy aspiration. This means buildings and organisations that do not adapt face increasing regulatory pressure, not decreasing.

BREEAM — Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method
The UK's most widely used sustainability assessment framework for new and refurbished buildings. Assesses performance across energy, water, materials, waste, pollution, transport and land use.

BREEAM ratings from lowest to highest: Pass, Good, Very Good, Excellent, Outstanding.

In practice: institutional investors routinely require Very Good or Excellent ratings for new development acquisitions. Planning authorities in many areas require BREEAM assessment as a condition of consent. Development funding increasingly depends on achieving minimum BREEAM standards.

Assessors want to hear: BREEAM ratings named correctly and connected to real commercial scenarios — not just defined as an assessment framework.

sections.h: 10.10 Renewable and Low Carbon Technologies
sections.body:
Clients ask surveyors about renewable technologies with increasing frequency — and they expect informed, commercially grounded advice.

Technologies surveyors should understand at a basic level:
— Solar PV: photovoltaic panels generating electricity from sunlight. Strong payback in commercial applications with high daytime consumption.
— Air Source Heat Pumps (ASHP): extract heat from outside air to heat buildings. Effective replacement for gas boilers in well-insulated buildings.
— Ground Source Heat Pumps (GSHP): higher efficiency than ASHP but require more space and higher capital cost.
— Battery storage: stores excess renewable energy for use when generation is low. Increasingly cost-effective alongside solar PV.
— Combined Heat and Power (CHP): simultaneous generation of electricity and heat. Suitable for large commercial or residential schemes.

Clients need advice on: feasibility for their specific property; capital cost versus running cost savings; payback period; impact on EPC rating; planning requirements.

Assessors want to hear: that you can advise clients on these options at a commercially aware level — and that you know when to refer to a specialist.

sections.h: 10.11 Valuation and Commercial Implications
sections.body:
The connection between sustainability and value is now well-established in institutional and investment markets — and it is spreading rapidly into all asset classes.

Poor sustainability performance affects value through:
— Reduced income potential: MEES non-compliance eliminates letting income
— Increased void risk: poor-rated buildings take longer to let and attract weaker covenants
— Higher financing costs: lenders apply risk premiums or refuse to lend against non-compliant assets
— Mandatory capital expenditure: upgrade costs to meet current and future standards
— Accelerated obsolescence: assets that cannot be upgraded at viable cost become stranded

Strong sustainability performance affects value through:
— Premium rents from ESG-committed occupiers
— Stronger investor demand and lower exit yields
— Lower operational costs reducing net income erosion

Assessors want to hear: sustainability linked to specific valuation inputs — not just described as a positive attribute.

sections.h: 10.12 APC Advice Examples and Scenarios
sections.body:
Practise these scenarios before your interview. They reflect the type of questions that come up regularly.

Scenario 1 — MEES risk in a portfolio.
A client owns six F and G-rated commercial units. Leases expire within 18 months.
Strong approach: advise that reletting without improvement will be unlawful; assess the upgrade cost for each unit; model the impact on capital value and yield if units remain void; recommend a prioritised improvement programme.

Scenario 2 — New development BREEAM requirement.
A developer client wants BREEAM Very Good for a new commercial scheme. Planning has been secured with BREEAM as a condition.
Strong approach: explain the category structure and performance requirements; advise on the cost premium for Very Good versus Good; confirm the programme implications of the assessment process.

Scenario 3 — EPC impact on acquisition value.
A client is acquiring a commercial asset. Due diligence reveals the EPC rating has dropped from D to F since the previous marketing exercise.
Strong approach: explain the MEES implications for the current letting; quantify the estimated upgrade cost; advise on the programme to achieve compliance; reflect the risk in your acquisition advice and recommended price adjustment.

Assessors want to hear: sustainability advice that is commercially specific — not generic environmental commentary.

sections.h: 10.13 2026 Sustainability Updates — EPC, BNG and Future Homes
sections.body:
Three significant sustainability changes came into effect or are anticipated in 2026 that surveyors must understand.

EPC Methodology Shift (Second Half of 2026)
The current single-metric EPC rating (A–G based on energy cost) is being replaced by a multi-metric approach assessing energy use, carbon emissions and fabric efficiency separately. Key changes:
— EPCs issued under the new methodology will carry a 5-year validity, reduced from 10 years
— Existing EPCs remain valid for their original 10-year term
— The change affects MEES compliance assessments — a building with a current valid EPC may need reassessment sooner under the new regime
— Portfolio managers must audit their EPC expiry dates in light of the new validity period

Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) Expansion (May 2026)
Mandatory BNG requirements — requiring a minimum 10% net gain in biodiversity — have expanded to cover Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects (NSIPs). Previously applying to most planning applications in England, BNG now applies to major infrastructure schemes including roads, rail, energy and water projects. Surveyors advising on development viability or site acquisition in the infrastructure sector must factor BNG delivery costs into appraisals.

Future Homes Standard (Published March 2026 — in force March 2027)
The Future Homes Standard will require new homes to produce 75–80% fewer carbon emissions than homes built under previous regulations. Key implications:
— New residential developments will need to meet significantly higher fabric and services standards
— Gas boilers will effectively be prohibited in new homes
— Development viability and build cost assessments must account for higher specification requirements
— Valuation and investment advice on new residential stock must reflect the higher compliance specification

Assessors want to hear: that you understand how these changes affect practical advice — EPC expiry management, BNG cost in development viability, and the impact of the Future Homes Standard on new residential schemes.

sections.h: 10.14 Paris Agreement, Net Zero Carbon and the UK Policy Framework
sections.body:
The Paris Agreement and Net Zero Carbon framework underpin all UK sustainability legislation and are tested in Sustainability competency interviews across all pathways.

The Paris Agreement 2015

The Paris Agreement is the international climate treaty adopted in December 2015 under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). It is the foundational document of global climate policy and every RICS APC candidate at Level 1 is expected to know what it is and what it commits signatories to.

The key commitment: Limit global average temperature increase to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. The 1.5°C target is the threshold below which the most severe climate impacts can be avoided.

Why 1.5°C matters in practice: The difference between 1.5°C and 2°C warming is significant — more extreme weather events, greater sea level rise, more frequent flooding and more severe impacts on ecosystems. In property terms, assets in flood plains, coastal locations and areas at risk from extreme heat face materially different risk profiles depending on which trajectory the world takes.

Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) — each signatory country submits its own plan for reducing emissions. The UK's NDC is legally enshrined in the Climate Change Act 2008 as amended.

UK Net Zero — Climate Change Act 2008 (amended 2019)

The UK was the first major economy to legislate for net zero. The Climate Change Act 2008, amended in 2019, commits the UK to achieving net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.

Carbon budgets — the UK operates through a system of five-year carbon budgets set by the Climate Change Committee (CCC), an independent statutory advisory body. Each budget sets a ceiling on the total greenhouse gases the UK can emit in that period. The Sixth Carbon Budget (2033–2037) requires a 78% reduction in emissions from 1990 levels.

What net zero means: Net zero does not mean zero emissions — it means any remaining emissions are balanced by carbon removal (through tree planting, carbon capture and storage or other mechanisms). For the built environment, which accounts for approximately 40% of UK carbon emissions, the pathway to net zero requires:
— Elimination of gas boilers in new homes (Future Homes Standard)
— Significant improvement in energy efficiency of existing stock
— Electrification of heating and transport
— Embodied carbon reduction in construction materials

Embodied Carbon vs Operational Carbon

— Operational carbon — emissions from running a building (heating, cooling, lighting). This is what EPC ratings measure.
— Embodied carbon — emissions from manufacturing, transporting and installing building materials, and from demolition and disposal. Increasingly important as operational carbon is reduced through better insulation and electrification — embodied carbon becomes proportionally more significant.

In your APC interview: Know the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C target and why it matters. Know the UK's 2050 net zero commitment and how it is legally structured. Be able to distinguish operational from embodied carbon. Assessors frequently ask: what does net zero mean for the built environment specifically? Have a pathway-relevant answer ready.

🎓
Discuss this with Michael
Sustainability and your professional context

"Sustainability used to be optional. It is not anymore. Tell me about a project where sustainability featured — an EPC, a planning condition, a client's ESG requirement, anything. If it has not come up yet in your work, tell me where you think it will. Either way, we have material to work with."

quiz.q: Which factor is MOST likely to drive a client to improve a building's energy performance?
opts: MEES compliance and reduced operating costs
The number of car parking spaces
