title: Inclusive Professional Practice
intro: Surveyors rarely work alone. Every significant project involves a team — and the quality of that team's communication, coordination and professional culture directly affects the quality of the outcome for the client.

sections.h: Sprint Inclusive Professional Practice — What the Panel Will Ask You
sections.body:
Inclusive Professional Practice covers teamworking, diversity and inclusion. Candidates often underestimate this competency — treating it as a tick-box exercise rather than a genuine professional standard. The panel notices.

This is also one of the competencies where personal experience is most valuable. Real examples from your own practice score far better than theoretical answers.

The three scenarios assessors use most

Scenario 1 — Tell me about a time you worked effectively as part of a team

The answer assessors want: A specific example. Your role in the team, how you contributed, how you communicated, how you handled any disagreement or difficulty, and what the outcome was. The panel is not looking for a perfect team experience — they are looking for self-awareness and professional behaviour.

What risks referral: "I am a good team player." That is not an answer. Give a real example with your specific contribution and what you learned.

Scenario 2 — What does inclusive practice mean to you in a professional context?

The answer assessors want: Inclusion means creating an environment where everyone can contribute effectively regardless of background, identity or circumstance. In practice this means considering accessibility in built environment advice, ensuring diverse perspectives are included in decision-making, and understanding that RICS has specific expectations around inclusive professional practice as a mandatory competency.

What risks referral: A generic answer about treating people equally. The panel wants to see that you understand inclusion as a professional obligation — not just a personal value.

Scenario 3 — A colleague behaves in a way that excludes or undermines a team member. What do you do?

The answer assessors want: You do not ignore it. Depending on severity you address it directly with the colleague, raise it with a line manager or follow your firm's HR procedures. You understand that inclusive practice is everyone's responsibility — not just management's. You document the situation if it is serious.

What risks referral: "I would stay out of it — it is not my business." The panel is testing professional responsibility and ethical awareness.

Two things every candidate must know cold

  1. The Equality Act 2010 — nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation
  2. RICS inclusive environments competency — the mandatory requirement to consider accessibility and inclusion in built environment practice

What the panel is really assessing

Is this candidate the kind of professional who makes teams and workplaces better? Inclusive practice is about character as much as competence. Show them both.

sections.h: 11.1 Introduction
sections.body:
This module covers two distinct but closely related mandatory competencies — Diversity, Inclusion and Teamworking, and Inclusive Environments.

Both competencies are required at Level 1 by every APC candidate regardless of pathway. They share a common thread: how the modern Chartered Surveyor relates to, includes and serves people — whether colleagues within a professional team or users of the built environment.

Competency 1 — Diversity, Inclusion and Teamworking covers how you work within teams, how you contribute to an inclusive workplace culture and how you evidence professional collaboration in your Summary of Experience.

Competency 2 — Inclusive Environments covers how the physical and built environment is designed and delivered to be accessible and usable by everyone — underpinned by Building Regulations Part M, BS 8300 and the Equality Act 2010.

These are two separate competencies in your SoE. You must evidence both individually. This module covers them together because they are complementary — but your Summary of Experience must address each one distinctly.

Both competencies are required to Level 1 — knowledge and understanding. You do not need to evidence personal application (Level 2) or reasoned advice (Level 3) for either of these unless your pathway guide specifies otherwise.

The Nine Protected Characteristics — Equality Act 2010

Every APC candidate must know all nine protected characteristics and be able to give a practical built environment example for each:

1. Age — e.g. ensuring accessible design for elderly occupiers; age-neutral recruitment in surveying firms
2. Disability — physical access, reasonable adjustments, BS 8300 compliance
3. Gender reassignment — inclusive workplace policies, privacy in facilities design
4. Marriage and civil partnership — applies in employment context only
5. Pregnancy and maternity — flexible working, risk assessments for pregnant workers on site
6. Race — inclusive hiring, cultural competency in client service
7. Religion or belief — prayer facilities in building design, flexible working for religious observance
8. Sex — gender pay gap reporting, inclusive workplace culture
9. Sexual orientation — inclusive workplace, no discrimination in service provision

Neurodiversity in the Workplace

Neurodiversity refers to the natural variation in human brain function and behavioural traits — including dyslexia, ADHD, autism spectrum conditions, dyscalculia and dyspraxia. An estimated 15-20% of the UK population is neurodivergent.

For RICS APC candidates:
— Neurodivergent employees may be considered disabled under the Equality Act 2010 where their condition has a substantial and long-term adverse effect on their ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities
— Firms have a duty to make reasonable adjustments — adjusting working patterns, providing technology tools, altering communication styles
— RICS has published guidance on supporting neurodivergent professionals and candidates in the APC process
— Inclusive workplaces that support neurodivergent team members benefit from diverse thinking — relevant to both the Diversity and Teamworking competency and the wider business case for inclusion

Gender Pay Gap Reporting

Employers with 250 or more employees must report their gender pay gap annually to the government. The gender pay gap measures the difference between the average earnings of men and women across an organisation — it is not the same as unequal pay for equal work (which is already unlawful).

What must be reported:
— Mean and median gender pay gap
— Mean and median bonus gap
— Proportion of men and women receiving bonuses
— Proportion of men and women in each pay quartile

The construction and surveying sector has one of the largest gender pay gaps of any profession. RICS publishes its own gender pay gap report annually. Candidates should be aware of the gap in their sector and be able to discuss what their firm is doing to address it.

sections.h: 11.2 Learning Outcomes
sections.body:
After this module you will:

— Explain what effective team-working means in professional practice
— Recognise different team roles and how they contribute to team performance
— Understand the communication behaviours that support collaboration
— Identify barriers to team performance and describe how you have overcome them
— Explain what multi-disciplinary team coordination involves and why it matters
— Demonstrate accountability, reliability and shared ownership
— Answer APC questions at Level 2 with real, specific examples

Assessors want to hear: 'I contributed to a team outcome by doing...' — not 'good teams work by...'

sections.h: PART A — Diversity, Inclusion and Teamworking
11.3 What Team-Working Actually Means
sections.body:
Team-working is not the same as working alongside other people. It is the deliberate, disciplined effort to collaborate towards a shared objective — coordinating information, solving problems jointly, managing risks collectively and maintaining professional relationships even when under pressure.

In surveying practice, teams are rarely formed by choice. You work with whoever the project requires: architects, structural engineers, mechanical and electrical consultants, quantity surveyors, project managers, planning consultants, legal advisers and contractors. Each has different priorities, different professional languages and different ways of working.

The surveyor who adds most value in multi-disciplinary environments is the one who can coordinate effectively across those differences — not just within their own discipline.

Assessors want to hear: examples that involve genuine multi-disciplinary coordination — not just collaboration with colleagues in your own team.

sections.h: 11.4 Why Team-Working Matters
sections.body:
Strong team-working produces better professional outcomes — this is measurable in practice.

When teams work well:
— Fewer errors reach the client because collective review catches them
— Decisions are better because diverse perspectives have been considered
— Programme is maintained because handoffs between disciplines are managed properly
— Client confidence is stronger because they receive coordinated, consistent advice

When teams work poorly:
— Errors arise from poor handoffs between disciplines
— Contradictory advice damages client confidence and professional credibility
— Programme slips because dependencies between disciplines are not managed
— Disputes arise between team members that spill into client-facing situations

Assessors want to hear: a candidate who understands that their team contribution affects client outcomes — not just their own workload.

sections.h: 11.5 Team Roles and Communication
sections.body:
Understanding team roles makes you a more effective colleague and a stronger assessor answer — by recognising what each person contributes and adapting your own contribution accordingly.

Belbin team roles most relevant to surveying:
— Coordinator: keeps the team focused on the objective, manages the agenda and ensures decisions are made
— Implementer: turns plans into action, reliable and methodical
— Completer-Finisher: attention to detail, quality and accuracy — catches errors before they reach the client
— Shaper: drives progress, challenges the team to move forward
— Team Worker: maintains relationships, resolves tensions, supports colleagues
— Specialist: brings specific technical expertise the rest of the team does not have

Team communication best practice:
— Clear, concise updates rather than lengthy reports
— Agreed reporting lines so information reaches the right person
— Accurate handoffs — when your work becomes someone else's input
— Active listening in meetings — not preparing your response while others speak
— Openness to feedback without defensiveness

Assessors want to hear: that you recognise your own Belbin role and can describe how it contributes to the teams you work in.

sections.h: 11.6 Accountability and Shared Ownership
sections.body:
The most effective team members are those who take personal responsibility for their contribution — not just completing their own tasks but understanding how those tasks connect to everyone else's work.

In practice this means:
— Doing what you commit to doing, by the date you committed to
— Updating colleagues when your timescale or output changes — before it becomes a problem for them
— Owning mistakes when they happen and addressing them proactively rather than covering them
— Supporting colleagues who are under pressure, even when it is not strictly your responsibility
— Being the person others can rely on — which is different from being the person who works the most hours

Poor team accountability has direct commercial consequences: missed deadlines, increased client risk, programme delays and budget overruns.

Assessors want to hear: specific examples of accountability in practice — and ideally an example of how you responded when another team member was not delivering.

sections.h: 11.7 Working in Multi-Disciplinary Teams
sections.body:
Most significant surveying projects involve multiple disciplines working in parallel. Managing the interfaces between those disciplines — not just your own discipline's work — is one of the defining skills of a good surveyor.

The challenges of multi-disciplinary coordination:
— Different disciplines have different timescales, priorities and ways of working
— Information produced by one discipline becomes a critical input for another — delays have a cascade effect
— Technical disagreements between disciplines require professional resolution
— Client-facing communications need to be coordinated so the client receives one consistent message

APC candidates who have worked on projects involving multiple consultants have the richest examples to draw on for this competency. If you have coordinated information between an engineer and a contractor, chaired a progress meeting or resolved a design clash between disciplines, that is exactly what assessors want to hear about.

Assessors want to hear: your specific personal contribution to coordinating across disciplinary boundaries — not just a description of the project.

sections.h: 11.8 Barriers to Effective Team-Working
sections.body:
Understanding what goes wrong in teams means you can prevent it — and gives you better APC answers when asked about team challenges.

The most common barriers:
— Poor communication: unclear instructions, inconsistent updates, wrong channels
— Conflicting priorities: team members pulled in different directions by different clients or managers
— Unclear objectives: team members with different understandings of the same goal
— Silo working: disciplines or individuals that hoard information rather than sharing it
— Personality conflicts: differences in working style that become professional friction
— Uneven workload: some team members overwhelmed while others are underutilised

When conflict arises in a team: remain objective; address the issue not the person; focus on the shared professional objective; escalate if the conflict is affecting the project and cannot be resolved at team level.

Assessors want to hear: a specific team challenge you faced, how you responded, and what the outcome was.

sections.h: 11.9 2026 Workforce, Inclusion and the Modern Surveying Team
sections.body:
The 2026 professional and legislative environment has direct implications for team-working, diversity and inclusion in the built environment. Assessors at Level 2 expect candidates to connect this competency to the real professional world they work in.

The RICS Diversity and Inclusion Standard

RICS regulated firms are required to have a written diversity and inclusion policy. For candidates in larger firms, this policy shapes how teams are recruited, managed and developed. At Level 2, a candidate should be able to describe how their firm's approach to diversity and inclusion affected their own team experience — not just describe the policy in the abstract.

The RICS AI Standard and Team Working — March 2026

The mandatory RICS AI Standard (March 2026) creates new team-working obligations. Where AI tools are used in a surveying team, responsibility for outputs remains with the Chartered Surveyor. This creates a clear professional accountability structure within teams — the qualified professional cannot delegate professional responsibility to an AI tool, regardless of how the work is divided. At Level 2, this means evidencing how you personally checked, validated and took responsibility for work even where AI assisted in its production.

Mental Health and Wellbeing in the Built Environment

The built environment profession has significantly higher rates of mental health challenges than the national average. RICS and CIOB have both published guidance on supporting wellbeing in surveying teams. At Level 2, assessors may ask how you have contributed to a positive team environment — including supporting colleagues under pressure, managing workloads fairly and raising concerns appropriately. This is not a soft question — it is a professional one.

Remote and Hybrid Team-Working

The shift to hybrid working has changed how surveying teams operate. Managing relationships across remote and in-person settings, maintaining communication quality and ensuring equitable contribution from all team members regardless of location are practical Level 2 challenges. If your experience includes hybrid or remote team-working, this is directly relevant evidence for this competency.

In your APC interview: Connect your team-working experience to the real professional environment — mention firm-level D&I policy, the RICS AI Standard's accountability framework, and how you personally contributed to team effectiveness rather than simply describing what the team achieved together.

sections.h: 11.10 APC Level 1 Application — What Assessors Expect
sections.body:
Level 1 requires knowledge and understanding — not personal application examples. Most candidates either underprepare or overcomplicate this competency. The standard is accessible; the goal is demonstrating genuine professional awareness.

What assessors want to see at Level 1:
— You can define both competencies in your own words
— You know the key legislative framework: Equality Act 2010 (nine protected characteristics), RICS Diversity and Inclusion Standard, and the professional obligations those create
— You understand why these competencies matter — not just what they require
— You can reference at least one experience from your own practice that shows you have engaged with these issues, even at an observational level

What trips candidates at Level 1:
— Not knowing all nine protected characteristics (every APC candidate must know these)
— Conflating Diversity and Teamworking with Inclusive Environments — they are separate competencies, tested separately
— Describing the competency in purely abstract terms with no reference to your own context
— Treating inclusion as a values question rather than a professional standard

Your SoE statement for Level 1 — Diversity, Inclusion and Teamworking:
Your Summary of Experience entry should:
— Explain what you understand the competency to require
— Reference the Equality Act 2010 and RICS D&I Standard
— Describe at least one specific observation or experience from your own practice — team composition, firm D&I policy, a situation where inclusion affected the outcome
— Reflect briefly on what you learned or observed

Assessors want to hear: 'I understand what inclusive practice requires professionally — here is how I have seen it apply in my own work.'

sections.h: 11.11 APC Scenarios and Practice Questions
sections.body:
Use these to test your Level 1 knowledge before your interview.

Q1. What is the Equality Act 2010, and which nine characteristics does it protect?
Strong answer: The Equality Act 2010 consolidates previous anti-discrimination legislation in England, Scotland and Wales. It protects nine characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. In surveying practice it applies to how we treat clients, colleagues, and the users of the buildings and land we advise on.

Q2. What is the RICS Diversity and Inclusion Standard, and what does it require of firms?
Strong answer: RICS regulated firms must have a written diversity and inclusion policy. The Standard reflects the professional obligation to create inclusive workplaces and to promote diversity in the profession. At a firm level this includes inclusive recruitment, D&I training, and where applicable, gender pay gap reporting for firms of 250 or more employees.

Q3. Describe a time you worked effectively as part of a team. What was your specific contribution?
Strong answer: Use a specific real example. Name your role in the team, describe precisely what you personally did (not what 'we' did), explain how you coordinated with others, and describe the outcome. The panel is not looking for a perfect team experience — they are looking for self-awareness and professional behaviour.

Q4. What would you do if a colleague behaved in a way that excluded another team member?
Strong answer: I would not ignore it. Depending on severity I would address it directly with the colleague in the first instance, and if it continued or was serious I would escalate to my line manager and follow firm HR procedures. Inclusive practice is a professional obligation, not a personal preference — I have a responsibility to contribute to an inclusive working environment.

Q5. What does your firm do to promote diversity and inclusion?
Strong answer: Reference specific initiatives at your firm — D&I policy, gender pay gap reporting, RICS Inclusive Employer Quality Mark if held, flexible working policies, inclusive recruitment practices, or specific programmes your firm runs. Be specific and accurate — generic answers do not score well.

Q6. How does neurodiversity affect how you should manage your team?
Strong answer: Neurodivergent team members may be considered disabled under the Equality Act 2010 where their condition has a substantial and long-term adverse effect on their ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities. Firms have a duty to make reasonable adjustments — which may include adjusting working patterns, communication styles, or providing specific technology tools. Inclusive teams benefit from diverse thinking styles — neurodiversity is a professional asset as well as a legal obligation to accommodate.

Q7. What is the gender pay gap, and why is it relevant to the surveying profession?
Strong answer: The gender pay gap measures the difference between the average earnings of men and women across an organisation. It is not the same as unequal pay for equal work, which is already unlawful. Firms with 250 or more employees must report their gender pay gap annually. The construction and surveying sector has one of the largest gender pay gaps of any profession — RICS publishes its own annual report. A Level 1 candidate should understand this context and be able to describe what their firm is doing to address it.

sections.h: PART B — Inclusive Environments
11.12 What Inclusive Environments Means
sections.body:
Inclusive Environments is a standalone mandatory competency at Level 1 required by every APC candidate on all 22 pathways. It is distinct from Diversity, Inclusion and Teamworking — it specifically concerns the physical and service environment, not internal team culture.

Common mistake: Candidates often conflate Inclusive Environments with Diversity and Teamworking. They are separate competencies. Inclusive Environments is about designing and delivering physical spaces and services that everyone can use. Diversity and Teamworking is about how you work within teams and respect colleagues. Both are mandatory. Both are tested separately.
What Inclusive Environments Means

An inclusive environment recognises and accommodates differences in the way people use the built and natural environment. It facilitates dignified, equal and intuitive use by everyone. It does not physically or socially separate, discriminate or isolate. It readily accommodates and welcomes diverse user needs.

The CIC Essential Principles guide defines an inclusive environment as one that can be accessed and used safely, easily and with dignity by everyone — regardless of age, disability, gender, ethnicity or any other characteristic.

Why this matters for APC candidates:
You do not need to have personally designed an accessible building to evidence this competency at Level 1. You need to demonstrate that you understand what inclusive design means in the context of the property work you do and why it matters. Whether you work in valuation, property management, commercial agency or construction, inclusive environments has a direct bearing on your professional practice.

sections.h: 11.13 The Three Principles of Inclusive Design
sections.body:
The three principles of inclusive design provide a framework for thinking about whether an environment meets the inclusive standard — and for answering APC interview questions about what inclusive design actually means.

1. Inclusive
Usable by all people, to the greatest extent possible, without the need for adaptation or specialised design. The goal is a single solution that works for everyone — not separate provision for disabled users. Where a ramp and steps serve the same entrance, one solution would be better than two.

2. Responsive
Taking account of what people say they need and prefer. Inclusive design is not design imposed on behalf of users — it listens to the diversity of user needs and incorporates them. Consultation with disabled users, older people and other groups whose needs may differ is part of responsive design.

3. Flexible
Offering a choice of means of use where a single solution cannot accommodate all users. Where one solution cannot serve everyone, flexibility — multiple routes, adjustable fittings, alternative formats — is the next best standard.

In practice: These principles apply beyond physical buildings. A service environment — a conveyancing process, a property management service, a valuation methodology — can also be more or less inclusive in how it reaches and serves diverse users.

Assessors want to hear: A candidate who can articulate the three principles and connect them to real built environment examples from their own practice.

sections.h: 11.14 Building Regulations Part M
sections.body:
Part M of the Building Regulations sets the minimum legal requirements for accessibility in new buildings and extensions in England. It is the baseline legal standard — compliance is mandatory; going beyond it is best practice (covered by BS 8300).

Scope of Part M:
Part M applies to:
— All new buildings (dwellings and non-dwellings)
— Extensions to existing buildings
— Changes of use where access requirements are relevant

It does not automatically apply to existing buildings being retained without works, though the Equality Act 2010 imposes separate obligations on service providers with existing premises (see section 11.17).

The two parts of Part M:
— Part M4 — applies to dwellings (residential). Divided into three categories.
— Part M (non-dwellings) — applies to offices, retail, schools, public buildings, industrial buildings and all other buildings that are not dwellings.

Non-dwelling requirements under Part M:
For buildings other than dwellings, Part M requires that reasonable provision be made for people to access and use the building. This includes accessible entrances, sanitary accommodation, and internal circulation. The standard is 'reasonable provision' — the Approved Document M gives detailed guidance on what this means in practice.

Approved Document M:
The Approved Document to Part M is the technical guidance document that shows how compliance can be achieved. For APC candidates it is not necessary to memorise the technical dimensions, but you should understand that the Approved Document exists, what it covers, and that its guidance represents one way of demonstrating compliance with the regulation.

Assessors want to hear: A clear distinction between Part M4 (dwellings) and Part M (other buildings), and an understanding that Part M is a minimum legal standard, not a design aspiration.

sections.h: 11.15 Part M4 — The Three Dwelling Categories
sections.body:
Part M4 divides accessible dwelling standards into three categories. Every APC candidate must be able to describe all three and explain when each applies.

Category 1 — Visitable Dwellings
The minimum standard required for all new dwellings in England. A visitor using a wheelchair can reach and enter the building and use the entrance storey. Level or ramped access to the entrance, a step-free threshold, and minimum door widths are required. Category 1 is the default — it applies unless planning requires a higher standard.

Category 2 — Accessible and Adaptable Dwellings
A higher standard designed for dwellings that can be adapted over time to meet the changing needs of occupiers — particularly relevant for ageing populations. Requirements include step-free access throughout, wider doorways, accessible bathroom provision, and design that allows for future adaptation without structural works. Category 2 must be specified in planning conditions — it does not apply by default. Many local authorities include Category 2 requirements in their housing policies, particularly for affordable housing or housing for older people.

Category 3 — Wheelchair User Dwellings
The highest standard — fully designed for wheelchair users, whether in a wheelchair at the time of occupation or likely to need one. Requires all rooms on a step-free level, wider circulation spaces, accessible kitchen and bathroom design, and features that allow full independent use by a wheelchair user. Category 3 dwellings must be specified in planning conditions. They are typically required as a proportion of a larger residential development.

APC interview tips:
Candidates regularly confuse Category 2 and Category 3. Remember: Category 2 can be adapted for wheelchair users in the future. Category 3 is designed for wheelchair users from the outset. The planning trigger is the key distinction — neither Category 2 nor 3 applies by default.

Assessors want to hear: The name and description of each category, the key distinguishing features, and an understanding that Categories 2 and 3 must be triggered by planning conditions.

sections.h: 11.16 BS 8300:2018 — Design of an Accessible Built Environment
sections.body:
BS 8300:2018 is the British Standard providing guidance on the design of buildings and their approaches to meet the needs of disabled people. It goes beyond the minimum requirements of Part M and represents best practice — the standard a well-designed building should aspire to achieve.

Key areas covered by BS 8300:
— Accessible car parking and approach routes — number of accessible spaces, surface, gradient, lighting, route from parking to entrance
— Entrances — level or ramped access, automatic doors, clear widths, door furniture, thresholds, lobby design
— Internal circulation — corridor widths, passing places, turning circles for wheelchair users, floor surface textures, changes in level
— Sanitary facilities — accessible WC layout and dimensions, grab rail positions, alarm systems, ambulant accessible WCs
— Wayfinding — signage, layout logic, contrast for visually impaired users, tactile paving and surfaces
— Acoustic design — background noise levels, reverberation for hearing impaired users, hearing loop provision
— Visual environment — lighting levels, tonal contrast between surfaces, avoidance of glare

The relationship between BS 8300 and Part M:
Part M is the legal minimum. BS 8300 is the aspirational standard. A building complying with Part M may still fall short of BS 8300. In practice, many clients, occupiers and local authorities specify BS 8300 compliance — particularly for public buildings, offices and healthcare premises. As a surveyor advising on design, specification, or asset management, understanding where the two standards differ matters.

Assessors want to hear: A clear understanding that BS 8300 goes beyond Part M, the key areas it covers, and why it matters in practice.

sections.h: 11.17 The Equality Act 2010 — Reasonable Adjustments
sections.body:
The Equality Act 2010 imposes a duty on service providers to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. This duty is separate from Building Regulations — it applies to how services are delivered, not just how buildings are constructed.

The three types of reasonable adjustment:
1. Changing a provision, criterion or practice — adjusting policies, processes or ways of working that put disabled people at a disadvantage
2. Providing auxiliary aids and services — such as alternative formats (large print, audio, braille), assistance, or technology
3. Physical features — removing or altering physical features that make a building harder to use, or providing a reasonable means of avoiding them

Key features of the duty:
— The duty is anticipatory — firms must think about adjustments before a disabled person requests them. Waiting for a disabled client or customer to complain before acting is not compliance.
— The standard is reasonableness — what is reasonable depends on the nature of the service, the size and resources of the provider, and the practicality of the adjustment. Cost is a factor, but not an absolute defence.
— The duty is ongoing — as technology, building conditions and user needs change, the obligation to adjust continues.

In a surveying context:
— A surveying firm must consider whether its offices are accessible to disabled clients
— Written communications should be available in accessible formats on request
— A property manager advising a client on commercial premises must consider the Equality Act obligations on their client as a service provider
— A valuer advising on an asset let to service providers should flag Equality Act compliance as part of their assessment

Assessors want to hear: The anticipatory nature of the duty, the three types of adjustment, and at least one practical built environment example.

sections.h: 11.18 Inclusive Design in Commercial and Public Buildings
sections.body:
The application of inclusive design principles to commercial and public buildings goes well beyond physical access ramps and wheelchair-accessible toilets. A complete inclusive design strategy addresses how all types of users experience the built environment — including those with visual, hearing, cognitive, and mobility impairments.

Commercial offices:
— Step-free access from street to all occupied floors
— Accessible reception and visitor facilities
— Sufficient accessible toilet provision (not just a single 'disabled toilet' that is used for other purposes)
— Meeting rooms with hearing loops
— Wayfinding systems with tonal contrast and clear typography
— Parking provision with accessible bays at appropriate size and proximity to entrance

Retail premises:
— Level thresholds and wide enough aisles for wheelchair users
— Checkout counters at accessible height
— Visual merchandising and signage accessible to visually impaired customers
— Clear and accessible changing rooms
— Customer assistance policies that are proactively offered, not just available on request

Public and civic buildings:
— Highest standard of Part M and BS 8300 compliance expected
— Accessible hearing loops throughout public spaces
— Multiple wayfinding methods (visual, tactile, audio) where needed
— Emergency evacuation provision for wheelchair users (evacuation lifts or refuge areas)

Common surveying scenarios where inclusive design is relevant:
— Due diligence on a commercial acquisition: identify accessibility gaps that may affect value or create legal exposure
— Property management: ensure accessible WCs are maintained, not repurposed as storage
— Lease review: identify tenant obligations relating to access compliance
— Refurbishment advice: trigger for bringing non-compliant elements up to Part M / BS 8300 standard

Assessors want to hear: Examples from your own practice where inclusive design considerations affected advice, specification, or asset assessment.

sections.h: 11.19 Common Mistakes and APC Pitfalls — Inclusive Environments
sections.body:
Inclusive Environments is a competency that candidates frequently underestimate. These are the most common errors seen in APC interviews.

Mistake 1 — Conflating Inclusive Environments with Diversity and Teamworking
They are separate mandatory competencies. Inclusive Environments is about the built and physical environment. Diversity and Teamworking is about internal team culture and professional conduct. Both appear separately in the APC pathway guides and must be evidenced separately in the SoE.

Mistake 2 — Only mentioning wheelchair access
Inclusive environments address a wide range of users and impairments — visual, hearing, cognitive, age-related changes, temporary conditions. A candidate who only talks about wheelchair ramps is demonstrating a narrow understanding. APC panels will test whether you can think more broadly.

Mistake 3 — Treating Part M as the ceiling rather than the floor
Part M is the minimum legal standard. A well-designed inclusive building goes further — BS 8300 represents best practice. Assessors expect candidates to understand the relationship between the two and to know that compliance with Part M does not necessarily mean an inclusive outcome.

Mistake 4 — Not knowing the Part M4 categories
Every APC candidate must be able to describe Category 1, 2 and 3 dwellings accurately. This is a standard interview question for any candidate who works in residential property, housing or development. Confusing Category 2 and Category 3 is a common error.

Mistake 5 — Missing the Equality Act's anticipatory duty
The duty to make reasonable adjustments is anticipatory — it does not wait for a disabled person to complain. Candidates who describe only reactive responses will not score well. The panel is testing whether you understand that this obligation is proactive.

Mistake 6 — No connection to personal experience
Even at Level 1, candidates should be able to reference at least one observation or experience from their own practice. 'I understand the theory but have no experience of it' is not a strong answer. Even indirect experience — reading a report, attending a CPD, advising a client on compliance — is sufficient to connect the competency to your own work.

sections.h: 11.20 APC Level 1 Application — Inclusive Environments
sections.body:
What Level 1 looks like in your SoE

At Level 1 you must demonstrate knowledge and understanding — not personal application. You do not need to have personally designed an accessible building. Your Summary of Experience entry for Inclusive Environments should:
— Reference the regulatory framework: Building Regulations Part M, BS 8300:2018, and the Equality Act 2010
— Explain what inclusive design means in the context of your work and why it matters
— Show awareness of the diversity of user needs — not just wheelchair users
— Connect the competency to at least one observation or experience from your own professional practice

Example SoE approach (Level 1):
'During my work on [project type] I developed an understanding of the Inclusive Environments competency. I understand that Part M of the Building Regulations sets minimum access standards for new buildings and dwellings, with BS 8300:2018 representing best practice. I understand the Equality Act 2010's anticipatory duty on service providers to make reasonable adjustments. I have observed [specific example — accessible WC provision on a site visit / reviewing access compliance for a client / CPD training on inclusive design] and understand how these requirements apply to the built environment work I do.'\

In your APC interview — key questions to prepare:
— What is an inclusive environment?
— What legislation governs accessible design?
— What is the difference between Part M Category 1 and Category 2?
— What does the Equality Act require of a surveying firm in terms of service delivery?
— What is BS 8300, and how does it relate to Part M?
— Give an example from your work where inclusive design was relevant

Senior Professional Candidates — Managing People

For candidates on the Senior Professional route only, Managing People is an additional mandatory competency. It covers leadership styles and motivation techniques, managing performance, dealing with underperformance, appraisal processes and employment law awareness. If you are on the Senior Professional route, ensure your SoE includes evidence of managing people at a senior level — not just working within a team.

🎓
Discuss this with Michael
Inclusive practice and teamworking

"The Inclusive Professional Practice competency asks something most candidates find unexpectedly personal — it asks you to think about who gets left out. Tell me about a time you noticed that something — a space, a process, a team — was not working for everyone equally. That observation is the beginning of your evidence."

sections.h: 11.21 2026 Context — Inclusive Environments
sections.body:
The 2026 regulatory and professional environment includes several developments directly relevant to the Inclusive Environments competency.

EPC Validity Changes — H2 2026
New EPC regulations expected in the second half of 2026 will affect how energy performance is assessed and reported. While this primarily affects the Sustainability competency, EPC reforms also intersect with accessible housing standards — particularly where energy efficiency retrofits affect accessibility features (ramps, threshold levels, door widths) in existing dwellings.

RICS AI Standard — March 2026
The mandatory RICS AI Standard (March 2026) has implications for inclusive environments work. Where AI tools are used in property assessment, accessibility analysis, or inclusive design review, the Chartered Surveyor remains responsible for validating outputs. AI-generated accessibility reports must be checked against Part M, BS 8300 and the Equality Act standard before being relied upon in professional advice.

Building Remediation Bill — 2026
The Building Remediation Bill, announced in the King's Speech May 2026, accelerates remediation requirements for buildings with unsafe cladding. Where remediation works are undertaken, any changes to building fabric — including external staircases, entrances and circulation routes — must maintain or improve accessibility standards. Responsible persons must consider inclusive design obligations when planning remediation schemes.

Renters' Rights Act 2025 and the PRS Database
The Renters' Rights Act 2025 introduces a mandatory PRS database with a phased launch from late 2026. Landlords registering rental properties must provide compliance information that includes whether the property meets fitness for habitation standards. Accessible design requirements for rental properties, and the duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled tenants, remain in effect under the Equality Act 2010.

Awaab's Law — Social Rented Sector from October 2025
Awaab's Law (stage one) came into force for the social rented sector in October 2025, requiring social landlords to investigate and fix hazardous conditions within specific timeframes. Significant hazard work under stage two extends the regime from October 2026. While primarily focused on damp and mould, Awaab's Law reinforces the fitness for habitation standard that underpins inclusive, safe housing — relevant to any candidate working in social housing or residential property management.

sections.h: COMBINED ASSESSMENT
11.22 50 APC Questions — Diversity, Inclusion, Teamworking and Inclusive Environments
sections.body:
Use these questions to test your combined understanding of both mandatory competencies. These replicate the style and difficulty of questions you may face in your APC interview.

Part A — Diversity, Inclusion and Teamworking

1. Name all nine protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010.
2. What is the RICS Diversity and Inclusion Standard, and what does it require of regulated firms?
3. Describe the difference between direct discrimination and indirect discrimination under the Equality Act.
4. What is neurodiversity, and how does it interact with an employer's duty to make reasonable adjustments?
5. What is the gender pay gap? How is it measured, and which employers must report it?
6. Describe a specific team situation where you personally contributed to a positive team outcome. What was your role?
7. A colleague is consistently not delivering to deadline and it is affecting the project team. What do you do?
8. How does hybrid and remote working affect team cohesion and inclusive participation? What can a team lead do to mitigate this?
9. What does the RICS AI Standard (March 2026) mean for team accountability where AI tools are used?
10. How does mental health and wellbeing affect professional teams in the built environment sector? What are the professional obligations?
11. Describe the Belbin team role you most identify with. Why, and how does it affect how you contribute?
12. What is the difference between Diversity, Inclusion and Teamworking as a mandatory competency, and the values of diversity and inclusion generally?
13. A new team member is being excluded from informal communications and social events. What do you do?
14. What is an inclusive workplace, and how does the physical built environment of an office affect inclusion?
15. How do you manage conflicting priorities between disciplines in a multi-disciplinary team?
16. What does accountability within a professional team look like in practice?
17. A client has received conflicting advice from two members of your team. How do you respond?
18. How has the professional environment changed since 2020 in terms of diversity and inclusion expectations in the built environment sector?
19. What is the difference between equality and equity? How do both concepts apply to professional practice?
20. What would you say to a senior colleague who dismisses diversity and inclusion as irrelevant to client service?
21. How do you ensure that team decisions reflect diverse perspectives, particularly in a time-pressured project environment?
22. What is the RICS Inclusive Employer Quality Mark, and what does it signal about a firm's commitment to D&I?
23. Describe a time you received constructive criticism in a team setting. How did you respond?
24. What is unconscious bias, and how might it affect decision-making in a surveying team?
25. How does marriage and civil partnership as a protected characteristic apply in an employment context in professional practice?

Part B — Inclusive Environments

26. Define an inclusive environment. What makes a built environment inclusive?
27. What are the three principles of inclusive design?
28. What does Building Regulations Part M require? To which buildings does it apply?
29. What is Part M4 Category 1? What does it require?
30. What is Part M4 Category 2, and when does it apply?
31. What is Part M4 Category 3? How does it differ from Category 2?
32. What is BS 8300:2018? How does it relate to Part M?
33. Name four areas covered by BS 8300:2018.
34. What is the Equality Act 2010's reasonable adjustment duty for service providers? What makes it anticipatory?
35. Name the three types of reasonable adjustment under the Equality Act 2010.
36. A client's office entrance has a step that prevents wheelchair access. What are their obligations under the Equality Act?
37. You are advising on a refurbishment. How do you ensure the scheme meets accessible design standards?
38. What is a 'hearing loop' and when should it be provided?
39. What are the emergency evacuation implications of inclusive design in a multi-storey office building?
40. You are conducting due diligence on a commercial building acquisition. What accessible design checks would you carry out?
41. A property manager has converted the accessible WC to a storage room. What is the risk?
42. What is tactile paving, and when is it used in inclusive built environment design?
43. How does inclusive design apply to a lease renewal negotiation where the tenant is a service provider?
44. What is the CIC Essential Principles guide on inclusive design?
45. How does inclusive environments differ from designing for disability? Why does the distinction matter?
46. A planning authority requires 10% of units on a new development to be Category 3. What does this mean for the developer?
47. What visual design features support visually impaired users in a commercial building?
48. Describe how an inclusive environments review might form part of a dilapidations assessment.
49. How does the Renters' Rights Act 2025 interact with the duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled tenants in the private rented sector?
50. A surveying firm is asked to advise on the accessibility of a listed building. What are the key constraints and obligations?

sections.h: 11.23 Module Quiz — Combined Competency Assessment
sections.body:
The interactive quiz below tests your knowledge of both mandatory competencies — Diversity, Inclusion and Teamworking, and Inclusive Environments. Complete all questions and submit to see your score and correct answers.

The quiz covers:
— The Equality Act 2010 — protected characteristics and reasonable adjustment duty
— Team-working principles and professional conduct
— Building Regulations Part M and Part M4 categories
— BS 8300:2018 — design of an accessible built environment
— APC application — what Level 1 evidence looks like in practice

If any questions expose gaps in your knowledge, return to the relevant section above and review the content before your interview.

quiz.q: A team member misses a deadline, impacting the client deliverable. What is the MOST appropriate team-focused action?
opts: Raise it constructively and work together to replan the deliverable
Ignore it — it will resolve itself
Escalate immediately to senior management
Report it to the client directly

quiz.q: Your team produces conflicting messages to the client. What should you do FIRST?
opts: Avoid involvement
Clarify roles, agree a single coordinated message, and communicate jointly
Send your own version to correct everyone
Ask the client which version they prefer

quiz.q: A contractor highlights a design issue that affects structural load. What is your BEST team-working response?
opts: Tell the client it's not your responsibility
Urgently consult the structural engineer and coordinate a joint response
Advise the contractor to continue work
Wait for the next project meeting to raise it

quiz.q: Which behaviour MOST improves team performance?
opts: Sharing updates regularly and proactively
Avoiding meetings
Withholding information to avoid criticism
Completing tasks independently without updating others

quiz.q: Two colleagues disagree strongly over survey methodology. What should you do?
opts: Take sides with whoever you prefer working with
Facilitate a discussion focused on evidence, scope and objectives
Tell both colleagues to stop talking about it
Escalate to senior management immediately

quiz.q: Your team works across different locations. What supports effective team-working?
opts: Clear communication channels and agreed check-in points
No scheduled meetings to avoid disruption
Ad-hoc updates only when problems arise
Each person working completely independently

quiz.q: A colleague asks you for help with a task they don't understand. What is the MOST team-oriented response?
opts: Support them by explaining the task and helping them learn
Give them the answer so they stop asking questions
Tell them to only speak to senior staff
Ignore the request and focus on your own work

quiz.q: What BEST supports a positive team culture?
opts: Avoiding feedback discussions
Recognising success, sharing learning, and encouraging open communication
Blaming colleagues when issues arise
Keeping information to yourself

quiz.q: A new colleague joins your team and is unfamiliar with internal systems. What is the BEST team-working approach?
opts: Let them figure it out over several weeks
Provide guidance, share key documents, and support their onboarding
Tell them to search online for training videos
Ask them to shadow someone without any guidance

quiz.q: During a valuation project, another team member incorrectly interprets a lease clause. What should you do?
opts: Correct the error privately and explain the rationale, then update the team
Ignore it as it's not your responsibility
Publicly criticise them in the next team meeting
Rewrite their work without telling them

title: Revision, Mock Tests & APC Simulation
intro: You have covered all eleven mandatory competencies. Now it is time to stop studying and start performing. This module is not about learning new content — it is about pressure-testing what you know until you can deliver it under interview conditions without hesitation.

sections.h: 12.0 Sprint Learners — Start Here
sections.body:
This section is for candidates on the Final APC sprint.

Your recommended sprint sequence:

1. Work through the revision sheets in order (sections 12.2–12.11) — one competency at a time. Each sheet gives you the five things you must know, what assessors probe, and the common reasons candidates are referred. Treat each one as your pre-interview checklist.

2. Use Michael to go deeper — if a revision sheet raises a question or an area feels less secure, use Michael to explore it further. It can help you build and sharpen your answers across any competency.

3. Practise the mock interview multiple times — select your RICS pathway and run the full 60-minute simulator. The questions change each session. Most sprint candidates should run it at least three times before their assessment.

4. Write your eight assignment answers (section 12.13) — these are the questions most likely to reflect what your panel will probe. Write them out in full, time yourself, and review your reasoning.

A note on the revision sheets: they are designed as focused recall tools, not as standalone teaching. If you find an area where you want to build more depth, Michael is there to assist — ask it to explain a concept, challenge your answer, or work through a scenario with you.

Six focused weeks is enough to make a significant difference. Use every session with intention.

Assessors want to hear: structured, confident answers with real examples. That is what this module builds.

sections.h: 12.1 Introduction — Module 12 is Not Revision. It is Rehearsal.
sections.body:
There is a significant difference between knowing the material and being able to deliver it confidently when an assessor follows up your answer with 'And why did you advise that?' or 'What would you have done differently?'

The candidates who pass APC comfortably are those who have rehearsed — out loud, under time pressure, with structured answers. The candidates who are referred are often those whose knowledge was sound but whose delivery was hesitant, unstructured or unable to cope with probing follow-up questions.

This module gives you:
— Revision sheets for each of the eleven mandatory competencies
— The complete 60-minute mock interview structure
— The AI Mock Interview Simulator — timed, scored, specific to your pathway
— Level 3 thinking practice across all competencies
— The final eight APC assignment questions that mirror real interview scenarios

Use every tool in this module. Your APC is closer than you think.

sections.h: 12.2 Revision Sheet 1 — Ethics, Conduct and Professionalism
sections.body:
Revision sheet — not a teaching module. This sheet assumes you have existing knowledge of this competency from your professional experience and training. It is a pre-assessment reference to sharpen recall and highlight what assessors probe. If you are not yet confident in the depth of this competency, the full programme covers it in detail across dedicated modules.
Definition: Understanding and applying the RICS Rules of Conduct, Ethical Standards and professional behaviour expected of all members of the profession.

Level 1: Know the five Ethical Standards, the Rules of Conduct, the CHP, PII requirements, and conflicts of interest management.
Level 2: Show how you applied ethical judgement in a real professional situation.
Level 3: Give clear, reasoned, RICS-compliant advice on an ethical dilemma — weighing options and justifying your position.

Five things you must know without hesitation:
1. The five Ethical Standards: Integrity, High Standard of Service, Promote Trust, Treat Others with Respect, Take Responsibility
2. The RICS Rules of Conduct 2022
3. How to identify and manage a conflict of interest
4. The two-stage Complaints Handling Procedure
5. PII requirements including run-off cover

What assessors probe: conflicts of interest, pressure to amend advice, error discovery, gifts and hospitality, colleague misconduct.

Common referral reasons: no real examples given; forgetting to reference RICS rules; showing commercial bias over public interest.

The rule that underpins everything: public interest always overrides commercial interest.

2026 Updates: RICS President as of January 2026: Nick Maclean OBE RD FRICS (144th President). RICS Responsible Use of AI Standard (March 2026): mandatory written records, risk registers and client notification for AI use. Updated CPD Framework: 3-year rolling requirement with mandatory topics including Ethics, Sustainability and AI.

2025 Update — ECCTA Failure to Prevent Fraud (in force 1 September 2025)
The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 Failure to Prevent Fraud offence came into force 1 September 2025. Large organisations (250+ employees, £36m+ turnover or £18m+ balance sheet) are criminally liable if an associated person commits fraud for the organisation's benefit and the organisation lacked reasonable prevention procedures. The six prevention principles: Proportionate Procedures, Top-Level Commitment, Risk Assessment, Due Diligence, Communication and Training, Monitoring and Review. Assessors are testing this in autumn 2026.

sections.h: 12.3 Revision Sheet 2 — Client Care
sections.body:
Revision sheet — not a teaching module. This sheet assumes you have existing knowledge of this competency from your professional experience and training. It is a pre-assessment reference to sharpen recall and highlight what assessors probe. If you are not yet confident in the depth of this competency, the full programme covers it in detail across dedicated modules.
Definition: Delivering a professional service by understanding client needs, setting clear expectations, communicating effectively and managing instructions from first contact to completion.

Level 1: Client lifecycle, scope of service, complaints handling, service level agreements, terms of engagement.
Level 2: Show how you managed a real instruction — setting scope, managing expectations and handling a variation or complaint.

Five things you must know without hesitation:
1. The client lifecycle: Enquiry, Proposal, Instruction, Delivery, Handover, Aftercare
2. The golden rule: if it is not written and recorded, it is not agreed
3. The two-stage CHP and when each stage applies
4. How to handle a scope variation correctly
5. How to manage a client complaint professionally

What assessors probe: how you set scope, how you handled a difficult client situation, how you managed a variation, what your CHP process involves.

Common referral reasons: no mention of written scope; unable to explain the CHP; no real examples of managing expectations under pressure.

The principle that underpins everything: clear scope plus clear communication equals strong client care.

2025 Update — Renters' Rights Act 2025
Section 21 no-fault evictions abolished. All tenancies become periodic. Rent increases restricted to once per year. Private Rented Sector Database introduced — landlords must register or face criminal liability. Assessors ask: how does the abolition of Section 21 affect your advice to a residential landlord client?

sections.h: 12.4 Revision Sheet 3 — Communication and Negotiation
sections.body:
Revision sheet — not a teaching module. This sheet assumes you have existing knowledge of this competency from your professional experience and training. It is a pre-assessment reference to sharpen recall and highlight what assessors probe. If you are not yet confident in the depth of this competency, the full programme covers it in detail across dedicated modules.
Definition: The ability to communicate professionally in writing, verbally and through non-verbal means, and to negotiate effectively, ethically and in the client's interest.

Level 1: Communication principles, barriers to communication, PREP framework, negotiation styles, BATNA.
Level 2: Real examples of professional communication and negotiation — fee discussions, difficult conversations, written advice.

Five things you must know without hesitation:
1. PREP: Point, Reason, Example, Point
2. BATNA: Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement
3. Active listening and why it matters in negotiation
4. The five negotiation styles — and why collaborative is preferred
5. The discipline of following up every significant verbal discussion in writing

What assessors probe: a specific negotiation you led, how you structured your preparation, how you handled the other party's position, what the outcome was.

Common referral reasons: PREP not used in answers; unable to describe a specific negotiation; no evidence of written follow-up discipline.

The principle that underpins everything: effective communication is structured, clear and always confirmed in writing.

2025 Update — IPMS: All Buildings (post-June 2025)
RICS archived its Property Measurement 2nd Edition on 9 June 2025. IPMS: All Buildings (January 2023) is now the consolidated standard. Members must document which measurement basis has been used on any instruction. GEA = gross external. GIA = gross internal (IPMS 2). NIA = net internal usable (IPMS 3). 1 sq m = 10.764 sq ft. 1 hectare = 2.471 acres.

sections.h: 12.5 Revision Sheet 4 — Health and Safety
sections.body:
Revision sheet — not a teaching module. This sheet assumes you have existing knowledge of this competency from your professional experience and training. It is a pre-assessment reference to sharpen recall and highlight what assessors probe. If you are not yet confident in the depth of this competency, the full programme covers it in detail across dedicated modules.
Definition: Understanding legal duties, identifying hazards, assessing risks and implementing safe working practices in all surveying activities.

Level 1: Key legislation, CDM 2015 roles, risk assessment methodology, RAMS, incident reporting obligations.
Level 2: Show how you applied H&S in real practice — pre-visit preparation, site behaviour, RAMS review, PPE.

Five things you must know without hesitation:
1. Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 — the legal foundation
2. CDM 2015 — your role as a surveyor within the regulatory framework
3. The 5-step risk assessment model
4. RAMS: what they are, what they must contain, what to do if they are missing
5. RIDDOR: seven consecutive days incapacitation triggers reporting — not 24 hours

What assessors probe: a specific site visit from an H&S perspective, how you handle RAMS, what you do when hazards are identified, CDM roles.

Common referral reasons: unable to explain RAMS; citing 24 hours instead of seven days for RIDDOR; no specific site visit examples.

The principle that underpins everything: safety is a legal duty — not an optional professional courtesy.

2026 Updates: Building Safety Regulator is now fully independent (January 2026). New Building Safety Levy applies to most new residential development in England from October 2026. Two staircase rule mandatory for new residential buildings over 18 metres from September 2026.

sections.h: 12.6 Revision Sheet 5 — Accounting Principles and Procedures
sections.body:
Revision sheet — not a teaching module. This sheet assumes you have existing knowledge of this competency from your professional experience and training. It is a pre-assessment reference to sharpen recall and highlight what assessors probe. If you are not yet confident in the depth of this competency, the full programme covers it in detail across dedicated modules.
Definition: Understanding the financial concepts, statements and processes that underpin commercially aware advice in surveying.

Level 1 only — but explanations must be confident and contextualised.

Five things you must know without hesitation:
1. The three financial statements: P&L (performance), Balance Sheet (position at a point in time), Cash Flow (money moving in and out)
2. The difference between cash and profit — and why a profitable business can still fail
3. Variance analysis: Actual minus Budget. Positive variance is better than budget.
4. Capital allowances: available on qualifying plant and machinery in commercial property
5. The matching principle: expenses recorded in the same period as the revenues they generate

What assessors probe: explain the difference between cash and profit; what does a balance sheet show; why is cash flow important.

Common referral reasons: thinking profit equals cash; unable to explain financial statements clearly; no commercial context given to accounting knowledge.

The principle that underpins everything: a business can be profitable and still fail — cashflow is the financial reality that accounting profit does not always reflect.

2026 Capital Allowances Update: New 40% First-Year Allowance for new plant and machinery from January 2026 (including assets used for leasing). Main pool WDA reduced from 18% to 14% from April 2026. Full Expensing continues for companies at 100%.

sections.h: 12.7 Revision Sheet 6 — Business Planning
sections.body:
Revision sheet — not a teaching module. This sheet assumes you have existing knowledge of this competency from your professional experience and training. It is a pre-assessment reference to sharpen recall and highlight what assessors probe. If you are not yet confident in the depth of this competency, the full programme covers it in detail across dedicated modules.
Definition: Understanding how surveying businesses plan their services, resources and finances — and the commercial risks and opportunities they manage.

Level 1 only — but answers must be commercially specific, not generic.

Five things you must know without hesitation:
1. The seven components of a business plan
2. SWOT: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats
3. PESTLE: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental
4. Three commercial risks facing a surveying firm: market downturn, key staff departure, regulatory change — each with a specific explanation
5. KPIs: utilisation rate, fee recovery, revenue per fee earner, client satisfaction

What assessors probe: name three commercial risks, explain what a SWOT analysis shows, how does a surveying firm measure performance, what is resource planning.

Common referral reasons: generic answers without surveying context; unable to name three commercial risks specifically; no understanding of KPIs.

The principle that underpins everything: a business plan is a roadmap — market, resources, finances, risks and strategy all connected.

sections.h: 12.8 Revision Sheet 7 — Conflict Avoidance and Dispute Resolution
sections.body:
Revision sheet — not a teaching module. This sheet assumes you have existing knowledge of this competency from your professional experience and training. It is a pre-assessment reference to sharpen recall and highlight what assessors probe. If you are not yet confident in the depth of this competency, the full programme covers it in detail across dedicated modules.
Definition: Understanding how to prevent disputes, identify conflict early and advise clients on the most proportionate resolution mechanism.

Level 1: Dispute resolution routes, causes of conflict, RICS Conflict Avoidance Pledge, without prejudice communications.
Level 2: A real example of identifying conflict early and taking action to prevent escalation.

Five things you must know without hesitation:
1. The five dispute resolution routes in escalation order: Negotiation, Mediation, Adjudication, Arbitration, Litigation
2. The RICS Conflict Avoidance Pledge — by name
3. Adjudication: 28-day decisions, common in construction contracts
4. Without prejudice: protects settlement negotiations from being used as evidence
5. Early warning signs that a conflict is developing

What assessors probe: how do you identify conflict early, what does 'without prejudice' mean, which resolution route would you recommend and why.

Common referral reasons: wrong order of dispute resolution routes; unable to explain 'without prejudice'; no real conflict example given; Conflict Avoidance Pledge not mentioned.

The principle that underpins everything: most disputes are preventable through clear scope, proactive communication and early intervention.

sections.h: 12.9 Revision Sheet 8 — Data Management
sections.body:
Revision sheet — not a teaching module. This sheet assumes you have existing knowledge of this competency from your professional experience and training. It is a pre-assessment reference to sharpen recall and highlight what assessors probe. If you are not yet confident in the depth of this competency, the full programme covers it in detail across dedicated modules.
Definition: Understanding how data is created, used, stored, protected and disposed of in compliance with legislation and professional obligations.

Level 1 only — knowledge of GDPR, data lifecycle, security, breach response.

Five things you must know without hesitation:
1. The six GDPR principles — in order
2. The 72-hour ICO notification rule for serious data breaches
3. The distinction between personal data and special category data
4. The correct response to a data breach: report, document, follow procedure, notify if required, review
5. Storage limitation: data must not be retained indefinitely — disposal must be secure

What assessors probe: what are the six GDPR principles, what do you do when a data breach occurs, what is the 72-hour rule, what is special category data.

Common referral reasons: unable to name all six principles; unaware of the 72-hour rule; confusing personal data and special category data.

The principle that underpins everything: protect client data as if it were your own — accuracy, security and confidentiality are non-negotiable professional obligations.

sections.h: 12.10 Revision Sheet 9 — Sustainability
sections.body:
Revision sheet — not a teaching module. This sheet assumes you have existing knowledge of this competency from your professional experience and training. It is a pre-assessment reference to sharpen recall and highlight what assessors probe. If you are not yet confident in the depth of this competency, the full programme covers it in detail across dedicated modules.
Definition: Understanding sustainable practices, environmental legislation and how sustainability affects the value, compliance and commercial performance of built assets.

Level 1 for mandatory pathway — but connect every answer to commercial implications.

Five things you must know without hesitation:
1. The three sustainability pillars: Environmental, Social, Economic
2. MEES: the current minimum is E. F and G-rated commercial buildings cannot be let without improvement.
3. BREEAM ratings: Pass, Good, Very Good, Excellent, Outstanding. Institutional investors commonly require Very Good or Excellent.
4. Climate Change Act 2008: Net Zero by 2050. Legally binding.
5. EPCs: from second half of 2026, new EPCs under the multi-metric methodology carry 5-year validity (not 10); required on construction, sale or letting; do not show actual energy use.

What assessors probe: what does MEES mean for a landlord, what is the commercial consequence of a poor EPC rating, explain BREEAM, what does the Climate Change Act require.

Common referral reasons: unable to explain MEES consequences; confusing EPC with actual energy consumption; no commercial context given to sustainability knowledge.

The principle that underpins everything: MEES non-compliance makes a building unlettable — and therefore significantly lower in value.

2026 Updates: EPC multi-metric methodology — 5-year validity from H2 2026. BNG expanded to NSIPs from May 2026 (10% minimum gain). Future Homes Standard, published March 2026, with regulations in force from March 2027.

sections.h: 12.11 Revision Sheet 10 — Team-Working, Diversity and Inclusion
sections.body:
Revision sheet — not a teaching module. This sheet assumes you have existing knowledge of this competency from your professional experience and training. It is a pre-assessment reference to sharpen recall and highlight what assessors probe. If you are not yet confident in the depth of this competency, the full programme covers it in detail across dedicated modules.
Definition: Working collaboratively with colleagues and multi-disciplinary teams to deliver shared objectives while maintaining professional relationships.

Level 1: Team roles, communication behaviours, barriers to performance.
Level 2: Real examples of your personal contribution to a team or multi-disciplinary project.

Five things you must know without hesitation:
1. Belbin roles: Coordinator, Implementer, Completer-Finisher, Shaper, Team Worker, Specialist
2. The most common cause of team underperformance: poor communication
3. Your personal contribution must be described using 'I' not 'we'
4. Multi-disciplinary coordination: managing interfaces between disciplines is as important as your own work
5. Accountability: doing what you commit to, updating others when things change

What assessors probe: describe your personal contribution to a team project, how did you handle a team conflict, what does your Belbin role tell you about how you work.

Common referral reasons: describing team activity without personal contribution; no multi-disciplinary examples; unable to name Belbin roles.

The principle that underpins everything: great teamwork is built on communication, accountability and respect — in that order.

sections.h: 12.12 Revision Sheet 11 — Inclusive Environments
sections.body:
Revision sheet — not a teaching module. This sheet assumes existing professional knowledge of this competency. It is a pre-assessment reference. If you need structured learning across this competency in full depth, that is in Module 11.
Mandatory Competency 11 — Inclusive Environments (Level 1)

What assessors test: Knowledge and understanding of the principles, legislation and standards that govern accessible and inclusive design in the built environment.

Key definition: An inclusive environment is one that can be accessed and used safely, easily and with dignity by everyone — regardless of age, disability, gender, ethnicity or any other characteristic. It does not physically or socially segregate, discriminate or isolate.

Three principles of inclusive design:
1. Inclusive — usable by all people without adaptation
2. Responsive — takes account of what people say they need
3. Flexible — offers choice where a single solution cannot accommodate all users

Building Regulations Part M — Access to and Use of Buildings:
— Category 1 — Visitable dwellings: minimum standard, all new dwellings
— Category 2 — Accessible and adaptable: adaptable as needs change, step-free access, wider doorways
— Category 3 — Wheelchair user dwellings: fully designed for wheelchair users

BS 8300:2018 — Design of an Accessible and Inclusive Built Environment:
Best practice standard beyond Part M minimum. Covers car parking, entrances, internal circulation, sanitary facilities, wayfinding, lighting, acoustic design. Represents what RICS expects of a competent professional.

Equality Act 2010 — Anticipatory Duty:
Service providers must make reasonable adjustments for disabled people before they are requested — not wait to be asked. In a surveying context: physical access to premises, alternative communication formats, flexible service delivery.

What Level 1 looks like in your SoE:
Reference Part M, BS 8300 and the Equality Act. Show awareness of the diversity of user needs. Explain how inclusive design principles apply to the property work you do. You do not need to have personally designed an accessible building — but you must understand the standards and why they matter.

Common assessor questions:
— What is an inclusive environment?
— What does Part M require for new dwellings?
— What is the difference between Category 1 and Category 2?
— What does the Equality Act require of a surveying firm?
— How does inclusive design differ from simply complying with Part M?

2026 note: The RICS AI Standard (March 2026) includes provisions for inclusive access to AI-assisted services — if your firm uses AI tools in service delivery, you must consider whether their use is accessible to clients with disabilities.

sections.h: 12.13 Level 3 Thinking — Applying It to Every Competency
sections.body:
Only Ethics formally requires Level 3. But the candidates who pass most comfortably are those who answer every question at Level 3 — even when it is not required.

Here is why: assessors will probe. A Level 2 answer invites a follow-up question. 'What would you have done if the client had rejected your advice?' 'What other options did you consider?' 'Why was that the best solution?'

If your answer to those follow-up questions is hesitant or incomplete, the assessor forms a view about your professional judgement. If your answer is structured, confident and justified, they form a very different one.

The Level 3 structure:
1. What options were available?
2. How did you evaluate the risks and implications of each?
3. What advice did you give and why?
4. How did the client respond and what was the outcome?

Apply that structure to every answer in your mock interview practice. After three or four rehearsals it becomes natural — and in the real interview, it will feel instinctive.

Reasoning, not recitation. Judgement, not knowledge. That is what makes a Chartered Surveyor.

sections.h: 12.14 Final Eight APC Assignment Questions
sections.body:
These eight questions are written in the style of real APC assessment questions. They require Level 3 thinking — options considered, risks weighed, advice justified.

Write a full response to each one before your interview. Time yourself. Read your answer back and ask: have I told the assessor what I decided and why — or just what happened?

1. Ethics and Professionalism
'Describe a situation where your professional judgement was tested. What options did you consider, what did you decide, and why?'

2. Client Care
'Tell me about a time you managed a difficult client expectation. How did you communicate the situation and what was the outcome?'

3. Communication and Negotiation
'Describe a negotiation you led that required balancing technical accuracy with commercial pressure. How did you ensure your advice remained impartial?'

4. Health and Safety
'Give an example of how you prepared for a site inspection where significant H&S risks were present. What specific controls did you put in place and why?'

5. Accounting and Commercial Awareness
'Explain how financial information influenced a piece of professional advice you gave. What indicators did you consider and how did they shape your recommendation?'

6. Conflict Avoidance
'Describe a situation where a disagreement between parties could have escalated into a formal dispute. What early interventions did you take and how effective were they?'

7. Data Management
'Provide an example of a situation where you managed sensitive or confidential information. How did you ensure your handling was compliant with GDPR and your professional obligations?'

8. Sustainability
'Tell me about a time when sustainability considerations changed or significantly influenced your professional advice. What legislation or standards did you rely on and what alternatives did you present?'

sections.h: 12.15 The 60-Minute APC Mock Interview
sections.body:
The structure of your APC interview:
