0:00–0:10 | Case Study Presentation (10 minutes)
You present your case study for 10 minutes exactly. The panel then asks targeted questions on: decision making; risk management; costs and commercial judgement; technical standards; ethics within the project. This section is weighted heavily — preparation and rehearsal make an enormous difference.

0:10–0:22 | Pathway Technical Questions (12 minutes)
The panel asks 4–6 questions specific to your RICS pathway. The AI Mock Simulator in this module generates questions specific to your chosen pathway so you can practise the questions most likely to come up across all 22 RICS pathways.

0:22–0:42 | Mandatory Competency Questions (20 minutes)
7–10 questions across Ethics, Client Care, Communication, H&S, Accounting, Commercial Awareness, Data Management, Sustainability, Conflict Avoidance and Teamworking. The revision sheets in this module are your preparation for this section.

0:42–0:52 | Ethics Scenarios (10 minutes)
2–4 realistic scenarios: conflicts of interest, gifts and hospitality, incorrect reporting, confidentiality breach, unsafe client instructions, duty to public interest. Assessors are testing your instincts — practise your responses until they are automatic.

0:52–1:00 | Final Wrap-Up (8 minutes)
'Is there anything you would like to add or clarify?' 'What would you do differently in your case study?' 'Why should we award you chartered status today?'

That last question is the one candidates prepare least for. Prepare an answer. Know what you want to say. It is your final opportunity to leave the assessors with a confident, professional impression.

Use the AI Mock Interview Simulator below to practise all five sections under timed conditions. Do it at least twice before your real interview.

sections.h: 12.16 AHA Rent Review Notice Validity — Rural Pathway
sections.body:
You’ve been instructed to serve a rent review notice on behalf of a landlord under an Agricultural Holdings Act 1986 tenancy. The tenant’s agent disputes that the notice is valid. Talk me through it.

Tests: Valuation, Agriculture, Landlord and Tenant. Comes up in most Rural interviews.

The model answer starts by separating the legal question from the valuation question — a rent review that hasn’t been validly triggered never gets to the point of discussing figures, and assessors want to see you check the foundations before building on them.

Key elements:

1. Regime identification. The first check is always which Act governs the tenancy — Agricultural Holdings Act 1986 tenancies (pre-1995) and Agricultural Tenancies Act 1995 Farm Business Tenancies follow different rent review mechanisms entirely, and applying the wrong one invalidates everything that follows.

2. Notice period and form. AHA rent reviews require notice within a specific window before the review date, and must be in the prescribed form — a notice served outside that window, or in the wrong form, is defective regardless of intent.

3. Valid service. How the notice was served, and to whom, matters as much as its content. Service on the wrong party, or by a method not permitted, can invalidate an otherwise correct notice.

4. The rent review basis. Under AHA s.12, the review is to open market rent on specific statutory assumptions and disregards — you need to be able to explain what’s assumed and what’s disregarded, not just quote a figure.

5. Third party determination. If the parties can’t agree, AHA rent disputes go to arbitration or independent expert determination — knowing which route applies and when to invoke it is part of the competency, not an afterthought.

6. Negotiation first. Formal determination is a last resort. Assessors want to hear that you tried to negotiate on the evidence before escalating.

How to frame this:

“I first established which regime applied by checking the tenancy commencement date, before doing anything else.”

“I confirmed the notice met the prescribed form and minimum notice period before advising my client to serve it.”

“When the tenant’s agent challenged validity, I checked the service method against the Act before responding, rather than assuming it was fine.”

Three things assessors tick: 1) the correct regime identified before anything else, 2) notice validity checked rather than assumed, 3) third party determination only used once negotiation had genuinely failed.

Get the notice wrong and the rent review dies before it starts — assessors are listening for whether you checked validity before you did anything else.

sections.h: 12.16 HMRC Capital Allowances Enquiry — Taxation Allowances Pathway
sections.body:
HMRC opens a formal enquiry into a capital allowances claim you’ve prepared for a client’s new industrial unit. Talk me through your response.

Tests: Accounting principles and procedures, Capital allowances, Quantification and costing. Comes up in most Taxation Allowances interviews.

The model answer treats an HMRC enquiry as a test of your original working papers, not a fresh argument to construct — if the evidence trail was solid at the point of claim, the response is straightforward.

Key elements:

1. Working papers review. The first step is going back to your original apportionment methodology and confirming what was classified as qualifying expenditure, and why.

2. Structural vs plant and machinery. This is the grey area HMRC challenges most often — you need the case law tests fresh in mind, not just the headline categories.

3. Contemporaneous evidence. Cost breakdowns, specification documents, and invoices contemporaneous with the works carry far more weight than a reconstruction after the fact.

4. Enquiry process and timeline. HMRC enquiries follow a formal process with statutory deadlines for response — missing these has consequences independent of the merits of the claim.

5. Concede vs defend. Not every item is worth defending. Part of the competency is judging which marginal items to concede and which core claims to hold, rather than fighting everything reflexively.

6. Client communication. Managing expectations on cost, time, and outcome uncertainty throughout — an enquiry can run for months, and clients need realistic guidance, not false reassurance.

How to frame this:

“I went back to my original apportionment working papers before responding to HMRC, rather than constructing a new justification.”

“Where an item sat in the grey area between structure and plant, I revisited the relevant case law tests before taking a position.”

“I kept my client informed of realistic timescales and the possibility of partial concession from the outset.”

Three things assessors tick: 1) evidence-based response rather than defensive assumption, 2) correct reasoning on the structural/plant distinction, 3) transparent client management throughout.

A capital allowances claim is only as strong as the working papers behind it — assessors want to hear that you can defend your numbers, not just produce them.

sections.h: 12.16 Party Wall Act Notice Dispute — Building Surveying Pathway
sections.body:
Your client is planning works that fall under the Party Wall etc. Act 1996, and a neighbour disputes your Notice. Talk me through it.

Tests: Legal/regulatory compliance, Building pathology, Contract administration. One of the most frequently tested Building Surveying scenarios.

The model answer treats the Party Wall Act as a procedural discipline first and a technical building question second — most disputes come from getting the process wrong, not the construction detail.

Key elements:

1. Correct notice type. Section 1 (new wall on the line of junction), Section 2 (works to an existing party wall), or Section 6 (excavation near a neighbouring structure) each apply to different works — the wrong section invalidates the notice.

2. Notice periods and service. Each section carries its own minimum notice period, and the notice must be properly served on all relevant owners.

3. The neighbour’s options. On receipt, the adjoining owner can consent, dissent and appoint their own surveyor, or dissent and agree to a joint surveyor — all at the building owner’s cost. Candidates need to explain this accurately, not vaguely.

4. The Award. Where surveyors are appointed, they produce a Party Wall Award covering the works, access, and protective measures — understanding what an Award does and doesn’t cover is core to the competency.

5. Schedule of condition. A schedule of condition before works start protects both parties and is standard good practice, not an optional extra.

6. Escalation. If appointed surveyors can’t agree, the Act provides for a third surveyor to resolve the matter — knowing this mechanism exists, and when it’s invoked, matters.

How to frame this:

“I confirmed which section of the Act applied to the specific works before drafting the Notice.”

“When the neighbour dissented, I explained their right to appoint their own surveyor at the building owner’s cost.”

“I made sure a schedule of condition was agreed before works started, to protect both parties from later disputes.”

Three things assessors tick: 1) correct section identified for the works in question, 2) the neighbour’s statutory rights explained accurately, 3) schedule of condition treated as standard practice.

Get the wrong section or skip the schedule of condition, and you’ve created the dispute you were trying to avoid — assessors are listening for procedural precision here.

sections.h: 12.16 Payment and Pay Less Notice Mechanics — Quantity Surveying Pathway
sections.body:
You’re administering interim payments on a JCT contract and the employer wants to pay less than the sum in the contractor’s application. Talk me through what needs to happen.

Tests: Contract practice, Quantification and costing, Procurement and tendering. Comes up in almost every QS interview.

The model answer separates the valuation question from the notice mechanics entirely — under the Construction Act, getting the process wrong can override the true value of the work.

Key elements:

1. The notified sum principle. Under the Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996 (as amended), the sum stated in a valid Payment Notice becomes the notified sum due, regardless of the underlying valuation, unless properly challenged.

2. Payment Notice deadlines. Whoever is responsible for issuing the Payment Notice must do so within the contractual deadline — if none is issued, the application sum becomes the default notified sum.

3. Pay Less Notice. A separate notice, with its own deadline and required content, is needed to pay less than the notified sum — get the timing or content wrong and the employer must pay the notified sum in full.

4. Smash and grab risk. Defective or late notices expose the employer to a “smash and grab” adjudication, where the full notified sum is recovered irrespective of the true value of the work.

5. Valuing the work properly. The underlying valuation still matters — it just can’t substitute for correct notice procedure if a dispute arises.

6. Client communication. Making sure the employer understands these deadlines are contractual and absolute, well before they’re at risk of being missed.

How to frame this:

“I made sure the Payment Notice was issued within the contractual deadline, regardless of whether the valuation was fully finalised.”

“When the employer wanted to pay less, I explained the separate Pay Less Notice deadline and the smash and grab risk of missing it.”

“I kept the valuation and the notice mechanics separate in my own mind, so a payment dispute never became a notice dispute.”

Three things assessors tick: 1) correct statutory notice mechanics explained, 2) deadlines treated as absolute rather than negotiable, 3) awareness of adjudication risk from defective notices.

Miss a Pay Less Notice deadline and the employer pays the full notified sum regardless of the true value of the work — assessors want to know you understand this is a process test, not just a valuation one.

sections.h: 12.16 Section 25 Notice Validity — Commercial Real Estate Pathway
sections.body:
You’re instructed to serve a Section 25 notice on a tenant ahead of lease expiry, and the tenant’s advisor disputes whether it was validly served. Talk me through it.

Tests: Landlord and tenant, Legal/regulatory compliance, Client care. One of the most frequently tested Commercial Real Estate scenarios.

The model answer treats notice validity as a legal precision exercise, not paperwork — a defective Section 25 notice can hand the tenant rights they shouldn’t have, regardless of the landlord’s underlying intentions.

Key elements:

1. Notice type and timing. A Section 25 notice (landlord-initiated) must be served not less than six and not more than twelve months before the termination date specified — outside that window, the notice is invalid.

2. Prescribed form and content. The notice must be in the correct prescribed form, stating whether the landlord opposes renewal and, if so, on what grounds.

3. Valid service. Service must comply with Section 23 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1927 (which governs how notices under the 1954 Act are validly served) — the wrong method or the wrong recipient can invalidate an otherwise correctly timed and worded notice.

4. Grounds for opposition. Where a landlord opposes renewal, this must be based on one of the Act’s specific statutory grounds — client preference alone is not a valid ground.

5. The negotiation window. Before matters reach court, there is normally a window to negotiate new terms directly, which is usually the client’s preferred outcome over contested proceedings.

6. Client communication. Managing the landlord’s expectations on timeline, cost, and the real risk to their security of tenure position if procedure isn’t followed exactly.

How to frame this:

“I checked the notice fell within the six-to-twelve month window before advising my client to serve it.”

“When service was challenged, I confirmed the method used was permitted under the Act before responding to the tenant’s advisor.”

“I made sure my client understood which statutory grounds, if any, were realistically available before we opposed renewal.”

Three things assessors tick: 1) correct notice type and timing window identified, 2) service validity checked rather than assumed, 3) any grounds for opposition grounded in the statutory test, not client preference.

Get the timing or service wrong on a Section 25 notice and the tenant may gain rights they shouldn’t have — assessors are testing whether you treat this as a legal precision exercise, not paperwork.

sections.h: 12.16 Secured Lending Valuation and Professional Negligence — Valuation Pathway
sections.body:
A lender challenges your secured lending valuation six months after a loan default, alleging professional negligence. Talk me through your defence.

Tests: Valuation, Inspection, Client care. One of the most frequently tested Valuation scenarios.

The model answer treats a negligence allegation as a test of your file, not a test of whether your figure was right — valuation is a matter of professional judgement within a defensible range, and your defence rests on demonstrating that range was reasonably arrived at, properly evidenced, and properly recorded at the time.

Key elements:

1. Standard of care, not perfect hindsight. The legal test is whether a reasonably competent valuer, exercising reasonable skill and care at the time, could have reached a similar figure on the evidence then available — not whether your figure matches what the market later showed the property was worth.

2. Red Book compliance at the time of valuation. Confirming the valuation met the mandatory minimum reporting requirements under VPS 3 — purpose, basis of value, extent of investigation, assumptions and special assumptions, valuation approach and reasoning, and date of valuation — is the first line of defence.

3. Inspection and investigation record. VPS 2 requires proper records of inspections and investigations to maintain a clear audit trail — file notes, photographs, and a record of what was and was not verified are what actually protect you months or years later, not memory.

4. Comparable evidence hierarchy. Being able to show the comparables relied on at the valuation date, and where they sat in the hierarchy of evidence, demonstrates the figure was reasoned rather than arbitrary.

5. Assumptions and special assumptions. Where any assumption was made — about tenure, condition, or planning status — showing it was reasonable to make at the time, and was clearly disclosed in the report, is central to a defence.

6. Early engagement with PII insurers. Notifying your professional indemnity insurers promptly on receiving a negligence allegation is standard professional discipline — delay can itself create problems independent of the merits of the claim.

How to frame this:

I went back to my valuation file first, to confirm what evidence and assumptions were recorded at the time, before responding to the allegation.

I checked the report against the VPS 3 minimum reporting requirements to confirm it was Red Book compliant at the point it was issued.

I notified my professional indemnity insurers as soon as the allegation was raised, rather than trying to resolve it informally first.

Three things assessors tick: 1) understanding that the standard is reasonable care, not hindsight accuracy, 2) evidence of contemporaneous record-keeping and Red Book compliance, 3) recognising the professional discipline of prompt insurer notification.

A valuation is not negligent because the market later proved it wrong — it is negligent if a reasonably competent valuer could not have reached it on the evidence at the time. Assessors are testing whether you understand that distinction, not whether you can guarantee a figure will hold up forever.

sections.h: 12.16 NEC Compensation Event Time Bar — Infrastructure Pathway
sections.body:
Your contractor believes they have a valid compensation event under an NEC contract, but seven weeks have passed since they became aware of it and no notification has been submitted. Talk me through the situation and what you would advise.

Tests: Contract practice, Risk management, Client care. One of the most frequently tested Infrastructure scenarios.

The model answer treats the NEC compensation event notification period as an absolute contractual deadline, not a general guideline — under NEC3/NEC4 clause 61.3, missing it doesn't weaken the contractor's claim, it extinguishes it entirely, regardless of how genuine the underlying entitlement is.

Key elements:

1. The eight-week time bar is absolute. Under clause 61.3, if the contractor doesn't notify a compensation event within eight weeks of becoming aware of it, they lose all entitlement to a change in the prices, completion date, or key date for that event — there is no partial or proportionate outcome.

2. The exception that doesn't apply here. The time bar doesn't apply where the project manager should have notified the event under clause 61.1 (events arising from an instruction, certificate, or changed decision) but failed to — that's a narrow exception, not a general safety net, and doesn't rescue a contractor-side event the contractor was aware of.

3. "Becoming aware" is the trigger, not the event itself. The clock starts from when the contractor became aware the event happened, which can itself be a point of genuine dispute — but with one week left, this is not the moment to start litigating that question; it's the moment to notify immediately.

4. Urgent, unambiguous advice is needed now. With one week remaining, the professional priority is making sure the notification is submitted correctly and immediately — not debating the merits of the underlying claim, which can be assessed afterwards.

5. The employer-side incentive. It's worth understanding that the time bar operates in the employer's favour — some project managers may be inclined to let a deadline lapse rather than proactively remind the contractor, which is a live commercial dynamic on the other side of this scenario.

6. Document everything from this point. Whatever the outcome, the advice given and the timeline of events from this point forward should be clearly documented, given how commercially significant a missed deadline is.

How to frame this:

"I would advise the contractor to submit the notification immediately, regardless of any uncertainty about the exact date of awareness."

"I'd check whether this event falls under the project manager's own notification duty under clause 61.1, since that's the only exception to the time bar."

"I would not spend the remaining time debating the merits of the claim — that can be assessed after notification, but the deadline itself can't be recovered once missed."

Three things assessors tick: 1) understanding that the eight-week bar is binary, not proportionate, 2) correctly identifying the narrow clause 61.1 exception rather than treating it as a general safety net, 3) prioritising immediate action over debating the underlying merits with time running out.

The NEC compensation event time bar doesn't care how strong the underlying claim is — miss the deadline and the entitlement is gone. Assessors are testing whether you understand this as a binary, procedural risk, not a commercial negotiation.

sections.h: 12.16 Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024 Currency Test — Residential Pathway
sections.body:
A leaseholder client asks whether they should proceed now with a Section 42 lease extension under current law, or wait for the anticipated changes under the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024. Talk me through how you would advise them.

Tests: Legal/regulatory compliance, Client care, Communication and negotiation. Increasingly common given ongoing leasehold reform.

The model answer treats this as a currency-of-knowledge test as much as a legal one — the correct answer requires knowing precisely which parts of the 2024 Act are actually in force today, not just that reform is happening.

Key elements:

1. Current law still governs the calculation. As things stand, a Section 42 lease extension premium is still calculated under the unamended Leasehold Reform, Housing and Urban Development Act 1993 — including marriage value where the unexpired term is below 80 years. The 2024 Act's abolition of marriage value and move to 990-year extensions is not yet in force.

2. What has actually changed already. The two-year ownership rule was removed in January 2025 — a leaseholder no longer has to wait two years after purchase before serving a lease extension or enfranchisement notice. That's a real, current change worth confirming with the client, since some clients (or their other advisers) may still assume the old rule applies.

3. What hasn't commenced yet, and why. The headline reforms — marriage value abolition and standardised valuation rates — require a government consultation on the replacement rates, resolution of identified technical flaws in the Act via further primary legislation, and the outcome of an ongoing Court of Appeal challenge from freeholder groups. None of that has concluded.

4. No credible timeline exists. Government statements point to these provisions being switched on once the technical and valuation-rate issues are resolved, but practitioner commentary consistently suggests this is unlikely before late 2026 at the earliest, with many expecting 2027–2028. Giving a client a confident prediction here would be professionally reckless.

5. The genuine trade-off to explain. Proceeding now gives certainty under known rules and stops the lease term running down further (relevant if it's approaching the 80-year marriage value threshold). Waiting risks years of delay for a benefit that isn't guaranteed to materialise on any particular timeline, or in the form currently proposed.

6. Document the advice given. Given the genuine uncertainty and the fact the client may feel differently about the outcome depending on how legislation develops, the advice given — and that it was based on the position as it stood at the time — should be clearly recorded.

How to frame this:

I explained that the premium calculation today still includes marriage value under current law, and that the abolition isn't yet in force.

I confirmed the two-year ownership rule no longer applies, since that's a genuine change already in effect that some clients aren't aware of.

I gave the client the current factual position and the genuine uncertainty around timing, rather than guessing when or whether the reform would come into force.

Three things assessors tick: 1) correctly distinguishing what's actually in force from what's merely proposed, 2) resisting the temptation to predict legislative timing with false confidence, 3) documenting the advice clearly given the genuine uncertainty involved.

Leasehold reform is one of the most talked-about topics in residential property right now — and one of the easiest to get wrong by assuming proposed changes are already law. Assessors are testing whether you actually know the difference.

sections.h: 12.16 JCT Formal Communication — Project Management Pathway
sections.body:
Question: Describe the formal communication process under a JCT contract and explain why this matters in your role as project manager.

This question tests both Communication and Negotiation (mandatory, Level 2) and Contract Practice (technical competency) — it is frequently asked in Project Management APC interviews.

The model answer — what assessors want to hear:

Under JCT contracts — whether the Standard Building Contract, Design and Build or other standard forms — formal communication is not optional or procedural. It is the mechanism by which legal rights and obligations are created, preserved and enforced. As project manager, understanding and applying formal communication correctly is part of competent contract administration.

Key elements to cover in your answer:

1. Written Notices
All formal notices must be in writing and served to the correct address as specified in the Contract Particulars. A notice served to the wrong address or in the wrong form may be invalid — which can have significant consequences for time, cost and the client's legal position.

2. Electronic Communication — JCT 2024 Update
JCT 2024 introduced specific provisions for electronic communication, distinguishing between Standard Notices and Critical Notices. Critical Notices — such as termination — have more stringent requirements and cannot simply be served by email without satisfying the contract's specific provisions. This distinction matters and assessors will probe whether you know it.

3. Architect / Contract Administrator Instructions
Only the Architect or Contract Administrator can issue instructions under the contract. If the employer wants a change, that instruction must go through the CA — not directly to the contractor. A project manager must understand this hierarchy and ensure the instruction trail is clean and documented.

4. Confirmation of Verbal Instructions (CVI)
Verbal instructions given on site are not formally binding until confirmed in writing via a CVI. The contractor has the right to dissent if a verbal instruction is not formally confirmed. On site, the practical discipline of confirming verbal instructions promptly protects both the programme and the audit trail.

5. Notices of Delay and Extension of Time
The contractor must notify the CA in writing when a delay is reasonably apparent. This notice must identify the Relevant Event. If the contractor fails to give timely notice, their entitlement to an Extension of Time may be affected. As project manager, you monitor the contractor's compliance with this obligation and advise the CA accordingly.

6. Payment Notices
Strict timescales govern payment applications, interim certificates and pay-less notices. Missing a payment notice deadline can result in the employer losing the right to withhold payment — even if there is a genuine dispute. This is a common area of contractor claims and project managers must track these timescales rigorously.

How to frame this in your APC interview:

Do not just describe the process. Describe how you applied it. Assessors want to hear:

— "I ensured all instructions were issued in writing through the CA and that verbal instructions on site were followed up with a CVI the same day."

— "When the contractor served a delay notice I reviewed it against the contract to confirm it identified a Relevant Event and was served within the required timeframe before advising the CA on the merits of any Extension of Time."

— "I maintained a formal correspondence register throughout the project to ensure the audit trail was complete and that all notices were served correctly under the Contract Particulars."

Three things assessors tick for this competency:
1. Audit trail — all decisions confirmed in writing, properly recorded
2. Contract specifics — you checked the specific contract version (JCT 2016 or 2024) and any bespoke amendments
3. Collaborative working — JCT 2024 mandatory collaborative working provisions exist to resolve issues before they become disputes

The line that separates a good answer from a strong one: Most candidates describe the process. Strong candidates describe the consequences of getting it wrong — and how they ensured they did not.

sections.h: 12.16 Fire Risk Assessment Lapse — Facilities Management Pathway
sections.body:
During a routine review, you discover that a building's fire risk assessment hasn't been reviewed in over two years, despite a significant change of use in one part of the building. Talk me through what you would do.

Tests: Health and safety, Legal/regulatory compliance, Risk management. One of the most frequently tested Facilities Management scenarios.

The model answer treats this as an immediate compliance and life-safety issue, not an administrative backlog item — a lapsed fire risk assessment isn't just a paperwork gap, it's a live breach of a duty that carries criminal liability under the Fire Safety Order.

Key elements:

1. Identify the responsible person. The Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 places the duty on a "responsible person" — the employer, the person in control of the premises, or the owner. Before anything else, you need to establish exactly who holds that duty in this specific building, since it may not be you personally.

2. The assessment is a living document, not a one-off. A fire risk assessment must be reviewed whenever there's reason to believe it's no longer valid — a significant change of use is a textbook trigger for review, and the fact this wasn't picked up sooner is itself a process failure worth addressing.

3. Immediate risk assessment, not just paperwork. Before worrying about the record itself, the priority is understanding whether the change of use has created a genuine, current fire risk — arrange an urgent, competent review of the affected area rather than treating this as something that can wait for the next scheduled cycle.

4. This is a criminal compliance matter. Breach of the risk assessment duty under the Order is a criminal offence, with penalties including unlimited fines and, in serious cases, imprisonment. This isn't a commercial risk to be weighed against cost — it needs to be treated with that level of seriousness from the outset.

5. Escalate and document immediately. Notify the responsible person (or relevant senior stakeholder) without delay, commission an updated assessment from a competent assessor, and document the timeline of discovery and remedial action clearly — this protects both the occupiers and the professional position of everyone involved.

6. Fix the underlying process, not just this instance. Once the immediate risk is addressed, the real question is why the change-of-use trigger wasn't caught by the existing review process — and what needs to change so this doesn't happen again.

How to frame this:

My first step was establishing exactly who the responsible person was for this building, since the duty doesn't automatically sit with me.

I treated this as an urgent life-safety issue first, and a compliance paperwork issue second — commissioning an immediate updated assessment rather than waiting for the next scheduled review.

I documented the discovery and the remedial steps taken clearly, given the criminal liability that attaches to this duty.

Three things assessors tick: 1) correctly identifying the responsible person rather than assuming it's automatically the candidate, 2) treating the lapse as an urgent life-safety matter, not just an administrative gap, 3) addressing the underlying process failure, not just the immediate instance.

A lapsed fire risk assessment isn't a scheduling problem — it's a live legal exposure and a genuine safety risk. Assessors are testing whether you understand the seriousness of that distinction, not just the theoretical content of the regulations.

sections.h: 12.16 CIL Commencement Notice Deadline — Planning and Development Pathway
sections.body:
Your client is due to start development in two days' time, and you realise the Community Infrastructure Levy Commencement Notice hasn't been submitted yet. Talk me through what you would do, and why the timing matters so much.

Tests: Legal/regulatory compliance, Accounting principles, Risk management. One of the most frequently tested Planning and Development scenarios.

The model answer treats the Commencement Notice deadline as an absolute, unforgiving procedural requirement — under Regulation 67 of the CIL Regulations 2010, the notice must reach the authority no later than the day before development starts, and the regulations are strict even where a genuine mistake was made.

Key elements:

1. The deadline is absolute, not a guideline. The Commencement Notice must be received by the collecting authority no later than the day before the day development commences — there's no grace period, and the Planning Inspectorate has upheld surcharges even where an applicant sent an informal letter expressing clear intent, because it wasn't in the correct form.

2. The consequence is a genuine financial penalty. If the notice isn't submitted in time, the authority must impose a surcharge equal to 20% of the chargeable amount or £2,500, whichever is lower — and the client also loses the ability to pay by instalments, meaning the full liability becomes due immediately.

3. Submitting the right form, to the right place, matters as much as timing. A notice submitted to the wrong department (such as building control rather than the actual collecting authority function) has been held not to satisfy the requirement — it needs to reach the correct collecting authority function, in the prescribed form.

4. Get written acknowledgement. Given how strict and unforgiving these regulations are, obtaining the authority's written acknowledgement of receipt is essential — without it, a dispute over whether the notice was properly received becomes very difficult to win.

5. This is urgent, not optional admin. With two days remaining, submitting the correctly completed notice today, to the confirmed correct address, and chasing written confirmation of receipt, is the immediate priority — not something to fit in once other tasks are cleared.

6. Once development starts, it's too late to fix. Once development commences, the CIL liability becomes fixed and generally can't be challenged under the regulations — there's no opportunity to correct a missed notice retrospectively.

How to frame this:

I treated this as an immediate priority rather than routine admin, given how unforgiving the CIL regulations are around timing.

I confirmed exactly which authority function the notice needed to go to, since submitting it to the wrong department wouldn't satisfy the requirement.

I made sure we obtained written acknowledgement of receipt from the authority, rather than just assuming the notice had been properly received.

Three things assessors tick: 1) understanding that the deadline is absolute with no grace period, 2) recognising the genuine financial consequence — surcharge plus loss of instalment payment rights, 3) prioritising written confirmation of receipt, not just submission.

The CIL regulations don't care whether missing the deadline was a genuine oversight — the surcharge applies regardless. Assessors are testing whether you treat this with the procedural seriousness it demands, not whether you know CIL exists in the abstract.

sections.h: 12.17 Loan Covenant Breach — Property Finance and Investment Pathway
sections.body:
A client's loan facility is approaching its quarterly compliance test date, and your review suggests the loan-to-value covenant is likely to be breached. Talk me through how you would advise them.

Tests: Property finance and funding, Investment management, Accounting principles. One of the most frequently tested Property Finance and Investment scenarios.

The model answer treats a covenant breach as a situation requiring immediate, transparent engagement rather than a problem to be quietly managed until the test date arrives — lenders generally respond far better to early warning than to a surprise breach.

Key elements:

1. Identify the exact mechanism first. Confirm precisely how the loan-to-value covenant is calculated and tested under the facility agreement — the specific valuation basis required, the testing frequency, and whether any cure period or grace mechanism exists before a breach becomes a formal Event of Default.

2. Diagnose the cause. A covenant breach can be driven by a falling asset value, an increased loan balance, or both — the right response differs depending on which is driving the issue, so this needs to be established before recommending any course of action.

3. Engage the lender proactively, before the test date. Lenders generally prefer early, transparent engagement to discovering a breach after the fact — approaching them ahead of time preserves goodwill and negotiating position that's harder to recover once a formal default has technically occurred.

4. Consider the available remedies. Options typically include a partial loan repayment (cash sweep) to bring the ratio back into compliance, an additional equity injection from the sponsor, providing additional security, or negotiating a covenant waiver or amendment with the lender.

5. Get a robust, defensible valuation. Since valuation is usually the key lever in an LTV test, ensure the valuation used is current, properly instructed, and methodologically sound — not artificially optimistic to avoid the breach, which would compromise professional independence and create a much larger problem if later challenged.

6. Document the advice given. Given the financial significance of a covenant breach, the advice given and the reasoning behind the recommended course of action should be clearly recorded.

How to frame this:

"I first confirmed exactly how the covenant was calculated and tested under the facility agreement, rather than assuming a standard mechanism."

"I identified whether the breach was being driven by falling value or rising debt, since that changed which remedy made sense to recommend."

"I advised engaging the lender proactively ahead of the test date, rather than waiting to see if the breach would actually materialise."

Three things assessors tick: 1) understanding the specific covenant mechanism rather than treating all covenants generically, 2) correctly diagnosing the cause before recommending a remedy, 3) recognising that proactive lender engagement is almost always better than waiting for a formal breach to occur.

A covenant breach isn't just a numbers problem — it's a relationship and timing problem. Assessors are testing whether you understand that the response needs to start well before the test date, not after.

sections.h: 12.18 Lease Break Clause Exercise — Corporate Real Estate Pathway
sections.body:
Your organisation holds a lease with a break option coming up, and the business has decided to exercise it. Talk me through what you would need to get right, and why the conditions matter so much.

Tests: Landlord and tenant, Legal/regulatory compliance, Business alignment. One of the most frequently tested Corporate Real Estate scenarios.

The model answer treats break clause conditions as a strict, unforgiving checklist rather than a general statement of intent — English courts have consistently held that conditions precedent to a break must be complied with exactly, and there's little room for "close enough."

Key elements:

1. Notice form and timing must be exact. The break notice must be served in exactly the form and within exactly the timeframe the lease specifies — courts have made clear that even a technically clear notice fails if it doesn't match the precise requirements set out in the lease.

2. Vacant possession is the classic pitfall. If the lease requires vacant possession, this generally means the premises must be free of people, of the tenant's moveable property and fixtures, and of any legal interests — case law has shown that even leaving partitioning or having contractors still on site at the break date can be enough to invalidate the break.

3. Rent and other payment conditions are strictly enforced. If the lease requires all rent (or "all sums") to be paid up to the break date, this needs careful checking — including any outstanding interest on previously late payments, which is a common oversight.

4. Once served, a break notice can't be taken back. The organisation needs to be genuinely certain before the notice is served, since it can't be unilaterally withdrawn once given.

5. A surveyor should be instructed to manage compliance. Given how strictly these conditions are construed and how easily a technical slip can invalidate the break, RICS guidance (the Code for Leasing Business Premises) recommends limiting break conditions to the essentials, and a surveyor's involvement in managing compliance is standard, prudent practice.

6. Document everything. Given the financial exposure of a failed break (being locked into the lease for a further term), the steps taken to satisfy each condition should be clearly recorded, including dates, communications, and evidence of vacant possession.

How to frame this:

"I treated every condition in the break clause as something that had to be satisfied exactly, not just substantially, given how strictly the courts have interpreted these in the past."

"I paid particular attention to vacant possession, making sure nothing was left on site that could be argued to prevent it — including things as easy to overlook as partitioning or a lingering contractor."

"I made sure the organisation understood the break notice couldn't be withdrawn once served, so the decision needed to be genuinely final before we acted."

Three things assessors tick: 1) understanding that break conditions require strict, not substantial, compliance, 2) correctly identifying vacant possession as the most common and easily-missed pitfall, 3) recognising the irreversible nature of a served break notice.

A lease break clause doesn't reward good intentions — it rewards exact compliance. Assessors are testing whether you understand that a single overlooked detail can cost the organisation a further lease term.

sections.h: 12.19 Research Methodology Challenge — Management Consultancy Pathway
sections.body:
You've presented a strategic recommendation to a client board based on your research findings, and a board member challenges the methodology behind your data, questioning whether your conclusions are robust enough to justify the investment. Talk me through how you would respond.

Tests: Research methodologies and techniques, Consultancy services, Client care. One of the most frequently tested Management Consultancy scenarios.

The model answer treats a methodology challenge as a normal, healthy part of rigorous consultancy work, not a personal attack — the right response depends on genuinely understanding your own methodology well enough to defend it honestly, including its real limitations.

Key elements:

1. Know your own methodology cold. Before anything else, you need to be able to explain precisely what research was done — sample size, data sources, whether it was primary or secondary research, and how any qualitative input was weighted alongside quantitative data.

2. Distinguish correlation from causation. A common weak point under genuine challenge is a recommendation that implies more causal certainty than the underlying data actually supports — be ready to explain precisely what your evidence does and doesn't establish.

3. Acknowledge genuine limitations honestly. Every piece of research has limitations — sample size constraints, data recency, a specific market context that may not generalise perfectly. Acknowledging this honestly builds more credibility than pretending the analysis is beyond challenge.

4. Separate data robustness from professional judgement. A recommendation can still be sound professional judgement even where the underlying data has genuine limitations — as long as that's disclosed, and the judgement itself is reasoned and defensible on the evidence available.

5. Offer to strengthen the evidence, where appropriate. If the challenge reveals a genuine gap, offering further research, a pilot, or sensitivity testing shows you're engaging with the substance of the challenge, not just defending a position reflexively.

6. Stay composed and professional throughout. Treating rigorous challenge as an attack, rather than a legitimate part of the process, undermines your credibility more than any weakness in the methodology itself would.

How to frame this:

"I explained exactly what the research methodology involved — the sample size and data sources — before addressing the specific concern raised."

"I was honest about the genuine limitations of the data, rather than defending it as beyond challenge."

"Where the challenge identified a genuine gap, I offered to strengthen the evidence with further research rather than simply holding my original position."

Three things assessors tick: 1) genuine command of your own methodology, not just the headline conclusion, 2) honest acknowledgement of real limitations rather than defensive denial, 3) professional composure under legitimate challenge.

A methodology challenge tests whether your recommendation was built on genuine analytical rigour or just a confident conclusion. Assessors are testing whether you can tell the difference — and defend the former honestly, rather than bluffing the latter.

sections.h: 12.20 Rights of Light — Land and Resources Pathway
sections.body:
A neighbour has raised concerns that your client's development may infringe their right to light, but your client wants to proceed with construction regardless. Talk me through how you would advise them.

Tests: Access and rights over land, Risk management, Client care. One of the most frequently tested Land and Resources scenarios, particularly for candidates specialising in rights of light.

The model answer treats this as a genuine legal risk requiring careful, proactive management — not a pricing problem that can be resolved later with a cheque, and not something planning permission makes safe.

Key elements:

1. Planning permission does not extinguish the right. A right to light is a private property right, and having planning permission for the development is no defence to a rights of light claim — this is a common and dangerous misconception that needs correcting for the client immediately.

2. Injunctions are still a real risk, not a thing of the past. Since Coventry v Lawrence (2014), courts have more flexibility to award damages instead of an injunction, and the rigid Shelfer test is no longer applied mechanically — but courts can and still do grant injunctions, including after construction is complete, particularly where a developer has proceeded "with their eyes open" after being warned.

3. Conduct matters enormously to the outcome. Courts have penalised developers who acted in a "high-handed" or "unneighbourly" manner after a claim was raised — proceeding regardless of a raised concern, rather than engaging properly, significantly increases the risk of an injunction rather than damages.

4. Early engagement is the best risk management. The right approach is to address rights of light risk as early as possible — ideally before or during planning, not after a neighbour has already raised a formal concern — through proper light modelling, negotiation, and where appropriate, a negotiated release.

5. Damages, if awarded, are not automatically small. Where damages are awarded instead of an injunction, courts have assessed them on a hypothetical negotiation basis, historically awarding around a third of the developer's profit attributable to the infringing part of the scheme — a genuinely significant sum, not a token payment.

6. Advise proceeding at risk only with full, documented understanding. If the client insists on proceeding despite the concern, that decision needs to be made with full knowledge of the genuine risk, clearly documented — not on the assumption that rights of light claims are toothless or that damages will always be modest.

How to frame this:

"I made clear that planning permission provided no protection against a private rights of light claim, since these are separate legal frameworks entirely."

"I explained that proceeding after a concern had been raised, without proper engagement, increased the risk of an injunction rather than reducing it."

"I recommended early, proper engagement — including a professional light assessment — rather than treating this as something to resolve financially after the fact."

Three things assessors tick: 1) correctly distinguishing planning permission from private property rights, 2) understanding that injunction risk remains real post-Coventry v Lawrence, particularly where conduct is poor, 3) recommending early engagement rather than a reactive, after-the-fact approach.

Rights of light claims punish developers who proceed carelessly after a warning far more than those who engage properly from the outset. Assessors are testing whether you understand that the client's conduct, not just the legal technicalities, shapes the ultimate risk.

sections.h: 12.21 Section 36 Enforcement Notice Time Limit — Building Control Pathway
sections.body:
An owner argues that a Section 36 enforcement notice can no longer be served on their unauthorised building work because more than 12 months have passed since completion. Talk me through whether they're correct.

Tests: Legal/regulatory compliance, Building control inspections, Risk management. Tests currency of knowledge on a recently changed area of law — one of the most frequently tested Building Control scenarios.

The model answer corrects a genuinely common and dangerous misconception — the 12-month time limit the owner is relying on was replaced by a 10-year limit under the Building Safety Act 2022, and getting this wrong could mean wrongly advising a client that they're safe from enforcement when they aren't.

Key elements:

1. The old 12-month limit is no longer current law. Before the Building Safety Act 2022, a Section 36 enforcement notice couldn't be served more than 12 months after completion of the contravening work — but this was extended to 10 years, effective from 1 October 2023 (with slightly different timing for Wales). Advice based on the old 12-month rule is now simply wrong.

2. Don't confuse this with the separate prosecution time limit. A different, shorter time limit applies to prosecuting the underlying contravention as an offence under Section 35 — generally six months from when the offence occurred — which is a genuinely separate mechanism from the Section 36 enforcement notice route, and conflating the two is a common candidate error.

3. The notice mechanism itself hasn't changed. A Section 36 notice still requires the owner to alter or remove non-compliant work, and if they don't comply, the authority can carry out the work itself and recover the cost — what changed is how long the authority has to act, not the substance of what the notice requires.

4. Some exceptions still apply. A Section 36 notice generally can't be served where plans were properly deposited, the work matches those plans, and it was executed in accordance with any conditions the authority imposed when passing the plans — a specific statutory protection worth knowing precisely, not just in outline.

5. Injunction powers sit outside this time limit entirely. Separately from the Section 36 notice mechanism, a local authority (or others) can apply for an injunction to require removal of non-compliant work — and this route isn't subject to the same time limit, though it's typically reserved for the most serious cases given the cost involved.

6. Advise based on current law, not outdated training. Given how significant this change is, and how recently it came into force, a Building Control surveyor giving advice based on stale knowledge could seriously mislead a client about their actual risk exposure.

How to frame this:

"I corrected the assumption immediately — the 12-month limit was extended to 10 years under the Building Safety Act 2022, so the notice could still validly be served."

"I made sure not to conflate the Section 36 enforcement time limit with the separate, shorter Section 35 prosecution time limit, since they're genuinely different mechanisms."

"I checked whether the specific plans-deposited exception applied here before confirming the notice could be served."

Three things assessors tick: 1) correctly identifying the current 10-year time limit rather than the outdated 12-month rule, 2) distinguishing the enforcement notice route from the separate prosecution time limit, 3) checking for the specific statutory exception before giving definitive advice.

This is exactly the kind of area where relying on training from a few years ago gives dangerously wrong advice. Assessors are testing whether you actively keep your legal knowledge current, not just whether you learned the rules once.

sections.h: 12.22 What Happens After Your Interview
sections.body:
What Happens After Your Interview

Once your interview ends, here's what to actually expect — verified against RICS's own published process, not assumption.

If you pass: you'll be notified by email. Congratulations — you're chartered.

If you're referred: you'll receive a referral report by email within 21 days of your result, explaining specifically why the assessors reached that decision. This report is the single most useful document you'll receive if you need to resit — it tells you precisely what to work on, not just that something fell short.

Your right to appeal — and what it actually is. You have 21 days from the date your referral report is issued to appeal. It's important to be precise about what an appeal actually does: it is not a route to argue that you deserved to pass. An independent panel of three chartered surveyors, with no connection to you or your employer and no prior knowledge of your interview, reviews only whether the assessment process itself was conducted fairly — administrative and procedural matters, not the merits of the assessors' judgement. Even if an appeal succeeds, it doesn't grant membership — your original interview is disregarded and you're given a fresh one.

If you need to resit: from 1 January 2026, candidates have up to five attempts to pass, and any attempts made before that date don't count toward the total. A resit carries its own fee, payable when you next apply.

The honest reassurance here: a referral is a specific, actionable outcome with a clear process attached to it — not an ambiguous dead end. If it happens, you'll know precisely why, and precisely what your options are.

title: Understanding Your Referral Properly
desc: Read the referral report calmly and accurately — and understand what it is really telling you.

sections.h: CR1.1 How to Read the Referral Report Without Panic
sections.body:
The referral report is not a verdict on your ability as a surveyor. It is a record of what the assessors could not score — and those are different things.

Most referred candidates read the letter once, feel devastated, and then either avoid it or read it repeatedly looking for validation of how they feel. Neither approach is useful. The letter contains specific, structured information that tells you exactly what to focus on for your resit — if you read it the right way.

How to read the referral report productively:

Read it once, in full, without annotating. Just read it as information. Let the initial emotional response pass before you do anything else with it.

On the second reading, separate what is said about written submission from what is said about interview performance. These are different problems requiring different solutions. A candidate whose written submission was adequate but who performed poorly under questioning has a different resit priority from one whose submission had structural weaknesses.

On the third reading, note each flagged competency and ask one question per competency: did the assessors say I lacked knowledge, or that I did not demonstrate application? The answer tells you whether you have a content problem or a communication problem.

What the language of referral letters typically means:

"The candidate was unable to demonstrate..." — the knowledge or application existed but was not shown clearly. Communication problem.

"The candidate lacked sufficient evidence of..." — the written submission did not contain the right type of evidence. Structural problem.

"The candidate struggled to articulate..." — verbal performance under questioning. Pressure and preparation problem.

"The candidate's responses were at Level 1..." — the answers described knowledge rather than evidencing application. The most common referral cause.

The most important thing to understand: The referral letter names where the problem was visible — not necessarily where it originated. A candidate referred on Client Care may have an evidencing problem that runs through every mandatory competency, not just Client Care. The letter is a symptom. This programme helps you find the cause.

sections.h: CR1.2 Identifying Patterns in Assessor Feedback
sections.body:
Referral letters rarely flag isolated, unconnected weaknesses. There is almost always a pattern — and finding it is the most valuable thing you can do before your resit.

The most common patterns in referral feedback:

Pattern 1 — Consistent Level 1 across multiple competencies
The assessors noted Level 1 responses in three or more competencies. This is not three separate problems. This is one problem — the candidate is not structuring answers to demonstrate application. The fix is the same for all three competencies.

Pattern 2 — Strong written submission, weak interview performance
The written submission was broadly adequate but the candidate could not defend or expand on it under questioning. This is a preparation and pressure problem, not a knowledge problem. More mock interview practice is the fix — not more content revision.

Pattern 3 — Good technical pathway, weak mandatory competencies
The candidate demonstrated reasonable technical competency for their pathway but was referred on mandatory competencies — typically Ethics, Client Care or Health and Safety. This is very common. Candidates preparing for their APC naturally focus on their pathway and underinvest in the mandatory content. The fix is targeted mandatory competency preparation.

Pattern 4 — Inconsistency across similar competencies
Strong on some mandatory competencies, weak on others, with no obvious technical reason. This often indicates that the candidate's preparation was uneven — they revised some competencies thoroughly and others superficially. The fix is systematic coverage, not just more time.

Exercise: List every competency flagged in your referral letter. Against each one, note whether the assessor language suggests a knowledge gap, an evidencing problem or a verbal performance issue. When you have done this for all flagged competencies, look for the pattern. In most cases you will find that one or two underlying causes explain the majority of your referral reasons.

sections.h: CR1.3 Separating Technical Gaps from Performance Gaps
sections.body:
This distinction is the most important thing to understand before you begin your resit preparation. Getting it wrong means spending weeks solving the wrong problem.

A technical gap means you did not know something, or knew it insufficiently. The assessors asked about the Building Safety Regulator and you could not describe its powers. They asked about the ECCTA Failure to Prevent Fraud offence and you had not heard of it. The fix is content — learning the thing you did not know.

A performance gap means you knew it but could not demonstrate it. You understood Client Care at Level 2 but your answers described your role rather than evidenced your application. You knew what professional judgement means but could not articulate a specific situation where you exercised it. The fix is structural — learning how to present what you already know in the format assessors need to score it.

Most referred candidates have far more performance gaps than technical gaps. They knew their subject. They could not show it under pressure in the format required.

How to tell the difference in your own case:

For each flagged competency, answer this question honestly: if someone asked you to explain it in a relaxed conversation over coffee, could you do it? If yes — you have a performance gap, not a technical gap. The knowledge is there. The demonstration was not.

If you genuinely could not explain it even in a relaxed setting, you have a technical gap. Both the APC Industry Briefing and Module 6 of this programme address the most common technical gaps in mandatory competencies updated for 2026 legislation.

The implication for your resit preparation: If your referral was primarily caused by performance gaps, spending the next eight weeks learning more content will not fix it. You need to spend that time rebuilding how you structure and articulate what you already know. Modules 3, 5 and 8 of this programme address that directly.

sections.h: CR1.4 What the Referral Report Is Really Telling You
sections.body:
Underneath the formal language of the referral report is a simpler message. Learning to hear that message clearly is the first step to addressing it.

The RICS assessment panel is not trying to fail candidates. Their job is to establish whether you can demonstrate the competencies required to practise professionally as a Chartered Surveyor. When they refer a candidate, they are saying: we could not score you against the standard — not that you do not meet the standard.

That distinction matters enormously. A candidate who leaves the room having said things the assessors could not score is in a completely different position from a candidate who genuinely lacks competence. The first candidate needs to learn how to demonstrate what they know. The second needs to develop what they know before demonstrating it.

The referral report as a roadmap:

Reframe the referral letter. Instead of reading it as a list of failures, read it as a specification for your resit. The flagged competencies are not your weaknesses — they are your priorities. The language used to describe each gap tells you what type of answer was missing. The pattern across all flagged competencies tells you the most efficient fix.

A candidate who reads the referral letter as a roadmap and builds their preparation around it will approach their resit completely differently from one who reads it as a verdict and tries to cover everything more thoroughly.

Practical exercise before moving to Module 3:
Write one sentence for each flagged competency that begins: "The assessors could not score me on [competency] because I [specific reason]." Not because you were bad or not ready — because of a specific, addressable thing. This exercise forces precision and is the foundation of your resit strategy.

intro: Start here. Before you can fix what went wrong, you need to understand exactly what the referral letter is telling you — and what it isn't.

title: Should I Keep My Case Study?
intro: Decide with confidence whether to improve your existing case study or select a new project — before you invest time rebuilding evidence around the wrong one.

sections.h: CR2.1 Why This Decision Matters
sections.body:
Many referred candidates spend weeks improving the wrong case study. Before deciding to strengthen what you have, it’s worth understanding why your referral happened in the first place — was the problem the underlying project, the evidence you provided, or how you performed under questioning? Those are three genuinely different problems, and only one of them means the project itself needs replacing.

If your referral was primarily about performance under pressure — hesitation, weak structure, not defending your reasoning — that’s very unlikely to mean the project was wrong. If it was about a genuine lack of Level 3 evidence, professional judgement, or personal contribution within the project itself, that’s a different and more serious signal.

sections.h: CR2.2 Structured Assessment — Score Your Case Study Honestly
sections.body:
Work through this with Michael, scoring your case study honestly against each of the following:

Personal responsibility and contribution — was this genuinely your decision-making, or could “we” quietly replace “I” throughout without changing the substance?

Breadth of competencies demonstrated — does it actually give you material to speak to across your declared competencies, or does it lean heavily on just one or two?

Opportunities to evidence Level 3 — are there real decision points where you weighed options and advised, not just described what happened?

Professional judgement and decision-making — can you point to at least one moment where you made a genuine judgement call, not just followed instruction?

Commercial awareness — does it show you understood the financial or business context you were operating in?

Ethical considerations — did anything in the project touch on ethics, conflicts of interest, or professional conduct you can speak to?

Availability of supporting evidence — do you actually have diary entries, documents, or records to back up what you’d say about it?

Ability to withstand follow-up questioning — if an assessor pushed hard on any single decision, could you defend it, or would you be exposed?

sections.h: CR2.3 Keep It, Improve It, or Replace It?
sections.body:
Based on that assessment, Michael will give you a working recommendation:

Keep it — the project is genuinely strong enough. The work now is about improving how it’s presented and defended, not the project itself.

Improve it — the project is fundamentally suitable, but needs stronger evidence or clearer explanation of your role and reasoning.

Replace it — another project available to you is likely to give a materially better opportunity to demonstrate competence at the level you need.

This is a genuine recommendation, not an automatic verdict — you know details of your own experience Michael doesn’t, and the final call is yours.

sections.h: CR2.4 If You Choose a New Case Study
sections.body:
What makes a genuinely strong APC case study — real complexity, real personal decision-making, a clear outcome you can speak to with evidence.

How to identify a stronger project from your own recent experience — look for instructions or projects where you made multiple professional decisions you can name and defend individually.

Common mistakes when selecting a replacement — picking something bigger but less personally-led, or something with no real judgement calls to point to. Scale and complexity are not the same as personal professional contribution.

sections.h: CR2.5 Preparing for Defence
sections.body:
Once you’ve made your decision — keep, improve, or replace — the next step is the same either way: identify the questions you’re actually likely to face.

— What are the likely assessor questions on this specific project?
— Where are the areas of genuine challenge or weakness?
— Which decisions will you need to justify, and can you do so clearly?
— What professional judgement will you need to explain, in your own words, under pressure?

If you want deep, iterative coaching on defending the specific document you’ve now decided to move forward with — anticipating follow-up questions, strengthening how clearly you explain your decisions, and practising your defence with Michael — that’s exactly what Case Study Review is built for. This section has told you what to do; Case Study Review is where you go to actually do it properly.

title: What APC Assessors Actually Score
desc: Reset your understanding of what assessors are looking for — and what the 'safe pair of hands' standard really means.

sections.h: CR3.1 Level 1, Level 2 and Level 3 — The Reset
sections.body:
You have been through an APC assessment. You know what the levels are. The question is whether you understand what they look like in practice well enough to produce them under pressure.

Most referred candidates could define Level 1, 2 and 3 if asked. The problem is not definition — it is execution. They know what Level 2 means in theory. They write Level 1 answers in practice.

Level 1 — Knowledge and Understanding
You can describe what something is, how it works and why it matters. Assessors expect this as a baseline. They do not score it at Level 2. A candidate who demonstrates Level 1 knowledge on a Level 2 competency will be referred on that competency regardless of how comprehensive their knowledge is.

Example Level 1 answer: "Client Care involves maintaining clear communication with clients, managing their expectations, understanding the terms of engagement and acting in their best interests at all times."

This is accurate. It demonstrates understanding. It does not evidence application. It scores Level 1.

Level 2 — Application
You can show a specific situation where you applied your knowledge, made a professional decision and acted on it. The key word is specific. Not "in my experience" or "typically I would" — a named situation, a decision made, an action taken.

Example Level 2 answer: "On a specific instruction, I identified that the client had not received the letter of engagement before works commenced. I prepared a revised letter, obtained written confirmation from the client before proceeding and updated the file accordingly to ensure the terms were formally agreed."

This evidences application. Assessors can score it at Level 2.

Level 3 — Professional Judgement and Reasoned Advice
You can show a situation where you evaluated options, weighed risks and gave professional advice or made a professional decision. Level 3 requires a problem, options considered, judgement exercised and a recommendation or decision with reasoning.

The shift from Level 2 to Level 3 is not about complexity — it is about the presence of reasoned options and professional accountability for a decision.

sections.h: CR3.2 Professional Judgement — What It Looks Like in Practice
sections.body:
Professional judgement is the quality assessors are most interested in and the quality candidates most commonly fail to demonstrate. Understanding exactly what it means is essential for your resit.

Professional judgement is not having an opinion. It is not knowing the right answer. It is the ability to evaluate a professional situation, identify the relevant principles and standards, consider the options available, weigh the risks and make a reasoned recommendation or decision — and to own that decision professionally.

What professional judgement looks like in an assessor answer:

A Level 3 answer typically contains:
— A situation with genuine professional complexity (not a routine task)
— Identification of the relevant principle, standard or legal obligation engaged
— Two or more options considered, with reasons why each was viable or not
— A decision or recommendation made, with professional justification
— An outcome, and reflection on what the situation taught you

What professional judgement does not look like:

— Describing what you generally do in similar situations
— Explaining what the correct answer is without situating it in a real decision
— Giving a recommendation without the options considered that preceded it

A practical test: After writing or speaking any Level 3 answer, ask yourself: could a junior colleague have given that answer? If yes, it is probably not demonstrating professional judgement. Professional judgement requires experience, reasoned evaluation and professional accountability — things a junior colleague cannot provide.

sections.h: CR3.3 The Safe Pair of Hands Standard
sections.body:
"Safe pair of hands" is the informal standard assessors use when evaluating candidates. Understanding it changes how you prepare.

The RICS assessment is not designed to find exceptional candidates. It is designed to establish whether a candidate can be trusted to practise professionally without supervision — to act ethically, serve clients competently, manage risk appropriately and exercise sound judgement in professional situations.

A safe pair of hands candidate:
— Knows when they need to refer a matter to someone more senior or specialist
— Does not take on work beyond their competence without disclosing it
— Documents their professional decisions and reasoning
— Identifies and manages conflicts of interest proactively
— Gives advice they can defend professionally, not advice designed to please the client
— Knows what the current legislation and professional standards require of them

What this means for your answers:

Assessors are not impressed by candidates who always knew exactly what to do. They are impressed by candidates who demonstrate sound professional process — who identified the issue, considered the right principles, sought appropriate advice where needed, documented their reasoning and arrived at a defensible professional position.

A candidate who says "I was unsure about the CDM obligations so I sought advice from our health and safety consultant before proceeding" demonstrates better professional judgement than one who confidently describes a situation where they handled everything themselves without any uncertainty.

Reframe your answers around process and principles, not just outcomes. The assessors want to know you are safe to let loose in the profession unsupervised.

sections.h: CR3.4 Why Communication and Reflection Matter
sections.body:
Two qualities distinguish candidates who pass from those who are referred on otherwise similar content: the ability to communicate clearly under pressure, and genuine professional reflection.

Communication under pressure:

The assessment room is stressful. Candidates who have not practised verbalising their professional knowledge under questioning conditions often find that knowledge they have solidly will not come out clearly when they need it. Words become imprecise. Sentences become long and circular. Examples become vague.

Assessors are evaluating not just what you know but whether you can communicate it clearly and precisely as a professional. A candidate who pauses, thinks and gives a clear, structured answer demonstrates better professional communication than one who speaks quickly and at length but imprecisely.

Professional reflection:

Reflection is what distinguishes a practitioner who learns from their experience from one who merely accumulates it. Assessors look for evidence of reflection in how candidates describe professional situations — do they just describe what happened, or do they show that they evaluated it, drew conclusions and changed their practice as a result?

A reflective answer sounds like: "On reflection, if I were handling a similar situation again, I would identify the potential conflict of interest earlier in the instruction process — before engagement rather than after work had commenced."

That one sentence demonstrates more professional maturity than three paragraphs of factual description. It shows the candidate can evaluate their own practice against professional standards — which is exactly what a safe pair of hands does.
